SDE-2 LLD Handbook

Low-level design from objects to SDE-2 interviews in 11 modules and 17 worked problems, practice first: every lesson opens with a question to try, every diagram steps through, every snippet of Java was compiled and run, and a practice tracker brings each problem back for spaced review.

How this handbook teaches

The goal is not to memorize 23 patterns or 17 solutions. The goal is to look at a new prompt, find the objects and the rules they protect, notice where change will come from, and write clean code that runs, inside a time box. So the handbook asks you to think before it explains.

  • Try before you read. Every lesson opens with a short question. Answer it on paper first; getting it wrong is what makes the explanation stick.
  • Pressure first, pattern second. Each pattern starts from the code smell it fixes and ends with when it is the wrong tool. Only the 14 patterns that LLD rounds actually use get a full lesson; the rest get one line each in the smell drills.
  • Analogy, then mechanism, then trade-off. Depth sits in folded "Go deeper" sections.
  • Step through every diagram. Diagrams with a step bar reveal one part at a time. Predict the next part before pressing Next.
  • Real, tested code. Every Java file in this handbook was compiled with Java 17 and run; the output blocks are the real output. Code marked with a red dot is the version to avoid; green is the fix.
  • Production notes. Green "In production" boxes show where the idea lives in the JDK, Spring, and payment systems, so the handbook serves your day job too.
  • Interview signals. Purple boxes say what interviewers listen for at SDE-2 and what lifts an answer above the bar.
  • Live tools. A pattern picker, an LRU simulator, a round timer, a mock rubric, and a machine coding starter project.

How to study one module

  1. Clear the revision queue above at the start of each session: redo those problems from a blank page.
  2. For each lesson: answer the "Try it first" question, read the short part, step through the figure, then read the code and type it out once. Typing, not pasting, is how the shapes get into your hands for the machine coding round.
  3. Say it out loud: what problem the idea solves, and when it is the wrong choice.
  4. Do the self-check quiz at the end, then tick lessons as studied.
  5. Tick the mastery checklist only when each item is true with your notes closed.

How to practice a problem

  1. Pick the round format and start the timer on the interview playbook: 45 to 60 minutes for an LLD discussion (requirements, class diagram, key flows, key code), 90 to 120 minutes for machine coding (code that runs).
  2. Then open the problem and compare section by section. Answer each guided deep dive before revealing it.
  3. Set an honest status at the top of the problem page. The handbook schedules a review.
  4. Redo it from memory when it comes due, faster each time. Then try the practice prompts in the tracker that use the same ideas.

Where your progress is saved

Lesson ticks, mastery checks, readiness checks, and problem statuses save automatically to your account, privately: nobody else who opens this page sees them, and they follow you to other devices. The indicator in the top bar shows where the latest change went. If the page cannot reach your account (for example in a private window), it saves in this browser instead, and the tracker has a backup and restore box.

Scope

This handbook covers what SDE-2 LLD and machine coding rounds test, in the depth they test it: object-oriented modeling, UML that interviewers read, SOLID, 14 design patterns, state machines, concurrency inside one process, the tables and REST APIs that LLD rounds ask for, scoping a one-line prompt, and the craft of writing a runnable, extensible solution in 90 minutes. Code is Java 17; everything also runs on Java 21.

It deliberately leaves out: distributed systems (the HLD handbook covers them), framework internals beyond where a pattern appears, and the rarely used Gang of Four patterns beyond a one-line description. If an interviewer asks about one of those, the smell drills page gives you the sentence you need.

Module 1: Objects and responsibilities

Low-level design decides which objects exist, what each one knows, and what each one does, so the code is correct today and cheap to change tomorrow. This module builds the object thinking every later module uses: encapsulation that protects rules, interfaces that hide choices, composition over inheritance, polymorphism instead of type switches, and value objects that cannot reach a bad state.

9 lessons3 figures6 mastery checks

On this page

  1. 1.1What LLD is and how it is judged
  2. 1.2Objects: state, behavior, identity
  3. 1.3Encapsulation: protect invariants
  4. 1.4Abstraction: program to an interface

  6. 1.6Polymorphism replaces conditionals
  7. 1.7Value objects and immutability
  8. 1.8Common mistakes

Warm-upWarm-up: one line each
  1. A BankAccount has a public setBalance(double) method. Name two things that can go wrong.
    Reveal

    Any caller can set any balance, so the rule "no overdraft" and the audit trail can be bypassed. And double cannot represent most decimal amounts exactly, so money drifts by fractions of a paisa.

  2. Interface or abstract class for "things that can receive a notification"?
    Reveal

    An interface. It names a capability that unrelated classes can have, and a class can implement many interfaces. Use an abstract class when closely related types share state and code.

  3. Why do experienced engineers say "prefer composition over inheritance"?
    Reveal

    A subclass depends on the parent's internals, so parent changes break it; combinations of features multiply subclasses; and Java allows only one parent. Composition lets you combine and swap parts, even at runtime.

  4. Two Money objects both hold 10.00 INR. Should a.equals(b) be true? Should a == b?
    Reveal

    equals should be true because a value object is defined by its values. == compares references and is usually false. Implement equals and hashCode together, or use a record.

  5. The same if (vehicle instanceof Car) ... else if (vehicle instanceof Bike) ... appears in three services. What is the fix?
    Reveal

    Move the varying behavior into the types (vehicle.hourlyRate()), or into a strategy chosen once. Then a new vehicle type is one new class instead of three edits.

1.1What LLD is and how it is judged

Try it first3 minutes

Two solutions to the same parking lot problem both pass the demo. List four things that would make an interviewer prefer one of them.

Reveal the answer
  1. Change cost: adding a vehicle type or a pricing rule touches one place, not five.
  2. Clear responsibilities: each class has one job and a name that says it; no ParkingLotManager that does everything.
  3. Correctness at the edges: invalid input, a full lot, a ticket paid twice, two cars racing for the last spot.
  4. Readability and testability: small methods, dependencies passed in, behavior you can test without a database.
Idea

Low-level design turns requirements into classes, interfaces, relationships, and method signatures. High-level design decides services, data stores, and how they talk over the network.

Analogy

HLD is the city map: districts, roads, water mains. LLD is the floor plan of one building: rooms, doors, and wiring. A great map with a bad floor plan still gives you a building nobody can live in.

Cost

Too little design gives tangled code. Too much gives speculative interfaces nobody needs. Aim for a design where the next likely change touches one class.

Interviews test LLD in two formats, and this handbook prepares you for both:

LLD discussion round Machine coding round
Length 45-60 minutes 90-120 minutes
You produce Requirements, class diagram, key flows, some code for the core classes A working, runnable program with a demo or tests
Judged on Modeling, responsibilities, patterns where they fit, extensibility, concurrency answers Working code first, then modularity, extensibility, edge cases, readability
Typical prompts Parking lot, elevator, movie booking, Splitwise Splitwise, snake and ladder, rate limiter, in-memory queue, cache

Four qualities sit behind every rubric:

  • Correct: the rules hold in every path, including errors and concurrent callers.
  • Clear: names and responsibilities that a reader understands without you explaining.
  • Changeable: the likely next requirement fits by adding a class, not by editing ten.
  • Simple: no pattern or interface that does not pay for itself today or for the next obvious change.
Interview signal

Say the change you are designing for out loud: "Pricing rules are the most likely thing to change, so pricing sits behind an interface." Interviewers score the reasoning, not the number of patterns.

1.2Objects: state, behavior, identity

Try it first2 minutes

List what a ParkingTicket object should know and what it should do.

Reveal the answer

It knows its ID, vehicle number, spot, entry time, and exit time. It does the things that need only that data: close itself on exit (once, and never before entry) and report how long the vehicle stayed. Fee calculation could live here too, but it usually depends on pricing rules that change, so it goes to a pricing strategy that reads the duration.

A class is a blueprint; an object is one instance of it at runtime. Every object has three things:

  • State: the values of its fields right now.
  • Behavior: its methods, which read and change that state.
  • Identity: it is distinguishable from other objects, even ones with equal state. Two tickets for the same car at the same time are still two tickets.

Objects with identity that matters over time are entities (an order, an account, a ticket). Objects defined only by their values are value objects (money, a date range, a coordinate); lesson 1.7 covers them.

ParkingTicket: data plus the behavior that needs it
class ParkingTicket {
    // what it knows (state)
    private final String id;            // identity: two tickets with equal fields are still different tickets
    private final String vehicleNumber;
    private final String spotId;
    private final Instant entryTime;
    private Instant exitTime;           // null while the vehicle is inside

    ParkingTicket(String id, String vehicleNumber, String spotId, Instant entryTime) {
        this.id = id;
        this.vehicleNumber = vehicleNumber;
        this.spotId = spotId;
        this.entryTime = entryTime;
    }

    // what it does (behavior that uses its own data)
    void close(Instant at) {
        if (exitTime != null) throw new IllegalStateException("ticket " + id + " already closed");
        if (at.isBefore(entryTime)) throw new IllegalArgumentException("exit before entry");
        exitTime = at;
    }

    Duration parkedFor(Instant now) {
        return Duration.between(entryTime, exitTime != null ? exitTime : now);
    }

    boolean isOpen() { return exitTime == null; }
    String id() { return id; }
}

The rule of thumb that drives most LLD decisions: put behavior with the data it needs. The ticket checks "closed twice" and "exit before entry" because it owns the times. If a service did these checks instead, every service that closes tickets would need to repeat them.

Key idea

An object is a small set of data plus the rules that keep that data valid. If a class only has getters and setters, its rules live somewhere else, usually duplicated.

1.3Encapsulation: protect invariants

Try it first3 minutes

A Wallet class has public BigDecimal balance; and services do w.balance = w.balance.subtract(x). Name three bugs this design invites.

Reveal the answer
  1. Nothing stops a negative balance; every service must remember the check.
  2. Nothing stops a negative or zero x, which turns a debit into a credit.
  3. History or audit entries can be skipped, because writing the balance and writing history are separate steps that each caller must do.
  4. Two threads can read the same balance and both subtract (a lost update, Module 9).

An invariant is a rule that must always hold for an object, such as "balance is never negative" or "a closed ticket has an exit time". Encapsulation keeps the data private and exposes only methods that preserve the invariants. It is not "add a getter and setter for every field": a public setter is a public field with extra typing.

Before: data is public, rules live in callers
class WalletBad {
    public BigDecimal balance = BigDecimal.ZERO;     // anyone can write anything
    public List<String> history = new ArrayList<>(); // anyone can clear it
}

class PaymentServiceBad {
    void pay(WalletBad w, BigDecimal amount) {
        // the rule "no negative balance" lives here, and in every other service that touches balance
        if (w.balance.compareTo(amount) >= 0) {
            w.balance = w.balance.subtract(amount);
            w.history.add("debit " + amount);
        }
    }
}
After: the wallet owns its rules
class Wallet {
    private BigDecimal balance = BigDecimal.ZERO;
    private final List<String> history = new ArrayList<>();

    void credit(BigDecimal amount) {
        requirePositive(amount);
        balance = balance.add(amount);
        history.add("credit " + amount);
    }

    void debit(BigDecimal amount) {
        requirePositive(amount);
        if (balance.compareTo(amount) < 0) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("insufficient balance: " + balance + " < " + amount);
        }
        balance = balance.subtract(amount);
        history.add("debit " + amount);
    }

    BigDecimal balance() { return balance; }                                // BigDecimal is immutable: safe to return
    List<String> history() { return Collections.unmodifiableList(history); } // read-only view, not the list itself

    private static void requirePositive(BigDecimal amount) {
        if (amount == null || amount.signum() <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("amount must be positive");
    }
}
Code that ranEncapsulation.java: the rest of the file, including the main method behind the output below
Encapsulation.java (everything not shown above)
class Demo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Wallet w = new Wallet();
        w.credit(new BigDecimal("500.00"));
        w.debit(new BigDecimal("120.50"));
        try { w.debit(new BigDecimal("1000")); throw new AssertionError(); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println(e.getMessage()); }
        try { w.history().clear(); throw new AssertionError(); } catch (UnsupportedOperationException e) { System.out.println("history is read-only"); }
        System.out.println("balance " + w.balance() + ", history " + w.history());
        WalletBad b = new WalletBad();
        b.balance = new BigDecimal("-999");  // compiles, and the object cannot stop it
        new PaymentServiceBad().pay(b, BigDecimal.ONE);
        assert b.balance.signum() < 0;
    }
}
Output (from running the code above)
insufficient balance: 379.50 < 1000
history is read-only
balance 379.50, history [credit 500.00, debit 120.50]

What changed:

  • Methods are named by intent (credit, debit), not by field (setBalance). Each one checks its rule and updates state and history together.
  • Getters do not leak mutable internals. history() returns a read-only view. Returning the list itself would let callers clear it.
  • Invalid states are impossible from outside. No caller, present or future, can make the balance negative.
Key idea

Defaults that pay off in every round: private fields, final where possible, no setters unless a real use case needs one, intent-named methods that validate, and read-only views or copies of collections.

Go deeper

Tell, don't ask

"Ask" code pulls data out of an object and decides outside it: if (w.balance().compareTo(x) >= 0) w.setBalance(...). "Tell" code asks the object to do the work: w.debit(x). Tell-style keeps the decision next to the data, so the rule exists once. When you see a chain of getters followed by a decision, consider moving that decision into the object that owns the data.

1.4Abstraction: program to an interface

Try it first3 minutes

OrderService.placeOrder contains new RazorpayGateway().charge(...). What does this cost when the business adds a second payment provider, and when you write a unit test?

Reveal the answer

Adding a provider means editing OrderService and adding a branch. A unit test cannot run without calling the real provider, because the service builds it internally. The fix: OrderService depends on a PaymentGateway interface and receives an implementation through its constructor.

An interface states what a component does; a class decides how. Code that depends on interfaces can work with any implementation: the real provider, a second provider, or a fake in tests.

Depend on the contract; receive the implementation
interface PaymentGateway {
    PaymentResult charge(String orderId, BigDecimal amount);
}

record PaymentResult(boolean success, String reference) {}

class RazorpayGateway implements PaymentGateway {
    public PaymentResult charge(String orderId, BigDecimal amount) {
        // call the provider's API here
        return new PaymentResult(true, "rzp_" + orderId);
    }
}

class StripeGateway implements PaymentGateway {
    public PaymentResult charge(String orderId, BigDecimal amount) {
        return new PaymentResult(true, "pi_" + orderId);
    }
}

class OrderService {
    private final PaymentGateway gateway;   // depends on the contract, not on a vendor

    OrderService(PaymentGateway gateway) {  // the caller (or Spring) decides which one
        this.gateway = gateway;
    }

    String placeOrder(String orderId, BigDecimal amount) {
        PaymentResult r = gateway.charge(orderId, amount);
        if (!r.success()) throw new IllegalStateException("payment failed for " + orderId);
        return r.reference();
    }
}
A test fake is just another implementation
class FakeGateway implements PaymentGateway {
    final List<String> charged = new ArrayList<>();
    public PaymentResult charge(String orderId, BigDecimal amount) {
        charged.add(orderId + ":" + amount);
        return new PaymentResult(true, "fake_" + orderId);
    }
}
// in a unit test: no network, and you can assert what was charged
// FakeGateway fake = new FakeGateway();
// new OrderService(fake).placeOrder("o1", new BigDecimal("99.00"));
// assertEquals(List.of("o1:99.00"), fake.charged);

Passing the dependency in through the constructor is dependency injection. Spring does it for you with @Service classes and constructor parameters, which is why Spring code is easy to test when it depends on interfaces.

Interface or abstract class?

Interface Abstract class
Purpose A capability or contract A partial implementation for closely related types
State No instance fields (constants only) Fields, constructors
Code default and static methods since Java 8 Any methods, including final template methods
How many per class Many One parent only
Use when Unrelated classes share a role (Notifier, PricingStrategy) Subtypes share real state and steps (AbstractExporter with a fixed export() skeleton)

Default to interfaces. Add an abstract class beneath an interface only when several implementations repeat the same fields and code.

Watch out

Do not create an interface for every class "just in case". An interface earns its place when there are two implementations today, a clear second one coming, or a need to fake it in tests.

1.5Inheritance vs composition

Try it first3 minutes

ReportExporter has subclasses CsvExporter and PdfExporter. Now each format needs optional encryption and optional compression. How many classes does an inheritance-only design need, and what is the alternative?

Reveal the answer

One class per combination: 2 formats x (encrypted, compressed, both) = 6 subclasses on top of the 2 formats, and a new option doubles the count again. The alternative is composition: Encrypting and Compressing wrappers that hold any exporter and add their step. Four classes cover every combination, chosen at runtime. That wrapper is the decorator pattern (Module 5).

Inheritance (extends) says "is a" and reuses the parent's code. Composition says "has a": an object holds other objects and delegates work to them. Inheritance is the tighter of the two, and the coupling shows up in three ways:

  • Fragile base class. A subclass depends on how the parent is implemented, not just on what it promises. Parent changes can silently break it.
  • Combination explosion. Independent variations multiply subclasses, as in the exporter example.
  • Single slot. A Java class has one parent, so using it for code reuse spends it.

The classic proof of the fragile base class comes from Effective Java. A set that counts additions overrides both add and addAll:

Inheritance: counts every element twice
// Count how many elements were ever added (Effective Java, Item 18)
class InstrumentedHashSet<E> extends HashSet<E> {
    int addCount = 0;

    @Override public boolean add(E e) {
        addCount++;
        return super.add(e);
    }

    @Override public boolean addAll(Collection<? extends E> c) {
        addCount += c.size();
        return super.addAll(c);   // HashSet.addAll calls add() for each element: counted twice
    }
}

HashSet.addAll happens to call add for each element, an implementation detail the subclass cannot see. The composed version holds a Set and forwards to it, so the inner set's internal calls never reach our counter:

Composition: holds a Set and delegates
class InstrumentedSet<E> {
    private final Set<E> inner;   // has-a: any Set implementation works
    private int addCount = 0;

    InstrumentedSet(Set<E> inner) { this.inner = inner; }

    boolean add(E e) {
        addCount++;
        return inner.add(e);
    }

    boolean addAll(Collection<? extends E> c) {
        addCount += c.size();
        return inner.addAll(c);   // inner calls its own add(), not ours: counted once
    }

    int addCount() { return addCount; }
    boolean contains(Object o) { return inner.contains(o); }
}
Code that ranComposition.java: the rest of the file, including the main method behind the output below
Composition.java (everything not shown above)
class Demo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        InstrumentedHashSet<String> a = new InstrumentedHashSet<>();
        a.addAll(List.of("x", "y", "z"));
        InstrumentedSet<String> b = new InstrumentedSet<>(new HashSet<>());
        b.addAll(List.of("x", "y", "z"));
        System.out.println("inheritance: addCount = " + a.addCount + " (expected 3)");
        System.out.println("composition: addCount = " + b.addCount());
        assert a.addCount == 6 && b.addCount() == 3;
    }
}
Output (from running the code above)
inheritance: addCount = 6 (expected 3)
composition: addCount = 3

When inheritance is the right tool:

  • A true is-a relationship where every subclass can stand in for the parent everywhere (Module 3, Liskov).
  • A parent designed for extension: documented hooks, a fixed skeleton (template method, Module 6), usually abstract.
  • Types that share an interface and real state, such as abstract class Account with SavingsAccount and CurrentAccount.
Key idea

Ask "is every B always an A, in every place an A is used?" If yes, inheritance is fine. If you mainly want to reuse some code, compose instead.

1.6Polymorphism replaces conditionals

Try it first2 minutes

The fee calculator below switches on vehicle type, and so do the spot finder and the report. What happens when electric cars arrive with their own rate and spot rules?

Reveal the answer

Every switch on vehicle type must change, in every class that has one. Miss one and you get a runtime IllegalArgumentException or, worse, a silent wrong default. With polymorphism, ElectricCar is one new class that answers hourlyRate() and spotSize() itself.

The switch that spreads
enum VehicleType { CAR, BIKE, TRUCK }

class FeeCalculatorBad {
    BigDecimal hourlyRate(VehicleType type) {
        switch (type) {                       // the same switch also lives in SpotFinder and Report
            case CAR:   return new BigDecimal("40");
            case BIKE:  return new BigDecimal("20");
            case TRUCK: return new BigDecimal("100");
            default:    throw new IllegalArgumentException("unknown type " + type);
        }
    }
}

Polymorphism means one call, many behaviors: vehicle.hourlyRate() runs the method of the object's runtime class (dynamic dispatch). Behavior that varies by type moves into the types, and callers stop caring which type they have.

Each type answers for itself
interface Vehicle {
    BigDecimal hourlyRate();
    SpotSize spotSize();
}

enum SpotSize { SMALL, MEDIUM, LARGE }

class Car implements Vehicle {
    public BigDecimal hourlyRate() { return new BigDecimal("40"); }
    public SpotSize spotSize() { return SpotSize.MEDIUM; }
}

class Bike implements Vehicle {
    public BigDecimal hourlyRate() { return new BigDecimal("20"); }
    public SpotSize spotSize() { return SpotSize.SMALL; }
}

// a new type is a new class; no existing switch changes
class ElectricCar implements Vehicle {
    public BigDecimal hourlyRate() { return new BigDecimal("30"); }
    public SpotSize spotSize() { return SpotSize.MEDIUM; }
}

class FeeCalculator {
    BigDecimal fee(Vehicle v, long hours) {
        return v.hourlyRate().multiply(BigDecimal.valueOf(hours));   // dynamic dispatch picks the right rate
    }
}

Polymorphism is not the only fix. When the varying behavior is a policy that changes independently of the type (weekend pricing, festival discounts), put it in a strategy object instead (Module 6). Rule of thumb: what a thing is belongs in its class; how the business treats it belongs in a strategy.

Overriding vs overloading

Overriding (same signature in a subclass) is resolved at runtime by the object's class. Overloading (same name, different parameter types) is resolved at compile time by the declared type of the argument. This catches people in interviews:

Two overloads
class Printer {
    String describe(Object o) { return "object"; }
    String describe(String s) { return "string"; }
}
Which one runs?
Printer p = new Printer();
Object o = "hello";            // static type Object, runtime type String
System.out.println(p.describe(o));         // prints "object": overloads are chosen at compile time
System.out.println(p.describe("hello"));   // prints "string"

Always put @Override on overriding methods. If the signature does not actually override (a typo, a different parameter type), the compiler then refuses it instead of quietly creating an overload.

Go deeper

Closed sets of types: sealed interfaces

When the set of types is closed and owned by you (a payment result is Success, Declined, or Pending), Java 17's sealed interfaces with records model it well, and Java 21's pattern-matching switch checks that every case is handled. That is the opposite trade-off: adding an operation is easy (one new switch), adding a type touches every switch, but the compiler finds them all. Use polymorphism when new types are the likely change, and a sealed hierarchy with exhaustive switches when new operations are.

1.7Value objects and immutability

Try it first3 minutes

Why is double wrong for money? And what goes wrong if a mutable object is used as a HashMap key and then changed?

Reveal the answer

double is binary floating point, so most decimal fractions are approximations: 0.1 + 0.2 prints 0.30000000000000004, and errors accumulate across many operations. A mutated key keeps sitting in the bucket chosen by its old hash code, so get with the same object returns null and the entry is effectively lost.

A value object is defined entirely by its values: two Money objects with 10.00 INR are interchangeable. Good value objects are:

  • Immutable: no setters; operations return new objects. They are safe to share, cache, use as map keys, and pass between threads.
  • Valid at construction: the constructor rejects bad input, so an invalid instance can never exist.
  • Equal by value: equals and hashCode are based on the fields. A Java record generates both, plus accessors.
Money as a record: validated, normalized, immutable
record Money(BigDecimal amount, Currency currency) {
    Money {                                         // compact constructor: validate and normalize once
        Objects.requireNonNull(amount);
        Objects.requireNonNull(currency);
        // INR has 2 fraction digits; 10.005 is rejected instead of silently rounded
        amount = amount.setScale(currency.getDefaultFractionDigits(), RoundingMode.UNNECESSARY);
    }

    static Money of(String amount, String currency) {
        return new Money(new BigDecimal(amount), Currency.getInstance(currency));
    }

    Money plus(Money other) {
        requireSameCurrency(other);
        return new Money(amount.add(other.amount), currency);   // a new object; this one never changes
    }

    Money minus(Money other) {
        requireSameCurrency(other);
        return new Money(amount.subtract(other.amount), currency);
    }

    boolean isNegative() { return amount.signum() < 0; }

    private void requireSameCurrency(Money other) {
        if (!currency.equals(other.currency)) throw new IllegalArgumentException("currency mismatch");
    }
}
Three equality facts worth knowing
Money a = Money.of("10.5", "INR");                 // stored as 10.50
Money b = Money.of("10.50", "INR");
System.out.println(a.equals(b) + " " + (a.hashCode() == b.hashCode()));   // true true
System.out.println(new BigDecimal("10.5").equals(new BigDecimal("10.50"))); // false: scale differs
System.out.println(0.1 + 0.2);                                             // 0.30000000000000004
Code that ranValueObjects.java: the rest of the file, including the main method behind the output below
ValueObjects.java (everything not shown above)
class MutablePoint {
    int x, y;
    MutablePoint(int x, int y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; }
    @Override public boolean equals(Object o) {
        return o instanceof MutablePoint p && p.x == x && p.y == y;
    }
    @Override public int hashCode() { return Objects.hash(x, y); }
}

class Demo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {

// ... (code shown above) ...

        assert a.equals(b);
        try { Money.of("10.005", "INR"); throw new AssertionError(); } catch (ArithmeticException e) { System.out.println("10.005 INR rejected"); }
        System.out.println(a.plus(b) + " " + a.minus(b).minus(b).isNegative());
        Map<MutablePoint, String> owners = new HashMap<>();
        MutablePoint p = new MutablePoint(1, 2);
        owners.put(p, "alice");
        p.x = 5;                                    // mutate a key after insertion
        System.out.println(owners.get(p));          // null: the entry sits in the bucket for the old hash
        System.out.println(owners.containsKey(new MutablePoint(1, 2)));   // false: equals now fails
        assert owners.get(p) == null;
    }
}
Output (from running the code above)
true true
false
0.30000000000000004
10.005 INR rejected
Money[amount=21.00, currency=INR] true
null
false

Two details in that code matter in fintech interviews:

  • BigDecimal.equals compares scale: 10.5 and 10.50 are not equal, but compareTo returns 0. Normalizing the scale in the constructor makes record equality behave. Many payment systems avoid the issue by storing amounts as a long count of minor units (paise or cents).
  • Rounding is a business decision. RoundingMode.UNNECESSARY makes an impossible amount fail loudly. When rounding is needed (splitting 100 into 3), choose the mode deliberately and decide where the leftover paisa goes (Problem 7).

And the reason keys must be immutable:

A mutable key
class MutablePoint {
    int x, y;
    MutablePoint(int x, int y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; }
    @Override public boolean equals(Object o) {
        return o instanceof MutablePoint p && p.x == x && p.y == y;
    }
    @Override public int hashCode() { return Objects.hash(x, y); }
}
Mutating a key after insertion
Map<MutablePoint, String> owners = new HashMap<>();
MutablePoint p = new MutablePoint(1, 2);
owners.put(p, "alice");
p.x = 5;                                    // mutate a key after insertion
System.out.println(owners.get(p));          // null: the entry sits in the bucket for the old hash
System.out.println(owners.containsKey(new MutablePoint(1, 2)));   // false: equals now fails
Key idea

The equals and hashCode contract: objects that are equal must have equal hash codes. Override both or neither, base them on the same immutable fields, and prefer records for value objects.

1.8Common mistakes

Common mistakes

  • Getters and setters for every field. The object has no rules, so the rules end up duplicated in services.
  • A god class (ParkingLotManager, BookingService with 40 methods) that knows every entity's data and does all the work.
  • Inheritance for code reuse, leading to fragile parents and subclass explosions.
  • double for money, or a mutable Money class.
  • Returning internal collections from getters, so callers can change an object behind its back.
  • instanceof chains or type switches spread across services instead of polymorphism or a strategy.
  • Missing @Override, so a typo creates an overload that never runs.
  • An interface for every class, including ones with one implementation and no test need.

1.9Self-check

Self-checkFive more, after the lessons
  1. What is an invariant? Give one for a Seat in a movie booking system.
    Reveal

    A rule that must always hold for an object. For a seat: "a seat that is BOOKED has exactly one booking ID", or "a seat cannot move from AVAILABLE to BOOKED without being HELD".

  2. Why does returning Collections.unmodifiableList(items) protect a class better than returning items?
    Reveal

    Callers get a read-only view, so they cannot add, remove, or clear elements behind the object's back. Changes still go through methods that enforce the rules.

  3. Your OrderService builds its own EmailSender. Why does that hurt testing, and what is the fix?
    Reveal

    A test cannot replace the sender, so it either sends real email or cannot run. Depend on a Notifier interface passed into the constructor, and pass a fake in tests.

  4. Give a case where inheritance is the right choice.
    Reveal

    A real is-a hierarchy with substitutable subtypes and shared state, such as abstract class Account with SavingsAccount and CurrentAccount, or a base class with a fixed algorithm skeleton and documented hooks (template method).

  5. new BigDecimal("2.0").equals(new BigDecimal("2.00")) returns what, and why does it matter?
    Reveal

    false, because equals includes scale. Amounts that are numerically equal can fail equality and map lookups. Normalize scale or compare with compareTo, or store minor units as a long.

Module 2: Relationships and UML

A class diagram is how you think out loud in an LLD round. This module teaches just enough UML to draw one quickly and correctly: the class box, the six relationships and how each becomes Java, multiplicities, and the two dynamic diagrams worth drawing, sequence and state.

9 lessons5 figures6 mastery checks

On this page

  1. 2.1How much UML you need
  2. 2.2Reading a class box
  3. 2.3The six relationships
  4. 2.4Multiplicity and navigability
  5. 2.5From diagram to code
  6. 2.6Sequence diagrams
  7. 2.7State diagrams
  8. 2.8Common mistakes
  9. 2.9Self-check
Warm-upWarm-up: one line each
  1. An arrow with a hollow triangle at one end. Solid line vs dashed line: what is the difference?
    Reveal

    Solid with a hollow triangle is inheritance (extends). Dashed with a hollow triangle is realization (implements). The triangle always points at the parent or interface.

  2. Order and OrderLine, or Team and Player: which pair is composition?
    Reveal

    Order and OrderLine. A line is created by its order, belongs to exactly one order, and dies with it. A player exists on their own and can join another team, so Team and Player is aggregation (or plain association).

  3. On a line between Customer and Order, where do you write 0..* to say "a customer has any number of orders"?
    Reveal

    Next to Order, at the far end from Customer. You read multiplicity from one class across the line to the number written at the other class.

  4. OrderService.place(Cart cart) uses the cart only inside that method. What relationship is that?
    Reveal

    A dependency: a dashed arrow from OrderService to Cart. Association would mean OrderService keeps a Cart in a field.

  5. Which three diagrams are worth drawing in a 45-minute LLD round?
    Reveal

    A class diagram (always), a sequence diagram for the trickiest flow, and a state diagram when an entity has a lifecycle (order, booking, elevator).

2.1How much UML you need

Try it first2 minutes

You have 45 minutes for "design a movie ticket booking system". Which diagrams would you draw, and which would you skip?

Reveal the answer

Draw a class diagram with the core entities and their relationships, a state diagram for the seat (available, held, booked), and a sequence diagram for "hold seats, then pay, then confirm" if there is time. Skip use case diagrams, activity diagrams, package diagrams, and deployment diagrams: they cost minutes and the interviewer rarely asks.

Idea

Diagrams are a thinking tool first. They let you and the interviewer agree on the model before you write code that is expensive to change.

Analogy

An architect sketches the floor plan before pouring concrete. The sketch is cheap to erase; the walls are not.

Cost

Every box takes time. Draw the classes the design argument needs and the relationships that carry meaning; leave out getters, setters, and trivial fields.

What to draw in each round:

Round Class diagram Sequence diagram State diagram
LLD discussion (45-60 min) Always, 6-12 classes One, for the flow with the most moving parts When an entity has a lifecycle
Machine coding (90-120 min) A rough sketch on paper or in comments, 5 minutes Rarely As a transition table in code
Design doc at work Yes, for the core model For cross-component flows For anything with statuses
Key idea

The precision that matters is the precision that changes the design: which class owns which, how many of each, and which side knows about the other. Exact UML syntax for everything else is optional.

2.2Reading a class box

Try it first2 minutes

Write the class box for a ParkingSpot that knows its ID, size, and parked vehicle, and can check fit, occupy, and release.

Reveal the answer

Three compartments: the name ParkingSpot; fields - id: String, - size: SpotSize, - vehicle: Vehicle; methods + canFit(v: Vehicle): boolean, + occupy(v: Vehicle): void, + release(): void. Fields are private, the methods callers need are public.

Conventions worth knowing:

  • Stereotypes go above the name in double angle brackets: <<interface>>, <<abstract>>, <<enum>> (formal UML prints each pair as one guillemet character). On a whiteboard, writing "interface" above the name is enough.
  • Abstract classes and methods are italic. On a whiteboard, write "abstract".
  • Enums list their constants in the field compartment.
  • Omit getters, setters, constructors, and toString. Show the methods that carry the design's rules.

2.3The six relationships

Try it first3 minutes

Classify each pair: (a) SavingsAccount and Account; (b) Circle and Shape (an interface); (c) Order and OrderLine; (d) Team and Player; (e) Invoice holding a Customer in a field; (f) InvoicePrinter.print(Invoice).

Reveal the answer

(a) Inheritance. (b) Realization. (c) Composition. (d) Aggregation. (e) Association. (f) Dependency. The figure below draws each one.

Relationship Meaning Lifetime In Java
Inheritance is a Subtype is permanently tied to its parent extends
Realization fulfils a contract Same implements
Composition owns, exclusively Part is created by the whole and dies with it private final field holding parts the whole creates
Aggregation has, but does not own Part exists independently, may be shared Field holding objects passed in
Association knows Long-lived reference A field
Dependency uses Only during a call Parameter, local variable, return type, static call

Two distinctions trip people up:

  • Association vs dependency is about time. If the reference is stored in a field, it is an association. If it only appears in a method signature or body, it is a dependency.
  • Composition vs aggregation is about ownership. If the whole creates the part, nobody else holds it, and deleting the whole deletes the part, it is composition. If parts are passed in and can outlive or be shared, it is aggregation.
On aggregation

The UML 2.5 specification itself says the precise meaning of aggregation varies by application area. Many teams draw only association and composition. In an interview, use the hollow diamond when "has but does not own" is the point you are making, and plain association otherwise.

2.4Multiplicity and navigability

Try it first3 minutes

Should Order hold its list of Payment objects, should Payment hold its Order, or both? What does "both" cost?

Reveal the answer

It depends on who needs to reach whom. Usually a payment records the orderId it pays for, and the order looks payments up through a repository when needed. Both directions as object references means every change must update both sides consistently, or the model contradicts itself. Prefer one direction, and reference by ID across independent entities.

Multiplicity says how many instances take part, written at the far end of the line:

Notation Meaning
1 exactly one
0..1 optional, at most one
* or 0..* any number, including zero
1..* at least one
2..4 a range

Navigability is shown with an open arrowhead: the arrow points to the class that is known. Customer --> Order means a customer can reach its orders; an order does not hold its customer object. Choose the direction from the use cases: "list a customer's orders" needs Customer -> Order or a repository query.

Two modeling rules that save trouble:

  • Prefer one-way references. Two-way references must be kept in sync by every method that changes them.
  • Reference by ID across independent entities. A Payment stores orderId, not an Order object. Inside one whole (an order and its lines), hold objects. This is the same boundary a database or a microservice split would draw later.

2.5From diagram to code

Try it first2 minutes

How does composition look different from aggregation in Java, given that both are just fields?

Reveal the answer

Composition: the whole creates the parts itself (lines.add(new OrderLine(...))), keeps them private, and never hands out the mutable collection. Aggregation: the parts are passed in from outside (team.add(player)), and the same object can be held by other wholes.

Every relationship becomes a specific code shape. Interviewers often check that your diagram and your code agree.

Composition: Order creates and owns its lines
// Composition: the order creates and owns its lines; a line never exists without its order
class Order {
    private final String id;
    private final List<OrderLine> lines = new ArrayList<>();

    Order(String id) { this.id = id; }

    void addLine(String sku, int qty) {
        lines.add(new OrderLine(sku, qty));        // created here, never handed in from outside
    }

    List<OrderLine> lines() { return Collections.unmodifiableList(lines); }
}

record OrderLine(String sku, int qty) {}
Aggregation: Team receives players that live on their own
// Aggregation: the team holds players that exist on their own and may join other teams
class Team {
    private final List<Player> players = new ArrayList<>();

    void add(Player p) { players.add(p); }        // received, not created
    int size() { return players.size(); }
}

class Player {
    final String name;
    Player(String name) { this.name = name; }
}
Association: a field
// Association: a long-lived reference held in a field
class Invoice {
    private final Customer billedTo;               // Invoice --> Customer
    Invoice(Customer billedTo) { this.billedTo = billedTo; }
    String customerName() { return billedTo.name(); }
}

record Customer(String name) {}
Dependency: a parameter
// Dependency: used briefly, as a parameter or local variable, then forgotten
class InvoicePrinter {
    String print(Invoice invoice) {                // InvoicePrinter ..> Invoice
        return "Invoice for " + invoice.customerName();
    }
}
Generalization and realization
// Inheritance (generalization) and realization (implements)
interface Shape { double area(); }                 // Circle ..|> Shape (realization)

abstract class Account {                           // SavingsAccount --|> Account (generalization)
    protected long balancePaise;
}

class SavingsAccount extends Account {}
class Circle implements Shape {
    private final double r;
    Circle(double r) { this.r = r; }
    public double area() { return Math.PI * r * r; }
}
Interview signal

When you draw a filled diamond, say why: "The booking owns its booked seats records, so they go when the booking is deleted." Saying the lifetime rule out loud shows the symbol was a decision, not decoration.

2.6Sequence diagrams

Try it first3 minutes

Sketch the calls when a car enters a parking lot and gets a ticket. Which object asks which?

Reveal the answer

The gate calls ParkingLot.park(vehicle). The lot asks a SpotAllocator for a free spot that fits, occupies that spot, creates a ticket with the entry time, saves it, and returns it to the gate. The figure below steps through it.

A sequence diagram shows one scenario over time: participants across the top, time flowing down, one arrow per call.

Conventions:

  • Solid arrow with a filled head: a call. Dashed arrow: a return value.
  • Self-call: an arrow that loops back to the same lifeline.
  • Notes or frames mark loops (loop), options (opt), and alternatives (alt). A note is enough on a whiteboard.
  • Keep it to one scenario and 5-10 messages. A sequence diagram that shows every branch is unreadable.

A sequence diagram is the quickest way to check your class diagram: every arrow needs a method on the receiving class, and every object on top needs a way to reach the next one.

2.7State diagrams

Try it first2 minutes

List the states of an e-commerce order and one transition that must be rejected.

Reveal the answer

Created, Paid, Shipped, Delivered, Cancelled, Returned. Reject cancelling a shipped order (in this model it must be delivered and then returned), and reject shipping an order that was never paid.

A state diagram shows the states one object can be in and the events that move it between them. Write transitions as event [guard] / action: the event triggers, the guard must be true, the action runs.

The diagram is also the spec for the code. Module 7 turns diagrams like this into an enum with a transition table, or into the State pattern when each state carries real behavior.

Key idea

Draw a state diagram whenever an entity has a status field. Most LLD bugs in vending machines, bookings, elevators, and orders are transitions nobody drew.

2.8Common mistakes

Common mistakes

  • Drawing every getter and setter, so the boxes hide the design.
  • Triangles pointing the wrong way. The triangle points at the parent or the interface.
  • Composition everywhere. Filled diamonds claim ownership and shared lifetime; use them only when that is true.
  • Missing multiplicities on the relationships that matter (one ticket per vehicle, many seats per show).
  • Two-way object references by default, which then drift out of sync.
  • A diagram that disagrees with the code, such as an association in the picture and a method parameter in the code.
  • Spending 15 minutes on notation in a round that rewards the model.

2.9Self-check

Self-checkFive more, after the lessons
  1. Draw (in words) the relationship between Library and Book if a book can move between library branches.
    Reveal

    Aggregation or association from Library to Book with multiplicity 1 to 0..*: the library holds books, but books exist independently and can move. Not composition, because a book outlives a branch.

  2. What does a dashed line with an open arrowhead mean?
    Reveal

    A dependency: the source uses the target temporarily (parameter, local variable, return type, or a static call).

  3. Why reference by ID across independent entities?
    Reveal

    It keeps entities loosely coupled, avoids loading big object graphs, avoids two-way sync bugs, and matches how data is stored and how services would be split later.

  4. Your class diagram shows Elevator with a List<Request> field. Is that association, aggregation, or composition, and what would you ask to decide?
    Reveal

    Ask whether requests exist outside the elevator. If the dispatcher creates a request and could move it to another elevator, it is aggregation (or association). If the elevator creates its own internal stop list, composition.

  5. What does the transition label pay [amount == total] / issueReceipt mean?
    Reveal

    On the pay event, if the guard amount == total holds, take the transition and run the action issueReceipt.

Phase 1: Object foundationsCoreVery high priority

Module 3: SOLID and design principles

Principles are how you justify a design in one sentence. This module teaches the two forces underneath all of them, cohesion and coupling, then SOLID with one before-and-after example each, then the everyday rules (DRY, KISS, YAGNI, Law of Demeter) and when following a principle too hard makes code worse.

9 lessons3 figures6 mastery checks

On this page

  1. 3.1Cohesion and coupling
  2. 3.2Single responsibility
  3. 3.3Open/closed
  4. 3.4Liskov substitution
  5. 3.5Interface segregation
  6. 3.6Dependency inversion and injection
  7. 3.7DRY, KISS, YAGNI, and the Law of Demeter
  8. 3.8Common mistakes
  9. 3.9Self-check
Warm-upWarm-up: one line each
  1. A class InvoiceService computes GST, renders a PDF, and saves to the database. Which principle does it strain, and why does it matter?
    Reveal

    Single responsibility. Three groups (finance, design, platform) each have a reason to change it, so their changes collide in one file and one test suite.

  2. Adding a new discount type means editing a long if-else in DiscountService. Which principle is that, and what is the usual fix?
    Reveal

    Open/closed. Put each discount behind a DiscountPolicy interface and pick the policy from a map built at startup, so a new type is a new class plus one line of wiring.

  3. FixedDepositAccount extends Account but its withdraw throws. Which principle breaks?
    Reveal

    Liskov substitution. Code written against Account expects withdraw to work and breaks when handed a fixed deposit.

  4. What is the difference between dependency inversion and dependency injection?
    Reveal

    Inversion is a design rule: high-level policy owns the interface, and details implement it. Injection is a technique: pass dependencies in (usually through the constructor) instead of creating them. Spring is a container that does the injection for you.

  5. Is copying the same three lines in two places always a DRY violation?
    Reveal

    No. DRY is about one piece of knowledge having one home. Two pieces of code that look alike but change for different reasons should stay separate.

3.1Cohesion and coupling

Try it first2 minutes

Without looking anything up: what do "high cohesion" and "low coupling" mean, and why do people always say them together?

Reveal the answer

Cohesion is how strongly the things inside one class belong together; high cohesion means everything in it serves one purpose. Coupling is how much one class depends on others; low coupling means few, narrow connections. Together they make a change local: the code that must change sits in one place, and few other places notice.

Idea

Group what changes together (high cohesion) and separate what changes for different reasons (low coupling). Every principle below is a specific way to do one of the two.

Analogy

A well-run kitchen has a pastry station, a grill station, and a dish station. A new dessert changes one station. A kitchen where every cook does a bit of everything makes every menu change a meeting.

Cost

Splitting too far creates classes so small that following one feature means opening ten files. Stop when each class has one clear reason to change.

How to measure coupling in practice: count how many classes a typical change touches, and how many imports and constructor parameters a class has. More than five or six collaborators in a constructor is usually a cohesion problem in that class.

3.2Single responsibility

Try it first3 minutes

List who would ask for changes to the InvoiceService below, and propose a split.

Reveal the answer

Finance asks for tax rule changes, design asks for layout changes, and the platform team asks for storage changes. Split into TaxCalculator, InvoiceRenderer, and InvoiceRepository, and keep a thin InvoiceService that coordinates them.

A class should have one reason to change. Robert Martin's sharper version: a module should be responsible to one actor, one group of people who request its changes. "One responsibility" does not mean "one method"; it means one owner.

Three owners in one class
class InvoiceService {
    private final Map<String, String> db = new HashMap<>();

    BigDecimal total(List<LineItem> items) {             // changes when finance changes tax rules
        BigDecimal sub = items.stream().map(LineItem::amount).reduce(BigDecimal.ZERO, BigDecimal::add);
        return sub.multiply(new BigDecimal("1.18")).setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_UP);
    }

    String render(String id, List<LineItem> items) {      // changes when the layout changes
        return "INVOICE " + id + "\n" + items.size() + " items, total " + total(items);
    }

    void save(String id, List<LineItem> items) {          // changes when storage changes
        db.put(id, render(id, items));
    }
}
One owner per class
class TaxCalculator {                                     // owner: finance rules
    private final BigDecimal rate;
    TaxCalculator(BigDecimal rate) { this.rate = rate; }

    BigDecimal total(List<LineItem> items) {
        BigDecimal sub = items.stream().map(LineItem::amount).reduce(BigDecimal.ZERO, BigDecimal::add);
        return sub.add(sub.multiply(rate)).setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_UP);
    }
}

class InvoiceRenderer {                                   // owner: presentation
    String render(String id, List<LineItem> items, BigDecimal total) {
        return "INVOICE " + id + "\n" + items.size() + " items, total " + total;
    }
}

interface InvoiceRepository {                             // owner: storage
    void save(String id, String document);
}

class InvoiceService2 {                                   // coordinates; holds no rules of its own
    private final TaxCalculator tax;
    private final InvoiceRenderer renderer;
    private final InvoiceRepository repo;

    InvoiceService2(TaxCalculator tax, InvoiceRenderer renderer, InvoiceRepository repo) {
        this.tax = tax; this.renderer = renderer; this.repo = repo;
    }

    String issue(String id, List<LineItem> items) {
        String doc = renderer.render(id, items, tax.total(items));
        repo.save(id, doc);
        return doc;
    }
}
Code that ranSrp.java: the rest of the file, including the main method behind the output below
Srp.java (everything not shown above)
record LineItem(String name, BigDecimal price, int qty) {
    BigDecimal amount() { return price.multiply(BigDecimal.valueOf(qty)); }
}

// ... (code shown above) ...

class Demo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<LineItem> items = List.of(new LineItem("pen", new BigDecimal("10.00"), 3), new LineItem("book", new BigDecimal("250.00"), 1));
        List<String> saved = new ArrayList<>();
        String doc = new InvoiceService2(new TaxCalculator(new BigDecimal("0.18")), new InvoiceRenderer(), (id, d) -> saved.add(id)).issue("INV-7", items);
        System.out.println(doc);
        assert doc.endsWith("330.40") && saved.equals(List.of("INV-7"));
        InvoiceService bad = new InvoiceService();

Output (from running the code above)
INVOICE INV-7
2 items, total 330.40
Key idea

The test: describe the class in one sentence without "and". "Calculates invoice totals with tax" passes. "Calculates totals and renders PDFs and saves invoices" fails.

3.3Open/closed

Try it first3 minutes

Marketing adds a STUDENT customer type with 15% off. With the if-else below, which files change and which tests rerun? Sketch a design where nothing existing changes.

Reveal the answer

DiscountServiceBad changes, and every test of it should rerun because any branch might break. Instead, give each discount its own class behind a DiscountPolicy interface, and have the service look the policy up in a map built at startup. STUDENT is then one line of wiring (or one new class if the rule is new).

Software entities should be open for extension, closed for modification. Adding behavior should mean adding code, not editing code that already works.

Every new type edits this method
class DiscountServiceBad {
    BigDecimal discount(String customerType, BigDecimal amount) {
        if (customerType.equals("REGULAR")) return BigDecimal.ZERO;
        if (customerType.equals("PREMIUM")) return amount.multiply(new BigDecimal("0.10"));
        if (customerType.equals("EMPLOYEE")) return amount.multiply(new BigDecimal("0.30"));
        // every new customer type edits this method, and its tests
        throw new IllegalArgumentException(customerType);
    }
}
New behavior is a new class
interface DiscountPolicy {
    BigDecimal discount(BigDecimal amount);
}

class NoDiscount implements DiscountPolicy {
    public BigDecimal discount(BigDecimal amount) { return BigDecimal.ZERO; }
}

class PercentOff implements DiscountPolicy {
    private final BigDecimal percent;
    PercentOff(String percent) { this.percent = new BigDecimal(percent); }
    public BigDecimal discount(BigDecimal amount) {
        return amount.multiply(percent).divide(BigDecimal.valueOf(100), 2, RoundingMode.HALF_UP);
    }
}

class DiscountService {
    private final Map<String, DiscountPolicy> policies;   // built once, at startup

    DiscountService(Map<String, DiscountPolicy> policies) { this.policies = policies; }

    BigDecimal discount(String customerType, BigDecimal amount) {
        DiscountPolicy p = policies.get(customerType);
        if (p == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("no policy for " + customerType);
        return p.discount(amount);
    }
}
Wiring at startup
DiscountService service = new DiscountService(Map.of(
        "REGULAR", new NoDiscount(),
        "PREMIUM", new PercentOff("10"),
        "EMPLOYEE", new PercentOff("30"),
        "STUDENT", new PercentOff("15")));   // new type: one line of wiring, no edits to the service
Code that ranOcp.java: the rest of the file, including the main method behind the output below
Ocp.java (everything not shown above)
class Demo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {

// ... (code shown above) ...

        BigDecimal d = service.discount("STUDENT", new BigDecimal("200.00"));
        System.out.println("student discount on 200.00 = " + d);
        assert d.compareTo(new BigDecimal("30.00")) == 0;
        assert new DiscountServiceBad().discount("PREMIUM", new BigDecimal("100")).compareTo(BigDecimal.TEN) == 0;
    }
}
Output (from running the code above)
student discount on 200.00 = 30.00

The pattern behind this fix is strategy plus a factory (Module 6). The switch does not disappear; it moves to one place where the objects are created, which is where variation belongs.

Watch out

OCP is about the changes you expect. You cannot close code against every change, and trying produces interfaces nobody implements twice. Apply it where a rule has already changed once or clearly will (pricing, discounts, payment methods, notification channels).

3.4Liskov substitution

Try it first3 minutes

BillPayer.payFrom(List<Account>) loops over accounts and withdraws from the first with enough balance. Someone adds FixedDepositAccount extends Account whose withdraw throws. What happens, and is the bug in BillPayer or in the hierarchy?

Reveal the answer

The first time a fixed deposit has enough balance, payFrom throws. The bug is in the hierarchy: FixedDepositAccount claims to be an Account but cannot keep Account's promise that withdraw works when the balance allows. Withdrawal is a capability only some accounts have, so it belongs in a separate interface.

Objects of a subtype must be usable anywhere the parent type is expected, without surprises (Barbara Liskov, 1987). In practice a subclass must not:

  • Demand more from callers (stronger preconditions, such as "amount must be under 1,000").
  • Promise less (weaker postconditions, such as "balance may not decrease").
  • Throw exceptions the parent's contract does not allow, or break the parent's invariants.
A subtype that breaks the parent's promise
class Account {
    protected long balance;
    Account(long balance) { this.balance = balance; }

    void withdraw(long amount) {
        if (amount > balance) throw new IllegalStateException("insufficient funds");
        balance -= amount;
    }
    long balance() { return balance; }
}

class FixedDepositAccount extends Account {
    FixedDepositAccount(long balance) { super(balance); }

    @Override void withdraw(long amount) {
        throw new UnsupportedOperationException("no withdrawals before maturity");   // breaks the parent's promise
    }
}

class BillPayer {
    void payFrom(List<Account> accounts, long amount) {
        for (Account a : accounts) {
            if (a.balance() >= amount) { a.withdraw(amount); return; }   // explodes on a fixed deposit
        }
    }
}
Model the capability, not the label
interface Withdrawable {                               // a capability, not every account has it
    long balance();
    void withdraw(long amount);
}

abstract class BankAccount {
    protected long balance;
    BankAccount(long balance) { this.balance = balance; }
    public long balance() { return balance; }
}

class SavingsAccount extends BankAccount implements Withdrawable {
    SavingsAccount(long balance) { super(balance); }
    public void withdraw(long amount) {
        if (amount > balance) throw new IllegalStateException("insufficient funds");
        balance -= amount;
    }
}

class FixedDeposit extends BankAccount {               // simply has no withdraw method
    FixedDeposit(long balance) { super(balance); }
}

class BillPayer2 {
    void payFrom(List<? extends Withdrawable> accounts, long amount) {   // the type says what it needs
        for (Withdrawable a : accounts) {
            if (a.balance() >= amount) { a.withdraw(amount); return; }
        }
        throw new IllegalStateException("no account can pay " + amount);
    }
}
Code that ranLsp.java: the rest of the file, including the main method behind the output below
Lsp.java (everything not shown above)
class Demo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try {
            new BillPayer().payFrom(List.of(new FixedDepositAccount(10_000), new Account(5_000)), 1_000);
            throw new AssertionError();
        } catch (UnsupportedOperationException e) {
            System.out.println("bad design: " + e.getMessage());
        }
        SavingsAccount s = new SavingsAccount(5_000);
        new BillPayer2().payFrom(List.of(s), 1_000);
        System.out.println("good design: savings balance " + s.balance());
        assert s.balance() == 4_000;
    }
}
Output (from running the code above)
bad design: no withdrawals before maturity
good design: savings balance 4000

The textbook example is Square extends Rectangle: setting a square's width must also change its height, which breaks code that sets width and height independently. The lesson is the same: "a square is a rectangle" is true in geometry and false for a mutable Rectangle class. Is-a must hold for behavior, not just for the English sentence.

Interview signal

Any override that throws UnsupportedOperationException is a Liskov smell. Say it in the interview and propose a role interface for the capability.

3.5Interface segregation

Try it first2 minutes

A PaymentProvider interface has charge, refund, createSubscription, and cancelSubscription. Cash on delivery supports only charge. What goes wrong?

Reveal the answer

Cash on delivery must implement three methods it cannot support, so it throws from them, which is a Liskov violation waiting to happen. Every client also depends on methods it never calls, so a change to subscriptions recompiles and retests refund code. Split into role interfaces: Chargeable, Refundable, SubscriptionCapable.

Clients should not be forced to depend on methods they do not use. Prefer several small role interfaces over one large one.

One fat interface
interface PaymentProvider {
    String charge(String customer, long amountPaise);
    void refund(String chargeId, long amountPaise);
    String createSubscription(String customer, String plan);
    void cancelSubscription(String subscriptionId);
}

class CashOnDelivery implements PaymentProvider {
    public String charge(String customer, long amountPaise) { return "cod-" + customer; }
    public void refund(String chargeId, long amountPaise) { throw new UnsupportedOperationException(); }
    public String createSubscription(String c, String p) { throw new UnsupportedOperationException(); }
    public void cancelSubscription(String s) { throw new UnsupportedOperationException(); }
}
Role interfaces: implement and depend on only what you use
interface Chargeable { String charge(String customer, long amountPaise); }
interface Refundable { void refund(String chargeId, long amountPaise); }
interface SubscriptionCapable {
    String createSubscription(String customer, String plan);
    void cancelSubscription(String subscriptionId);
}

class CardProvider implements Chargeable, Refundable, SubscriptionCapable {
    public String charge(String customer, long amountPaise) { return "card-" + customer; }
    public void refund(String chargeId, long amountPaise) { /* call the card network */ }
    public String createSubscription(String customer, String plan) { return "sub-" + plan; }
    public void cancelSubscription(String subscriptionId) { }
}

class CashOnDelivery2 implements Chargeable {           // implements only what it can do
    public String charge(String customer, long amountPaise) { return "cod-" + customer; }
}

class RefundService {
    private final Refundable provider;                   // depends only on the role it uses
    RefundService(Refundable provider) { this.provider = provider; }
    void refund(String chargeId, long amount) { provider.refund(chargeId, amount); }
}

The bonus is visible in RefundService: it accepts a Refundable, so passing cash on delivery is now a compile error instead of a runtime exception.

3.6Dependency inversion and injection

Try it first3 minutes

OrderNotifier creates a SmtpEmailClient inside itself. List two problems, and redraw the dependency so the business rule does not depend on SMTP.

Reveal the answer

You cannot test OrderNotifier without sending email, and switching to SMS or a different provider means editing the business class. Redraw: OrderNotifier depends on a MessageSender interface that it owns; EmailSender and SmsSender implement it; the sender is passed into the constructor.

High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules; both should depend on abstractions. And the abstraction belongs to the high-level side: the business rule says what it needs (send(to, text)), and the vendor code adapts to it.

Policy depends on a detail
class SmtpEmailClient {
    void sendMail(String to, String subject, String body) { /* SMTP details */ }
}

class OrderNotifierBad {
    private final SmtpEmailClient smtp = new SmtpEmailClient();   // policy depends on a detail

    void orderShipped(String email, String orderId) {
        smtp.sendMail(email, "Shipped", "Order " + orderId + " is on its way");
    }
}
Policy owns the interface; details implement it
// The high-level module owns the abstraction it needs...
interface MessageSender {
    void send(String recipient, String text);
}

class OrderNotifier {
    private final MessageSender sender;
    OrderNotifier(MessageSender sender) { this.sender = sender; }   // injected

    void orderShipped(String recipient, String orderId) {
        sender.send(recipient, "Order " + orderId + " is on its way");
    }
}

// ...and the details implement it
class EmailSender implements MessageSender {
    private final SmtpEmailClient smtp = new SmtpEmailClient();
    public void send(String recipient, String text) { smtp.sendMail(recipient, "Update", text); }
}

class SmsSender implements MessageSender {
    public void send(String recipient, String text) { /* call the SMS gateway */ }
}

Three related terms, often mixed up:

Term What it is
Dependency inversion (DIP) A design rule: policy owns abstractions, details implement them
Dependency injection (DI) A technique: pass dependencies in, usually through the constructor
Inversion of control (IoC) container A framework that creates objects and injects dependencies, such as Spring

Constructor injection is the default in Spring: a class with one constructor gets its parameters injected without any annotation, the fields can be final, and tests can pass fakes directly:

Testing with a lambda as the fake
List<String> sent = new ArrayList<>();
OrderNotifier notifier = new OrderNotifier((to, text) -> sent.add(to + ": " + text));   // a lambda as a fake
notifier.orderShipped("asha@example.com", "o-42");
// sent == ["asha@example.com: Order o-42 is on its way"]

3.7DRY, KISS, YAGNI, and the Law of Demeter

Try it first2 minutes

shipping.rate(order) calls order.getCustomer().address().city(). What does ShippingCalculator now depend on, and what would you change?

Reveal the answer

It depends on Order, Customer, and Address and on how they are connected. Any restructuring (customers with several addresses, a separate shipping address on the order) breaks it. Ask the order for what you need: order.shippingCity(), so one place knows the path.

Four everyday rules, each with its trap:

Rule Means Trap
DRY (don't repeat yourself) Each piece of knowledge has one authoritative home Merging code that only looks alike but changes for different reasons, creating coupling
KISS (keep it simple) Choose the simplest design that meets today's requirements Confusing simple with easy: a 300-line method is easy to write, not simple to read
YAGNI (you aren't gonna need it) Do not build for imagined requirements Ignoring requirements the interviewer clearly signaled ("we may add more vehicle types")
Law of Demeter Talk only to your direct collaborators, not their internals Adding pass-through methods for everything; fluent builders and streams are not violations
Reaching through objects
record Address(String city, String pincode) {}
record Customer(String name, Address address) {}

class OrderBad {
    private final Customer customer;
    OrderBad(Customer customer) { this.customer = customer; }
    Customer getCustomer() { return customer; }
}

class ShippingBad {
    double rate(OrderBad order) {
        // reaches through three objects: knows Order, Customer, and Address internals
        return order.getCustomer().address().city().equals("Bengaluru") ? 40 : 80;
    }
}
Ask the nearest object
class Order {
    private final Customer customer;
    Order(Customer customer) { this.customer = customer; }
    String shippingCity() { return customer.address().city(); }   // one place knows the path
}

class Shipping {
    double rate(Order order) {
        return order.shippingCity().equals("Bengaluru") ? 40 : 80;
    }
}
Key idea

Principles are tools for arguing about change cost, not rules to satisfy. In an interview, name a principle when it explains a decision you made ("pricing is behind an interface because of open/closed"), not as a checklist recital.

3.8Common mistakes

Common mistakes

  • Reciting SOLID without examples. Interviewers ask "show me where in your design".
  • Splitting every class into one-method classes in the name of single responsibility.
  • Interfaces for everything in the name of open/closed and dependency inversion, with one implementation each.
  • Inheritance that throws UnsupportedOperationException, a Liskov violation.
  • Fat interfaces that force empty or throwing implementations.
  • Creating dependencies with new inside business classes, which blocks testing and swapping.
  • DRY applied to look-alike code with different owners, producing a shared helper everyone is afraid to change.
  • Getter chains that couple a class to the structure of objects it does not own.

3.9Self-check

Self-checkFive more, after the lessons
  1. State the single responsibility principle in terms of actors, and give a test you can apply to a class.
    Reveal

    A class should answer to one actor, one group that requests its changes. Test: describe it in one sentence without "and", and list who would ask for changes; more than one group means split.

  2. Give three rules a subclass must follow to respect Liskov substitution.
    Reveal

    Do not strengthen preconditions, do not weaken postconditions, preserve the parent's invariants, and do not throw exceptions the parent's contract does not allow.

  3. In the dependency inversion principle, who owns the interface, and why does that matter?
    Reveal

    The high-level policy owns it. The interface then describes what the business needs, so swapping vendors means writing a new implementation, never changing the policy.

  4. Why is constructor injection preferred over field injection in Spring?
    Reveal

    Dependencies are explicit in the signature, fields can be final, the object is never half-built, and tests can construct it with fakes without a container.

  5. When is duplicated code acceptable?
    Reveal

    When the two copies represent different knowledge that changes for different reasons. Merging them would couple two owners. Duplicated knowledge, such as one tax rule written twice, is never acceptable.

Mastery checklist

Tick an item only when it is true with your notes closed.
