Phase 2: Patterns that earn their placeCoreHigh priority

Module 4: Creational patterns

Creational patterns answer three questions about making objects: which class to create, how to build a complex object so it is always valid, and how many instances should exist. This module covers the three you will use constantly (factory, builder, singleton), when dependency injection replaces them, and how to recognize the two you only need to name (abstract factory, prototype).

7 lessons3 figures6 mastery checks

On this page

  1. 4.1Why creation needs a pattern
  2. 4.2Factory
  3. 4.3Builder
  4. 4.4Singleton, and why DI usually wins
  5. 4.5Choosing a creational pattern
  6. 4.6Common mistakes
  7. 4.7Self-check
Warm-upWarm-up: one line each
  1. new EmailNotifier(), new SmsNotifier(), and new PushNotifier() appear behind an if-else in twelve places. What is the cost?
    Reveal

    Twelve places know the concrete classes. A new channel means twelve edits, and construction details (credentials, retries) are repeated. A factory keeps that knowledge in one place.

  2. A constructor takes (String, long, String, String, boolean, String). Name two problems.
    Reveal

    Call sites are unreadable (null, true means what?), and arguments of the same type are easy to swap without a compile error. A builder names each value.

  3. Why is a plain lazy singleton (if (instance == null) instance = new X()) unsafe with threads?
    Reveal

    Two threads can both see null before either writes, so two instances are created. Fix it with an enum, the holder idiom, or double-checked locking with volatile.

  4. Spring beans are singletons by default. Do you need the singleton pattern in a Spring app?
    Reveal

    Rarely. The container creates one instance and injects it, which gives one instance without global static access and keeps it replaceable in tests.

  5. What does a static factory method like Money.of("10", "INR") give you that a constructor cannot?
    Reveal

    A descriptive name, the freedom to return a cached instance or a subtype, and the ability to validate or normalize input before choosing what to create.

4.1Why creation needs a pattern

Try it first2 minutes

List three decisions hidden in the line Notifier n = new SmsNotifier(twilioKey, 3, Duration.ofSeconds(2)); that a caller should probably not be making.

Reveal the answer

Which implementation to use (SMS, and which vendor), how it is configured (the key, three retries, a two-second timeout), and whether a new instance is needed at all or a shared one would do. Each is a reason for that line to change, and none of them is the caller's business.

Idea

new couples the caller to one concrete class and to its construction details. Creational patterns move that knowledge to one place.

Analogy

A restaurant guest orders "the soup of the day"; the kitchen decides which soup and how to make it. If guests had to name the recipe and the stove setting, every menu change would need new guests.

Cost

Each pattern adds a class or two and some indirection. Use one when creation varies, is complex, or must be controlled; plain new is fine for simple value objects.

Question Pattern Typical LLD use
Which class? Factory Vehicle by type, notifier by channel, split strategy by type
How to build a valid complex object? Builder Requests and configs with many optional fields
How many instances? Singleton, or one instance injected by DI Logger, ID generator, configuration
A matching family of objects? Abstract factory AWS vs in-memory infrastructure, UI themes
A copy of a configured object? Prototype Game levels, templates, copy constructors

4.2Factory

Try it first3 minutes

Sketch how NotificationService.notify(channel, to, text) can send through email, SMS, or push without naming any of those classes, and how a new channel is added.

Reveal the answer

The service asks a factory for a Notifier by channel and calls send on it. The factory holds a map from channel to a supplier (constructor reference). A new channel is a new Notifier class plus one register line where the factory is wired. The service does not change.

A factory creates objects for callers so they depend only on an interface. Three forms, from simplest:

1. Simple factory: one method with the only switch on the type in the codebase. Fine when the set of types is small and owned by you.

One switch, in one place
class SimpleNotifierFactory {
    static Notifier create(Channel channel) {
        return switch (channel) {                   // the only switch on Channel in the codebase
            case EMAIL -> new EmailNotifier();
            case SMS -> new SmsNotifier();
            case PUSH -> new PushNotifier();
        };
    }
}

2. Registry factory: a map from key to Supplier. Adding a type is registration, not an edit, and tests can register fakes. This is the form to use in machine coding rounds.

Map-based factory
class NotifierFactory {
    private final Map<Channel, Supplier<Notifier>> makers = new EnumMap<>(Channel.class);

    NotifierFactory register(Channel channel, Supplier<Notifier> maker) {
        makers.put(channel, maker);
        return this;
    }

    Notifier create(Channel channel) {
        Supplier<Notifier> maker = makers.get(channel);
        if (maker == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("no notifier for " + channel);
        return maker.get();
    }
}

class NotificationService {
    private final NotifierFactory factory;
    NotificationService(NotifierFactory factory) { this.factory = factory; }

    String notify(Channel channel, String to, String text) {
        return factory.create(channel).send(to, text);   // never names a concrete class
    }
}
Wire it once at startup
NotifierFactory factory = new NotifierFactory()
        .register(Channel.EMAIL, EmailNotifier::new)
        .register(Channel.SMS, SmsNotifier::new)
        .register(Channel.PUSH, PushNotifier::new);
NotificationService service = new NotificationService(factory);
Code that ranFactory.java: the rest of the file, including the main method behind the output below
Factory.java (everything not shown above)
interface Notifier {
    String send(String to, String text);
}

class EmailNotifier implements Notifier {
    public String send(String to, String text) { return "email to " + to; }
}

class SmsNotifier implements Notifier {
    public String send(String to, String text) { return "sms to " + to; }
}

class PushNotifier implements Notifier {
    public String send(String to, String text) { return "push to " + to; }
}

enum Channel { EMAIL, SMS, PUSH }

// ... (code shown above) ...

final class Temperature {
    private final double celsius;
    private Temperature(double celsius) { this.celsius = celsius; }

    // named factory methods say what the double means; a constructor cannot
    static Temperature ofCelsius(double c) { return new Temperature(c); }
    static Temperature ofFahrenheit(double f) { return new Temperature((f - 32) * 5 / 9); }

    double celsius() { return celsius; }
}

class Demo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {

// ... (code shown above) ...

        for (Channel c : List.of(Channel.EMAIL, Channel.PUSH)) System.out.println(service.notify(c, "u1", "hi"));
        assert SimpleNotifierFactory.create(Channel.SMS) instanceof SmsNotifier;
        assert Math.abs(Temperature.ofFahrenheit(212).celsius() - 100) < 1e-9;
    }
}
Output (from running the code above)
email to u1
push to u1

3. Factory method (the original GoF form): a superclass declares abstract Notifier createNotifier(), and each subclass decides which concrete class to create. It appears in frameworks; in application code, the registry form is usually simpler.

Static factory methods (List.of, Optional.empty, Money.of, Duration.ofSeconds) are a lightweight cousin. They have names, can return cached or subtype instances, and can validate first:

Named creation beats an ambiguous constructor
final class Temperature {
    private final double celsius;
    private Temperature(double celsius) { this.celsius = celsius; }

    // named factory methods say what the double means; a constructor cannot
    static Temperature ofCelsius(double c) { return new Temperature(c); }
    static Temperature ofFahrenheit(double f) { return new Temperature((f - 32) * 5 / 9); }

    double celsius() { return celsius; }
}
FactoryCreational
Intent
Create objects without the caller naming the concrete class.
Use when
The class to create depends on input or configuration, or construction is complex and repeated.
Shape
create(key) backed by a switch or a Map<Key, Supplier<T>>; callers receive the interface.
Real world
Spring BeanFactory, java.util.Calendar.getInstance(), JDBC DriverManager.getConnection, Executors.newFixedThreadPool.
Avoid when
There is one implementation and no sign of a second. Use new.
Interview signal
Pair it with strategy: "the factory picks the split strategy from the expense type, so adding a split type is one class and one registration."

4.3Builder

Try it first3 minutes

A PaymentRequest has three required fields (order ID, amount, currency) and several optional ones (description, manual capture, idempotency key, metadata). What is wrong with (a) one constructor per combination, and (b) a no-argument constructor plus setters?

Reveal the answer

(a) Telescoping constructors: call sites full of null and true that nobody can read, and same-typed arguments are easy to swap silently. (b) Setters leave the object mutable and possibly half-built: nothing stops a request with manual capture and no idempotency key from being used, and nothing makes it safe to share.

Telescoping constructors
class PaymentRequestOld {
    PaymentRequestOld(String orderId, long amountPaise, String currency) { this(orderId, amountPaise, currency, null, false); }
    PaymentRequestOld(String orderId, long amountPaise, String currency, String description, boolean capture) { /* ... */ }
}
// new PaymentRequestOld("o1", 49900, "INR", null, true);   // what are null and true?

A builder collects values through named methods and creates the object in one step, after validating the whole combination:

Builder with required fields up front and whole-object validation
final class PaymentRequest {
    private final String orderId;            // required
    private final long amountPaise;          // required
    private final String currency;           // required
    private final String description;        // optional
    private final boolean autoCapture;       // optional, default true
    private final String idempotencyKey;     // optional
    private final Map<String, String> metadata;

    private PaymentRequest(Builder b) {
        this.orderId = b.orderId;
        this.amountPaise = b.amountPaise;
        this.currency = b.currency;
        this.description = b.description;
        this.autoCapture = b.autoCapture;
        this.idempotencyKey = b.idempotencyKey;
        this.metadata = Collections.unmodifiableMap(new LinkedHashMap<>(b.metadata));   // defensive copy
    }

    static Builder builder(String orderId, long amountPaise, String currency) {   // required fields up front
        return new Builder(orderId, amountPaise, currency);
    }

    static final class Builder {
        private final String orderId;
        private final long amountPaise;
        private final String currency;
        private String description;
        private boolean autoCapture = true;
        private String idempotencyKey;
        private final Map<String, String> metadata = new LinkedHashMap<>();

        private Builder(String orderId, long amountPaise, String currency) {
            this.orderId = Objects.requireNonNull(orderId);
            this.amountPaise = amountPaise;
            this.currency = Objects.requireNonNull(currency);
        }

        Builder description(String d) { this.description = d; return this; }
        Builder manualCapture() { this.autoCapture = false; return this; }
        Builder idempotencyKey(String k) { this.idempotencyKey = k; return this; }
        Builder metadata(String key, String value) { this.metadata.put(key, value); return this; }

        PaymentRequest build() {                   // validate the whole object once, here
            if (amountPaise <= 0) throw new IllegalStateException("amount must be positive");
            if (!autoCapture && idempotencyKey == null)
                throw new IllegalStateException("manual capture needs an idempotency key");
            return new PaymentRequest(this);
        }
    }

    @Override public String toString() {
        return orderId + " " + amountPaise + " " + currency + " capture=" + (autoCapture ? "auto" : "manual") + " " + metadata;
    }
}
Reads like a sentence
PaymentRequest req = PaymentRequest.builder("o-42", 49_900, "INR")
        .description("Annual plan")
        .manualCapture()
        .idempotencyKey("o-42-attempt-1")
        .metadata("source", "app")
        .build();

o-42 49900 INR capture=manual {source=app}

Details that separate a good builder from a long one:

  • Required fields go in builder(...), so they cannot be forgotten.
  • build() validates combinations that no single setter can check.
  • The product is immutable, with defensive copies of collections.
  • In real projects, Lombok's @Builder generates this; know how to write it by hand for interviews, and know that Lombok does not add validation unless you write it.
BuilderCreational
Intent
Build a complex, valid, immutable object step by step.
Use when
Four or more parameters, several optional, or rules that span fields.
Shape
Static nested Builder with fluent methods; private constructor that takes the builder; build() validates.
Real world
StringBuilder, HttpRequest.newBuilder(), Stream.builder(), Lombok @Builder, Spring UriComponentsBuilder.
Avoid when
Two or three required fields. A constructor or a record is clearer.
Interview signal
Mention validation in build() and immutability. That is what makes it more than a long chain of setters.

4.4Singleton, and why DI usually wins

Try it first3 minutes

Write the shortest thread-safe lazy singleton you know. Then argue why a Spring application rarely needs one.

Reveal the answer

The holder idiom (a private static nested class holding a static final instance) or an enum with one constant. Both rely on the JVM's thread-safe class initialization. In Spring, a bean is a singleton by default within the container: you get one instance, created by the container and injected where needed, so callers do not reach for global static state and tests can inject a different instance.

A singleton guarantees one instance and global access to it. The guarantee is easy to get wrong:

Lazy initialization without synchronization
class LazyConfigBroken {
    private static LazyConfigBroken instance;

    static LazyConfigBroken getInstance() {
        if (instance == null) {                 // two threads can both see null here
            instance = new LazyConfigBroken();  // and both create an instance
        }
        return instance;
    }
}

Three correct versions:

Enum singleton: simplest, thread-safe, safe against serialization and reflection
enum IdGenerator {
    INSTANCE;                                   // created once by the JVM, thread-safely

    private final AtomicLong next = new AtomicLong(1);

    long nextId() { return next.getAndIncrement(); }
}
Holder idiom: lazy and lock-free
class AppConfig {
    private AppConfig() { /* load files, expensive */ }

    private static class Holder {               // loaded only on first use of getInstance()
        static final AppConfig INSTANCE = new AppConfig();
    }

    static AppConfig getInstance() { return Holder.INSTANCE; }   // class init is thread-safe by the JVM spec
}
Double-checked locking: correct only with volatile
class Registry {
    private static volatile Registry instance;  // volatile is required: without it a thread can see a half-built object

    static Registry getInstance() {
        Registry r = instance;
        if (r == null) {
            synchronized (Registry.class) {
                r = instance;
                if (r == null) instance = r = new Registry();
            }
        }
        return r;
    }
}
Code that ranSingleton.java: the rest of the file, including the main method behind the output below
Singleton.java (everything not shown above)
class Demo {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        Set<Long> ids = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet();
        ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8);
        for (int t = 0; t < 8; t++) pool.submit(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < 10_000; i++) ids.add(IdGenerator.INSTANCE.nextId()); });
        pool.shutdown();
        pool.awaitTermination(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
        System.out.println("unique ids from 8 threads: " + ids.size());
        assert ids.size() == 80_000;
        assert AppConfig.getInstance() == AppConfig.getInstance() && Registry.getInstance() == Registry.getInstance();
        assert LazyConfigBroken.getInstance() != null;
    }
}
Output (from running the code above)
unique ids from 8 threads: 80000

The problem with singletons is not the instance count; it is global access. Code that calls Config.getInstance() hides a dependency, cannot easily run with a different config in a test, and shares state between tests. Dependency injection keeps "one instance" and drops "global access":

Singleton pattern One instance via DI (Spring default)
Who creates it The class itself The container, at startup
How code gets it X.getInstance() anywhere Constructor parameter
Dependencies visible No Yes, in the signature
Replace in tests Hard (static state) Pass a fake
Interview signal

In machine coding, a singleton for an ID generator or an in-memory store is acceptable and quick. Say the trade-off: "I'd inject this in a real service; here a singleton keeps the driver simple." That shows you know both.

4.5Choosing a creational pattern

Try it first2 minutes

For each, name the pattern: (a) tests should run against in-memory storage and queue, production against AWS, and the two must never be mixed; (b) a game level is expensive to set up and you need many slightly different copies; (c) a Report takes 9 parameters.

Reveal the answer

(a) Abstract factory: one factory creates a matching family (blob store and job queue). (b) Prototype: copy a configured instance (with a copy constructor) and adjust it. (c) Builder.

The two patterns you mostly need to recognize:

Abstract factory creates a family of related objects that must be used together, and switching the family is one decision:

One factory per family; one place to switch
interface BlobStore { void put(String key, byte[] data); }
interface JobQueue { void enqueue(String job); }

interface InfraFactory {                     // creates a family of objects that must match
    BlobStore blobStore();
    JobQueue jobQueue();
}

class AwsInfra implements InfraFactory {
    public BlobStore blobStore() { return (k, d) -> { /* S3 PutObject */ }; }
    public JobQueue jobQueue() { return job -> { /* SQS SendMessage */ }; }
}

class InMemoryInfra implements InfraFactory {  // for tests and local runs
    final Map<String, byte[]> blobs = new HashMap<>();
    final Queue<String> jobs = new ArrayDeque<>();
    public BlobStore blobStore() { return blobs::put; }
    public JobQueue jobQueue() { return jobs::add; }
}

class ReportJob {
    private final BlobStore store;
    private final JobQueue queue;
    ReportJob(InfraFactory infra) {          // one switch point: pass a different factory
        this.store = infra.blobStore();
        this.queue = infra.jobQueue();
    }
    void run(String id) {
        store.put("reports/" + id, new byte[] {1, 2, 3});
        queue.enqueue("email-report:" + id);
    }
}

Prototype creates new objects by copying an existing configured one. In Java, prefer a copy constructor or a copy() method over Cloneable, whose clone() is shallow by default and easy to get wrong with mutable fields.

Smell Pattern
new ConcreteType behind an if-else in many places Factory
Constructor with many parameters, several optional Builder
Objects of different families mixed by mistake Abstract factory
Expensive setup copied by hand Prototype (copy constructor)
Exactly one instance needed DI with one instance; enum singleton if no container

4.6Common mistakes

Common mistakes

  • A factory for a class with one implementation, adding indirection without value.
  • Factories that also hold business rules: the factory decides what to create, not how to price or validate.
  • Builders that skip validation, so invalid objects are built anyway.
  • Mutable products from builders, or products that share the builder's collections.
  • Lazy singletons without synchronization, or double-checked locking without volatile.
  • Singletons with mutable global state that tests share and leak between each other.
  • Calling getInstance() deep in business code instead of injecting the dependency.

4.7Self-check

Self-checkFive more, after the lessons
  1. Write (in words) a registry factory for split strategies in an expense-sharing app.
    Reveal

    A Map<SplitType, Supplier<SplitStrategy>> filled at startup (EQUAL -> EqualSplit::new, and so on); create(type) looks up the supplier and throws on an unknown type. The expense service calls factory.create(type).split(...).

  2. What exactly does volatile fix in double-checked locking?
    Reveal

    Without it, the write of the reference can become visible before the constructor's writes, so another thread can see a non-null but half-initialized object. volatile adds the happens-before ordering that prevents this.

  3. Why is the enum singleton considered the most robust form?
    Reveal

    The JVM creates the constant exactly once and thread-safely; serialization returns the same constant; and reflection cannot create a second enum instance.

  4. When would you not use a builder even though a class has five fields?
    Reveal

    When all five are required and of clearly different types, a constructor or a record is shorter and just as safe. Builders pay off with optional fields and cross-field rules.

  5. How does an abstract factory differ from a factory?
    Reveal

    A factory creates one kind of product chosen by a key. An abstract factory creates several kinds of products that must match (a family), and switching families is one decision.

Mastery checklist

Tick an item only when it is true with your notes closed.

Module 5: Structural patterns

Structural patterns arrange objects so they fit together without editing them. Four of them wrap one object in another (adapter, decorator, proxy, facade), and they look alike in a class diagram, so this module teaches each with a real use case, then a side-by-side comparison so you can name the right one. Composite rounds it off for trees.

8 lessons5 figures6 mastery checks

On this page

Warm-upWarm-up: one line each
  1. A vendor SDK takes amounts in rupees as a double and returns error codes as integers. Your code uses paise as long and readable reasons. Which pattern sits between them?
    Reveal

    An adapter. It implements your interface and translates units, names, and error codes at the boundary, so vendor quirks never leak into business code.

  2. You want logging, retries, and metrics around a payment gateway, in any combination, without editing the gateway. Which pattern?
    Reveal

    Decorator: each concern is a wrapper with the same interface that adds its step and delegates. Wrappers stack in any order.

  3. Spring's @Transactional on a method called from another method of the same class does nothing. Why?
    Reveal

    Spring applies @Transactional through a proxy around the bean. A call on this inside the class goes straight to the object, not through the proxy, so no transaction starts.

  4. What is the difference between a facade and a god class?
    Reveal

    A facade offers a simple entry point and coordinates subsystems that keep their own rules. A god class holds the rules of many subsystems itself.

  5. A product bundle can contain products and other bundles, and both have a price. Which pattern?
    Reveal

    Composite: Product and Bundle share an interface with price(), and a bundle's price sums its children.

5.1Adapter

Try it first3 minutes

Your checkout uses PaymentGateway.charge(orderId, amountPaise). Stripe's SDK wants a parameter map and returns an intent with a status string; a legacy bank API wants rupees as a double and returns integer codes. Where should each translation live?

Reveal the answer

In one adapter per vendor, each implementing PaymentGateway. StripeAdapter builds the parameter map and maps the status; BankAdapter converts paise to rupees and maps code 51 to "insufficient funds". Checkout code never sees a vendor type, so switching or adding vendors leaves it untouched.

Idea

An adapter makes an existing class usable through an interface it was not written for, by translating calls.

Analogy

A travel plug adapter. Neither the socket nor the laptop changes; the adapter in between makes them fit.

Cost

One more class per external dependency, and translation code you must test. It pays for itself the first time a vendor changes its API.

Our interface, written for our needs
interface PaymentGateway {
    PaymentResult charge(String orderId, long amountPaise);
}

record PaymentResult(boolean success, String reference, String failureReason) {}
Vendor code we cannot change
// third-party code we cannot change
class StripeClient {
    StripeIntent createPaymentIntent(Map<String, Object> params) {
        return new StripeIntent("pi_" + params.get("metadata[order_id]"), "succeeded");
    }
}
record StripeIntent(String id, String status) {}

class LegacyBankApi {
    /** returns 0 for success, 51 for insufficient funds, other codes for errors */
    int debit(String accountRef, double rupees) { return rupees > 10_000 ? 51 : 0; }
}
One adapter per vendor
class StripeAdapter implements PaymentGateway {
    private final StripeClient client;
    StripeAdapter(StripeClient client) { this.client = client; }

    public PaymentResult charge(String orderId, long amountPaise) {
        Map<String, Object> p = new HashMap<>();
        p.put("amount", amountPaise);                 // Stripe also uses the smallest currency unit
        p.put("currency", "inr");
        p.put("metadata[order_id]", orderId);
        StripeIntent intent = client.createPaymentIntent(p);
        boolean ok = intent.status().equals("succeeded");
        return new PaymentResult(ok, intent.id(), ok ? null : intent.status());
    }
}

class BankAdapter implements PaymentGateway {
    private final LegacyBankApi bank;
    private final String accountRef;
    BankAdapter(LegacyBankApi bank, String accountRef) { this.bank = bank; this.accountRef = accountRef; }

    public PaymentResult charge(String orderId, long amountPaise) {
        int code = bank.debit(accountRef, amountPaise / 100.0);   // translate units at the boundary only
        return switch (code) {
            case 0 -> new PaymentResult(true, "bank-" + orderId, null);
            case 51 -> new PaymentResult(false, null, "INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS");
            default -> new PaymentResult(false, null, "BANK_ERROR_" + code);
        };
    }
}

Adapter.java (everything not shown above)
// our contract, owned by our code

// ... (code shown above) ...

// ... (code shown above) ...

class Demo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        PaymentGateway stripe = new StripeAdapter(new StripeClient());
        PaymentGateway bank = new BankAdapter(new LegacyBankApi(), "ACC-1");
        System.out.println(stripe.charge("o1", 49_900));
        System.out.println(bank.charge("o2", 2_000_000));
        assert !bank.charge("o3", 2_000_000).success() && bank.charge("o4", 100).success();
    }
}
Output (from running the code above)
PaymentResult[success=true, reference=pi_o1, failureReason=null]
PaymentResult[success=false, reference=null, failureReason=INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS]
AdapterStructural
Intent
Let a class work through an interface it does not implement, by translating calls.
Use when
Integrating third-party SDKs, legacy systems, or any API whose shape you do not control.
Shape
Adapter implements the target interface and holds the adaptee (object adapter); it converts arguments, results, units, and errors.
Real world
InputStreamReader adapts an InputStream to a Reader; Arrays.asList adapts an array to a List; Spring MVC's HandlerAdapter.
Avoid when
You own both sides. Change the interface instead of adding a translator.
Interview signal
Say "translate at the boundary": units, error codes, and naming are converted once, in the adapter.

5.2Decorator

Try it first3 minutes

You need retries and logging around a flaky gateway. Does it matter whether logging wraps retries or retries wrap logging? What would each log?

Reveal the answer

It matters. Logging outside retries logs once per business call: one "charge" line and the final outcome. Logging inside retries logs every attempt, including the failures that were retried. Both are useful for different purposes; the order of wrapping is a design decision.

A decorator implements the same interface as the object it wraps, adds behavior before or after delegating, and can be stacked:

Two decorators: each adds one concern
class RetryingGateway implements PaymentGateway {
    private final PaymentGateway inner;
    private final int maxAttempts;
    RetryingGateway(PaymentGateway inner, int maxAttempts) { this.inner = inner; this.maxAttempts = maxAttempts; }

    public String charge(String orderId, long amountPaise) {
        for (int attempt = 1; ; attempt++) {
            try {
                return inner.charge(orderId, amountPaise);
            } catch (TransientFailure e) {
                if (attempt == maxAttempts) throw e;
                // real code: back off with jitter, and only retry if the provider is idempotent per orderId
            }
        }
    }
}

class LoggingGateway implements PaymentGateway {
    private final PaymentGateway inner;
    private final List<String> log;
    LoggingGateway(PaymentGateway inner, List<String> log) { this.inner = inner; this.log = log; }

    public String charge(String orderId, long amountPaise) {
        log.add("charge " + orderId + " " + amountPaise);
        try {
            String ref = inner.charge(orderId, amountPaise);
            log.add("ok " + ref);
            return ref;
        } catch (RuntimeException e) {
            log.add("failed " + e.getMessage());
            throw e;
        }
    }
}
Compose them at wiring time
PaymentGateway gateway = new LoggingGateway(new RetryingGateway(new FlakyGateway(2), 3), log);
gateway.charge("o-9", 25_000);
Code that ranDecorator.java: the rest of the file, including the main method behind the output below
Decorator.java (everything not shown above)
interface PaymentGateway {
    String charge(String orderId, long amountPaise);
}

class TransientFailure extends RuntimeException {
    TransientFailure(String m) { super(m); }
}

class FlakyGateway implements PaymentGateway {          // fails the first `failures` calls
    private int failures;
    FlakyGateway(int failures) { this.failures = failures; }
    public String charge(String orderId, long amountPaise) {
        if (failures-- > 0) throw new TransientFailure("timeout");
        return "ref-" + orderId;
    }
}

// ... (code shown above) ...

class Demo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<String> log = new ArrayList<>();

// ... (code shown above) ...

        log.forEach(System.out::println);
        assert log.equals(List.of("charge o-9 25000", "ok ref-o-9"));
        List<String> log2 = new ArrayList<>();
        PaymentGateway order2 = new RetryingGateway(new LoggingGateway(new FlakyGateway(2), log2), 3);
        order2.charge("o-10", 1);
        System.out.println("logging inside retry sees every attempt: " + log2);
    }
}
Output (from running the code above)
charge o-9 25000
ok ref-o-9
logging inside retry sees every attempt: [charge o-10 1, failed timeout, charge o-10 1, failed timeout, charge o-10 1, ok ref-o-10]

Why decorators beat subclasses here: each concern is one class, combinations happen at runtime, and the wrapped class never changes (open/closed). The same idea is all over the JDK: new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(new FileInputStream(path))) stacks three behaviors on a byte stream, and Collections.unmodifiableList(list) decorates a list with read-only behavior.

Watch out

Retrying a payment is only safe if the provider treats repeated requests for the same order as one charge (an idempotency key). A retry decorator around a non-idempotent call can charge a customer twice.

5.3Proxy

Try it first3 minutes

Exchange rates come from a slow remote API and change every few minutes. Callers use a RateService interface. How do you add caching without changing callers or the remote client?

Reveal the answer

A caching proxy that implements RateService, holds the real service, and returns a cached value while it is fresh. On a miss or an expired entry, it calls the real service and stores the result. Callers still depend on RateService, and the remote client is untouched.

A proxy has the same interface as the real object and controls access to it: it may delay creating it, cache its answers, check permissions, or call it over the network. Unlike a decorator, a proxy may decide not to call the real object at all.

A caching proxy with a TTL
interface RateService {
    BigDecimal rate(String from, String to);
}

class RemoteRateService implements RateService {      // slow: a network call
    int calls = 0;
    public BigDecimal rate(String from, String to) {
        calls++;
        return new BigDecimal("83.10");
    }
}

class CachingRateProxy implements RateService {
    private record Entry(BigDecimal value, Instant expiresAt) {}

    private final RateService real;
    private final Duration ttl;
    private final Clock clock;
    private final Map<String, Entry> cache = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();   // proxies are shared: make the cache thread-safe

    CachingRateProxy(RateService real, Duration ttl, Clock clock) { this.real = real; this.ttl = ttl; this.clock = clock; }

    public BigDecimal rate(String from, String to) {
        String key = from + "->" + to;
        Entry e = cache.get(key);
        if (e != null && clock.instant().isBefore(e.expiresAt())) return e.value();   // real object not called at all
        BigDecimal v = real.rate(from, to);
        cache.put(key, new Entry(v, clock.instant().plus(ttl)));
        return v;
    }
}
Kind Controls Example
Virtual When the real object is created Hibernate lazy-loading proxies
Caching Whether the real object is called @Cacheable, the rate proxy above
Protection Who may call it A permission check before a sensitive method
Remote Where it runs gRPC and RMI client stubs

How Spring uses proxies, and the self-call trap

Spring implements @Transactional, @Cacheable, and @Async by wrapping your bean in a proxy. Only calls that go through the proxy get the behavior. A JDK dynamic proxy shows the mechanism:

A dynamic proxy that records every call it sees
interface OrderOps {
    void placeOrder(String id);
    void audit(String id);
}

class OrderOpsImpl implements OrderOps {
    public void placeOrder(String id) {
        audit(id);                     // a call on `this`: it never passes through the proxy
    }
    public void audit(String id) { }
}

class Tracing {
    @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
    static <T> T wrap(T target, Class<T> type, List<String> seen) {
        InvocationHandler h = (proxy, method, args) -> {
            seen.add("proxy saw " + method.getName());   // where Spring would begin a transaction
            return method.invoke(target, args);
        };
        return (T) Proxy.newProxyInstance(type.getClassLoader(), new Class<?>[] {type}, h);
    }
}
The self-call never reaches the proxy
List<String> seen = new ArrayList<>();
OrderOps ops = Tracing.wrap(new OrderOpsImpl(), OrderOps.class, seen);
ops.placeOrder("o-1");
System.out.println(seen);      // [proxy saw placeOrder]: audit() ran, but the proxy never saw it
Interview signal

This is a favorite SDE-2 follow-up. The fixes: move the annotated method to another bean, call it through the injected proxy, or use AspectJ weaving. Saying why it happens (calls on this bypass the proxy) is what earns the credit.

5.4Facade

Try it first2 minutes

Placing an order means reserving stock, pricing, charging, and notifying. If payment fails, the reservation must be released. Where should that sequence and the undo step live?

Reveal the answer

In one checkout facade with a placeOrder method. It calls each subsystem in order and releases the reservation if a later step fails. Controllers and other callers make one call and do not need to know the sequence.

A facade gives clients one simple entry point to a set of collaborating objects:

One call for clients; the sequence and the compensation in one place
class CheckoutFacade {
    private final Inventory inventory;
    private final Pricing pricing;
    private final Payments payments;
    private final Notifications notifications;

    CheckoutFacade(Inventory i, Pricing p, Payments pay, Notifications n) {
        this.inventory = i; this.pricing = p; this.payments = pay; this.notifications = n;
    }

    /** One call for clients; the order of steps and the compensation live here. */
    String placeOrder(String orderId, String sku, int qty) {
        String reservation = inventory.reserve(sku, qty);
        String paymentRef;
        try {
            long amount = pricing.total(sku, qty);
            paymentRef = payments.charge(orderId, amount);
        } catch (RuntimeException e) {
            inventory.release(reservation, sku, qty);     // undo the earlier step
            throw e;
        }
        try {
            notifications.orderPlaced(orderId);           // best effort: a failed email must not undo a paid order
        } catch (RuntimeException e) {
            // log and retry later; the order stands
        }
        return paymentRef;
    }
}
Code that ranFacade.java: the rest of the file, including the main method behind the output below
Facade.java (everything not shown above)
class Inventory {
    final Map<String, Integer> stock;
    Inventory(Map<String, Integer> stock) { this.stock = stock; }
    String reserve(String sku, int qty) {
        if (stock.getOrDefault(sku, 0) < qty) throw new IllegalStateException("out of stock: " + sku);
        stock.merge(sku, -qty, Integer::sum);
        return "res-" + sku;
    }
    void release(String reservationId, String sku, int qty) { stock.merge(sku, qty, Integer::sum); }
}
class Pricing { long total(String sku, int qty) { return 49_900L * qty; } }
class Payments {
    boolean failNext;
    String charge(String orderId, long amount) {
        if (failNext) throw new IllegalStateException("card declined");
        return "pay-" + orderId;
    }
}
class Notifications { final List<String> sent = new ArrayList<>(); void orderPlaced(String id) { sent.add(id); } }

// ... (code shown above) ...

class Demo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Inventory inv = new Inventory(new java.util.HashMap<>(Map.of("BOOK", 3)));
        Payments pay = new Payments();
        CheckoutFacade checkout = new CheckoutFacade(inv, new Pricing(), pay, new Notifications());
        System.out.println(checkout.placeOrder("o1", "BOOK", 2) + ", stock left " + inv.stock.get("BOOK"));
        pay.failNext = true;
        try { checkout.placeOrder("o2", "BOOK", 1); throw new AssertionError(); } catch (IllegalStateException e) {
            System.out.println("declined; stock restored to " + inv.stock.get("BOOK"));
        }
        assert inv.stock.get("BOOK") == 1;
    }
}
Output (from running the code above)
pay-o1, stock left 1
declined; stock restored to 1

A facade coordinates; it does not absorb the subsystems' rules. Pricing rules stay in Pricing, stock rules in Inventory. If the facade starts computing discounts or checking stock levels itself, it is turning into a god class.

In production

In a Spring service, the @Service class your controller calls is usually a facade over repositories and clients. The compensation pattern above is the in-process version of a saga: in a distributed system each step would be a separate service, and the undo would be an event or a call to that service.

5.5Composite

Try it first3 minutes

Model a file system where you can ask any file or directory for its size, and a directory's size is the sum of everything inside it, at any depth.

Reveal the answer

An FsNode interface with size(). FileNode returns its own size. Directory holds a list of FsNode children and returns the sum of their sizes, which recurses naturally. Callers treat a single file and a whole tree the same way.

A composite lets clients treat a single item and a group of items uniformly, because both implement the same interface and groups delegate to their children.

Leaf and group share one interface
interface FsNode {
    String name();
    long size();                                       // same question for a file and a whole tree
    void print(String indent, StringBuilder out);
}

record FileNode(String name, long size) implements FsNode {
    public void print(String indent, StringBuilder out) {
        out.append(indent).append(name).append(" (").append(size).append(" B)\n");
    }
}

class Directory implements FsNode {
    private final String name;
    private final List<FsNode> children = new ArrayList<>();

    Directory(String name) { this.name = name; }

    Directory add(FsNode child) { children.add(child); return this; }
    List<FsNode> children() { return Collections.unmodifiableList(children); }

    public String name() { return name; }

    public long size() {                               // delegates to children, recursively
        long total = 0;
        for (FsNode c : children) total += c.size();
        return total;
    }

    public void print(String indent, StringBuilder out) {
        out.append(indent).append(name).append("/ (").append(size()).append(" B)\n");
        for (FsNode c : children) c.print(indent + "  ", out);
    }
}
Build a tree and ask the root
Directory root = new Directory("project")
        .add(new FileNode("README.md", 1_200))
        .add(new Directory("src")
                .add(new FileNode("Main.java", 4_096))
                .add(new FileNode("Util.java", 2_048)));
StringBuilder out = new StringBuilder();
root.print("", out);
Code that ranComposite.java: the rest of the file, including the main method behind the output below
Composite.java (everything not shown above)
class Demo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {

// ... (code shown above) ...

        System.out.print(out);
        assert root.size() == 7_344;
    }
}
Output (from running the code above)
project/ (7344 B)
  README.md (1200 B)
  src/ (6144 B)
    Main.java (4096 B)
    Util.java (2048 B)

Use it for trees where operations apply to both leaves and groups: file systems, nested menus, organization charts, product bundles, and expression trees (Add(Num(2), Mul(Num(3), Num(4)))).

5.6Telling the wrappers apart

Try it first2 minutes

For each, name the pattern: (a) wrap a list so writes throw; (b) a stub that sends method calls over gRPC; (c) one bookTrip() call that books a flight, a hotel, and a cab; (d) make a vendor's XML client look like your JSON interface.

Reveal the answer

(a) Decorator (it adds a behavior, read-only, with the same interface); some call it a protection proxy, and either answer with the reason is fine. (b) Remote proxy. (c) Facade. (d) Adapter.

Adapter Decorator Proxy Facade
Interface vs wrapped object Different: converts Same Same New and simpler
Purpose Make it fit Add behavior Control access Simplify use
Calls the wrapped object Always, translated Always, plus extra work Maybe not (cache, lazy, denied) Several objects, in sequence
Who creates the wrapped object The caller passes it in The caller passes it in Often the proxy itself (lazy) Injected subsystems
Example InputStreamReader BufferedInputStream Spring @Transactional CheckoutFacade
Key idea

Name the pattern by its intent, not its shape. "It wraps the gateway to add retries" is a decorator; "it wraps the gateway to translate the vendor's API" is an adapter, even though both diagrams show a class holding another.

5.7Common mistakes

Common mistakes

  • Vendor types leaking past the adapter, such as returning the SDK's response object to business code.
  • Decorators that change the contract, such as swallowing exceptions the interface promises to throw.
  • Ignoring wrap order: retry inside logging and logging inside retry produce different logs and metrics.
  • A retry decorator on a non-idempotent call, which can duplicate charges or messages.
  • Expecting @Transactional or @Cacheable to work on self-calls.
  • A facade that holds business rules, becoming the god class it was meant to hide.
  • Composite trees with type checks (if (node instanceof Directory)) in client code, which defeats the uniform interface.

5.8Self-check

Self-checkFive more, after the lessons
  1. Why should an adapter convert error codes into your own exception or result types?
    Reveal

    So business code handles one vocabulary of failures regardless of vendor. Switching vendors or adding a second one then changes only adapters.

  2. Give two differences between a proxy and a decorator.
    Reveal

    A proxy controls access and may not call the real object (cache hit, lazy creation, permission denied); a decorator always delegates and adds behavior. A proxy often creates or locates the real object itself; a decorator receives it from the caller.

  3. Why does java.io use decorators instead of subclasses for buffering, decompression, and character decoding?
    Reveal

    Those concerns combine freely. Subclasses would need one class per combination; decorators stack any combination at runtime from a few classes.

  4. Your facade's placeOrder charges the card and then the notification step throws. Should the payment be refunded?
    Reveal

    Usually not: a notification failure should not undo a successful order. Make notification asynchronous or best-effort with a retry, and compensate only for steps the order truly depends on.

  5. What makes the composite pattern support unlimited nesting?
    Reveal

    The group holds children typed as the shared interface, so a child can itself be a group. Operations recurse through the same method.

Mastery checklist

Tick an item only when it is true with your notes closed.

Module 6: Behavior that varies: strategy, template method, chain of responsibility

Most LLD problems have one rule that varies: how a fee is computed, how a spot is chosen, how an expense is split, which checks a request must pass. Strategy, template method, and chain of responsibility are three ways to make that variation pluggable. This module teaches each, the strategy plus factory combination that removes type switches for good, and how to choose between the three.

7 lessons4 figures6 mastery checks

On this page

  1. 6.1Strategy
  2. 6.2Strategy plus factory: killing the switch
  3. 6.3Template method
  4. 6.4Chain of responsibility

  6. 6.6Common mistakes
  7. 6.7Self-check
Warm-upWarm-up: one line each
  1. The shipping fee depends on a policy that marketing changes every quarter. Where should that rule live?
    Reveal

    Behind a ShippingStrategy interface, with one class (or lambda) per policy. Checkout holds a strategy and asks it for the fee, so a new policy never edits checkout.

  2. A switch (paymentMethod) that picks a fee formula appears in three places. What combination of patterns removes it?
    Reveal

    Strategy plus factory: one fee strategy per method, and one map from method to strategy built at startup. The three switches become one lookup.

  3. Three importers share the same steps (parse, validate, save) and differ in parsing. Which pattern keeps the steps in one place?
    Reveal

    Template method: an abstract base class with a final run() that calls the steps, and subclasses that fill in parse and save. Composition with strategies is the alternative.

  4. A withdrawal must pass KYC, limit, and fraud checks; the first failure stops it. Which pattern?
    Reveal

    Chain of responsibility (or its list form, a pipeline): each check either rejects or passes the request on.

  5. Can a Java lambda be a strategy?
    Reveal

    Yes. Any single-method interface is a functional interface, so p -> 0 can implement ShippingStrategy. Use a class when the strategy has fields, several methods, or deserves a name in the design.

6.1Strategy

Try it first3 minutes

Shipping costs can be a flat rate, depend on weight, or be free above an order value with one of the other rules below it. Sketch a design where checkout does not change when marketing invents a fourth rule.

Reveal the answer

A ShippingStrategy interface with costPaise(parcel). FlatRate, ByWeight, and FreeAbove implement it; FreeAbove holds another strategy for orders below the threshold. Checkout receives one strategy and calls it. A fourth rule is a fourth class.

Idea

Put each variant of an algorithm in its own class behind one interface, and let the context hold one of them. The context's code never branches on which one it has.

Analogy

A navigation app asks you to choose fastest, shortest, or no tolls. The app does the same thing either way (draw the route); only the routing rule is swapped.

Cost

One interface and one class per variant. For two variants that will never grow, an if is clearer.

Strategies, including one that wraps another
interface ShippingStrategy {
    long costPaise(Parcel p);
}

class FlatRate implements ShippingStrategy {
    private final long ratePaise;
    FlatRate(long ratePaise) { this.ratePaise = ratePaise; }
    public long costPaise(Parcel p) { return ratePaise; }
}

class ByWeight implements ShippingStrategy {
    public long costPaise(Parcel p) {
        long kg = (long) Math.ceil(p.weightKg());
        return 4_000 + Math.max(0, kg - 1) * 2_000;        // 40 rupees for the first kg, 20 for each extra
    }
}

class FreeAbove implements ShippingStrategy {             // wraps another strategy: free above a threshold
    private final long thresholdPaise;
    private final ShippingStrategy otherwise;
    FreeAbove(long thresholdPaise, ShippingStrategy otherwise) { this.thresholdPaise = thresholdPaise; this.otherwise = otherwise; }
    public long costPaise(Parcel p) {
        return p.orderValuePaise() >= thresholdPaise ? 0 : otherwise.costPaise(p);
    }
}

class Checkout {
    private final ShippingStrategy shipping;              // chosen by configuration or by the caller
    Checkout(ShippingStrategy shipping) { this.shipping = shipping; }

    long total(Parcel p) { return p.orderValuePaise() + shipping.costPaise(p); }
}
Code that ranStrategy.java: the rest of the file, including the main method behind the output below
Strategy.java (everything not shown above)
record Parcel(double weightKg, long orderValuePaise, boolean express) {}

// ... (code shown above) ...

class Demo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Parcel small = new Parcel(2.3, 30_000, false), big = new Parcel(2.3, 120_000, false);
        ShippingStrategy festival = p -> 0;                       // a one-line strategy needs no class
        ShippingStrategy expressFee = p -> p.express() ? 9_900 : 4_900;
        ShippingStrategy policy = new FreeAbove(99_900, new ByWeight());
        for (Parcel p : List.of(small, big)) System.out.println("order " + p.orderValuePaise() + " -> shipping " + policy.costPaise(p));
        assert new Checkout(policy).total(small) == 30_000 + 8_000 && new Checkout(policy).total(big) == 120_000;
        assert festival.costPaise(small) == 0 && expressFee.costPaise(new Parcel(1, 1, true)) == 9_900 && new FlatRate(5).costPaise(small) == 5;
    }
}
Output (from running the code above)
order 30000 -> shipping 8000
order 120000 -> shipping 0

Because ShippingStrategy has one method, lambdas work too:

One-line strategies
ShippingStrategy festival = p -> 0;                       // a one-line strategy needs no class
ShippingStrategy expressFee = p -> p.express() ? 9_900 : 4_900;
StrategyBehavioral
Intent
Make a family of algorithms interchangeable by putting each behind one interface.
Use when
A rule varies by configuration, user, region, or time, or a type switch picks between formulas.
Shape
Context holds a Strategy; implementations are classes or lambdas; a factory or map picks one.
Real world
Comparator passed to List.sort; Spring Security's AuthenticationProvider; retry and backoff policies in Resilience4j.
Avoid when
Two branches that will never grow, or variants that differ by one constant. Use a parameter.
Interview signal
Strategies appear in most LLD problems: spot allocation, pricing, splitting, elevator dispatch, eviction. Name the one in yours early.

6.2Strategy plus factory: killing the switch

Try it first3 minutes

Fees differ by payment method (card 2%, UPI free, netbanking flat 15 rupees, wallet 1%), and international cards pay 3.5%. Design the lookup so a new method or a special case does not edit existing code.

Reveal the answer

Two options. A map from method to fee rule handles the simple one-to-one case. For special cases that depend on more than the method (card and international), use a list of rules where each says supports(payment), ordered most specific first with a default last; the first rule that supports the payment computes the fee.

The strategy decides how; something still has to decide which. Two selection styles cover almost every interview:

Select by key: an EnumMap from method to rule
class FeeCalculator {
    private final Map<Method, FeeRule> rules = new EnumMap<>(Method.class);

    FeeCalculator() {
        rules.put(Method.CARD, p -> p.amountPaise() * 2 / 100);       // 2%
        rules.put(Method.UPI, p -> 0);
        rules.put(Method.NETBANKING, p -> 1_500);                     // flat 15 rupees
        rules.put(Method.WALLET, p -> p.amountPaise() / 100);         // 1%
    }

    long fee(Payment p) {
        FeeRule rule = rules.get(p.method());
        if (rule == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("no fee rule for " + p.method());
        return rule.feePaise(p);
    }
}
Select by condition: the first rule that supports the input
interface PricingRule {
    boolean supports(Payment p);    // decides whether it applies
    long feePaise(Payment p);
}

class InternationalCardRule implements PricingRule {
    public boolean supports(Payment p) { return p.method() == Method.CARD && p.international(); }
    public long feePaise(Payment p) { return p.amountPaise() * 35 / 1000; }   // 3.5%
}

class DomesticCardRule implements PricingRule {
    public boolean supports(Payment p) { return p.method() == Method.CARD; }
    public long feePaise(Payment p) { return p.amountPaise() * 2 / 100; }
}

class DefaultRule implements PricingRule {
    public boolean supports(Payment p) { return true; }
    public long feePaise(Payment p) { return 0; }
}

class RuleBasedFees {
    private final List<PricingRule> rules;           // order matters: most specific first
    RuleBasedFees(List<PricingRule> rules) { this.rules = rules; }

    long fee(Payment p) {
        return rules.stream().filter(r -> r.supports(p)).findFirst()
                .orElseThrow(() -> new IllegalStateException("no rule for " + p))
                .feePaise(p);
    }
}
Code that ranStrategyFactory.java: the rest of the file, including the main method behind the output below
StrategyFactory.java (everything not shown above)
enum Method { CARD, UPI, NETBANKING, WALLET }

record Payment(Method method, long amountPaise, boolean international) {}

interface FeeRule {
    long feePaise(Payment p);
}

// ... (code shown above) ...

class Demo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        FeeCalculator calc = new FeeCalculator();
        System.out.println("card fee on 1000.00: " + calc.fee(new Payment(Method.CARD, 100_000, false)));
        RuleBasedFees fees = new RuleBasedFees(List.of(new InternationalCardRule(), new DomesticCardRule(), new DefaultRule()));
        System.out.println("international card fee on 1000.00: " + fees.fee(new Payment(Method.CARD, 100_000, true)));
        assert fees.fee(new Payment(Method.UPI, 100_000, false)) == 0 && calc.fee(new Payment(Method.NETBANKING, 5, false)) == 1_500;
    }
}
Output (from running the code above)
card fee on 1000.00: 2000
international card fee on 1000.00: 3500
In production

In Spring, inject all implementations at once: a constructor parameter of type List<PricingRule> receives every bean that implements it (ordered by @Order), and Map<String, PricingRule> receives them keyed by bean name. A new rule is a new @Component; nothing else changes.

6.3Template method

Try it first3 minutes

CSV and JSON importers both parse, validate each row, save the valid ones, count rejects, and report. Only parsing and saving differ. How do you keep the sequence in one place, and stop a subclass from skipping validation?

Reveal the answer

An abstract FileImporter with a final run() that performs the steps in order and calls abstract parse and save methods, plus a hook isValid with a default. Subclasses fill in the blanks; final prevents them from changing the order or skipping steps.

A template method fixes an algorithm's skeleton in a base class and lets subclasses supply some steps:

A final skeleton with required steps and optional hooks
abstract class FileImporter {
    // the skeleton is fixed and final: subclasses cannot reorder or skip steps
    final ImportResult run(String content) {
        int saved = 0, rejected = 0;
        for (Row row : parse(content)) {
            if (isValid(row)) { save(row); saved++; }
            else rejected++;
        }
        afterImport(saved, rejected);
        return new ImportResult(saved, rejected);
    }

    protected abstract List<Row> parse(String content);      // required step
    protected abstract void save(Row row);                    // required step

    protected boolean isValid(Row row) {                      // hook with a sensible default
        return row.amountPaise() > 0;
    }

    protected void afterImport(int saved, int rejected) { }   // optional hook
}

class CsvImporter extends FileImporter {
    final List<Row> db = new ArrayList<>();

    protected List<Row> parse(String content) {
        return Arrays.stream(content.split("\n"))
                .map(line -> line.split(","))
                .map(f -> new Row(f[0].trim(), Long.parseLong(f[1].trim())))
                .toList();
    }

    protected void save(Row row) { db.add(row); }
}
Code that ranTemplate.java: the rest of the file, including the main method behind the output below
Template.java (everything not shown above)
record Row(String id, long amountPaise) {}
record ImportResult(int saved, int rejected) {}

// ... (code shown above) ...

interface Parser { List<Row> parse(String content); }
interface Sink { void save(Row row); }

class Importer {                                  // the same flow, assembled from parts
    private final Parser parser;
    private final Sink sink;
    Importer(Parser parser, Sink sink) { this.parser = parser; this.sink = sink; }

    ImportResult run(String content) {
        int saved = 0, rejected = 0;
        for (Row r : parser.parse(content)) {
            if (r.amountPaise() > 0) { sink.save(r); saved++; } else rejected++;
        }
        return new ImportResult(saved, rejected);
    }
}

class Demo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        CsvImporter csv = new CsvImporter();
        ImportResult r = csv.run("t1, 5000\nt2, -10\nt3, 250");
        System.out.println(r + " saved ids " + csv.db.stream().map(Row::id).toList());
        assert r.equals(new ImportResult(2, 1));
        List<Row> sink = new ArrayList<>();
        assert new Importer(c -> csv.parse(c), sink::add).run("a,1\nb,0").equals(new ImportResult(1, 1));
    }
}
Output (from running the code above)
ImportResult[saved=2, rejected=1] saved ids [t1, t3]

The same flow can be built by composition, passing a parser and a sink into one concrete class:

The composition alternative
interface Parser { List<Row> parse(String content); }
interface Sink { void save(Row row); }

class Importer {                                  // the same flow, assembled from parts
    private final Parser parser;
    private final Sink sink;
    Importer(Parser parser, Sink sink) { this.parser = parser; this.sink = sink; }

    ImportResult run(String content) {
        int saved = 0, rejected = 0;
        for (Row r : parser.parse(content)) {
            if (r.amountPaise() > 0) { sink.save(r); saved++; } else rejected++;
        }
        return new ImportResult(saved, rejected);
    }
}

Prefer composition when steps vary independently (any parser with any sink) or must change at runtime. Prefer a template method when the steps are coupled and the skeleton is the point, as in frameworks: the JDK's AbstractList, where you implement get and size and inherit the rest, and Spring MVC's AbstractController. Spring's JdbcTemplate keeps the fixed skeleton (get a connection, run, map rows, close) but takes the varying step as a callback, which is the composition version of the same idea.

6.4Chain of responsibility

Try it first3 minutes

An ATM holds 2,000, 500, and 100 rupee notes. Design the dispensing logic so a new denomination (200) can be added without editing the others.

Reveal the answer

A chain of handlers, one per denomination, ordered from largest to smallest. Each gives as many of its notes as it can and passes the remainder to the next. Adding 200 means inserting one handler between 500 and 100. The last handler throws if anything remains.

A chain of responsibility passes a request along a sequence of handlers. In the classic form, each handler does its part or passes the request on:

Each handler takes what it can and passes the rest
abstract class NoteDispenser {
    private final int denomination;
    private NoteDispenser next;

    NoteDispenser(int denomination) { this.denomination = denomination; }

    NoteDispenser then(NoteDispenser next) { this.next = next; return next; }

    void dispense(int amount, Map<Integer, Integer> out) {
        int count = amount / denomination;
        if (count > 0) out.put(denomination, count);
        int rest = amount % denomination;
        if (rest == 0) return;
        if (next == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("cannot dispense remaining " + rest);
        next.dispense(rest, out);                       // pass what is left down the chain
    }
}

class TwoThousands extends NoteDispenser { TwoThousands() { super(2000); } }
class FiveHundreds extends NoteDispenser { FiveHundreds() { super(500); } }
class Hundreds extends NoteDispenser { Hundreds() { super(100); } }
Build the chain once, use it for every withdrawal
NoteDispenser chain = new TwoThousands();
chain.then(new FiveHundreds()).then(new Hundreds());
Map<Integer, Integer> notes = new LinkedHashMap<>();
chain.dispense(3_700, notes);                   // {2000=1, 500=3, 100=2}

The more common form in business code is a pipeline: a list of checks run in order, stopping at the first rejection. Servlet filters and Spring Security's filter chain work this way.

A list of checks; the first rejection stops the request
record Withdrawal(String userId, long amountPaise, boolean kycDone, int todayCount) {}

interface Check {
    Optional<String> reject(Withdrawal w);              // empty = pass to the next check
}

class ChecksPipeline {
    private final List<Check> checks;
    ChecksPipeline(List<Check> checks) { this.checks = checks; }

    Optional<String> firstRejection(Withdrawal w) {
        for (Check c : checks) {
            Optional<String> r = c.reject(w);
            if (r.isPresent()) return r;                // stop at the first handler that rejects
        }
        return Optional.empty();
    }
}
Checks as lambdas
ChecksPipeline checks = new ChecksPipeline(List.of(
        w -> w.kycDone() ? Optional.empty() : Optional.of("KYC pending"),
        w -> w.amountPaise() <= 5_000_000 ? Optional.empty() : Optional.of("over single-withdrawal limit"),
        w -> w.todayCount() < 5 ? Optional.empty() : Optional.of("daily count exceeded")));
Code that ranChain.java: the rest of the file, including the main method behind the output below
Chain.java (everything not shown above)
class Demo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {

// ... (code shown above) ...

        System.out.println(notes);
        assert notes.equals(Map.of(2000, 1, 500, 3, 100, 2));
        try { chain.dispense(3_750, new LinkedHashMap<>()); throw new AssertionError(); } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) { System.out.println(e.getMessage()); }

// ... (code shown above) ...

        List<String> out = new ArrayList<>();
        out.add(checks.firstRejection(new Withdrawal("u1", 10_000, true, 0)).orElse("approved"));
        out.add(checks.firstRejection(new Withdrawal("u2", 9_000_000, true, 0)).orElse("approved"));
        out.add(checks.firstRejection(new Withdrawal("u3", 10_000, false, 9)).orElse("approved"));
        System.out.println(out);
        assert out.equals(List.of("approved", "over single-withdrawal limit", "KYC pending"));
    }
}
Output (from running the code above)
{2000=1, 500=3, 100=2}
cannot dispense remaining 50
[approved, over single-withdrawal limit, KYC pending]
Watch out

Order is part of the design. Cheap checks that reject the most requests go first; checks with side effects (reserving a limit) go last, after every check that could still reject.

6.5Choosing between the three

Try it first2 minutes

Name the pattern: (a) tax rules per country; (b) export to CSV, JSON, or PDF with identical open, header, rows, close steps; (c) a support ticket escalates from bot to agent to manager until someone resolves it; (d) a discount engine where several promotions may each adjust the price in turn.

Reveal the answer

(a) Strategy, picked by country. (b) Template method, or composition with a writer strategy. (c) Chain of responsibility (classic: each handler resolves or passes on). (d) A chain or pipeline where every handler runs and may adjust the price, in a defined order.

Strategy Template method Chain of responsibility
What varies One whole algorithm Some steps of a fixed algorithm Which handlers act, and in what order
Mechanism Composition: hold an interface Inheritance: override steps A linked chain or a list of handlers
Chosen At runtime At compile time (subclass) At assembly time (order of handlers)
How many run Exactly one One skeleton, with its steps Until one handles it, or all in order
Typical LLD use Pricing, allocation, splitting, scheduling Importers, exporters, report jobs Validation, approvals, note dispensing, logging levels
Pattern pickerPick the pressure you feel in the code. The picker names the pattern, its shape, and when it is the wrong tool.

6.6Common mistakes

Common mistakes

  • A strategy interface with one implementation forever, created for a rule that never varies.
  • The switch moved, not removed: a factory with a switch is fine once; the same switch in three places is not.
  • Strategies that reach into the context's internals instead of receiving what they need as parameters.
  • A template method without final, so subclasses override run() and skip validation.
  • Deep template hierarchies where behavior is spread across four levels of subclasses.
  • An unordered chain, or a chain that applies a side effect before a later check rejects the request.
  • A chain where no handler is guaranteed to handle, so requests silently fall off the end.

6.7Self-check

Self-checkFive more, after the lessons
  1. What is the difference between strategy and polymorphism on the entity itself?
    Reveal

    Polymorphism on the entity puts behavior that depends on what the thing is inside its class (vehicle.spotSize()). A strategy holds a policy that varies independently of the entity (weekend pricing for every vehicle). Use strategy when the rule changes without the type changing.

  2. Why put a default rule last in a supports-based list?
    Reveal

    So every input matches some rule. Without it, an unexpected input finds no rule and fails at runtime; with it, the fallback behavior is explicit and tested.

  3. What does final on a template method protect?
    Reveal

    The order and completeness of the algorithm. Subclasses can fill in steps and hooks but cannot reorder, skip, or bypass them.

  4. When would you prefer composition over a template method for an importer?
    Reveal

    When the parser and the destination vary independently (CSV to the database, CSV to a queue, JSON to the database), when they must change at runtime, or when you want to test steps in isolation.

  5. In a withdrawal pipeline, where does "reserve the daily limit" go, and why?
    Reveal

    Last, after every check that could still reject. Otherwise a later rejection leaves a reservation behind that must be undone.

Tick an item only when it is true with your notes closed.

Module 7: Events, commands, and state machines

Three behavioral patterns carry most LLD problems that have events, actions, or lifecycles. Observer lets one change notify many parts without knowing them. Command turns an action into an object you can queue, log, and undo. State machines, written as an enum transition table or as the State pattern, make illegal transitions impossible. The vending machine, elevator, booking, and order problems all rest on this module.
