Warm-upWarm-up: one line each
  1. When an order is placed you must email a receipt, add loyalty points, and record analytics. Why should OrderService not call those three services directly?
    Reveal

    It would depend on all three and change whenever a reaction is added or removed. Publishing an OrderPlaced event lets each reaction subscribe on its own; the order service stays the same.

  2. One observer throws an exception. What should happen to the others?
    Reveal

    They should still run. The publisher (or event bus) catches and records each listener's failure separately, unless the reactions must succeed or fail together, in which case they are not observers but steps of one transaction.

  3. How do undo and redo work with the command pattern?
    Reveal

    Each action is a command with execute and undo. Executed commands go on an undo stack; undo pops one, reverses it, and pushes it on a redo stack; redo moves it back. A new command clears the redo stack.

  4. An order is SHIPPED and someone calls cancel(). Where should that be rejected?
    Reveal

    In the order's state machine: the transition table has no CANCEL from SHIPPED, so the call throws. No caller should need to remember the rule.

  5. Enum with a transition table, or the State pattern?
    Reveal

    An enum table when states differ mainly in which transitions are allowed. The State pattern when each state has substantial behavior of its own across several operations.

7.1Observer

Try it first3 minutes

Placing an order must trigger a receipt email, loyalty points, and analytics. Next quarter, fraud scoring is added. Design it so adding fraud scoring does not touch the order code, and a loyalty outage does not block receipts.

Reveal the answer

The order service publishes an OrderPlaced event to an event bus. Email, loyalty, analytics, and later fraud each subscribe independently. The bus calls listeners one by one and catches each listener's exceptions, so a loyalty outage is recorded and the others still run. Adding fraud scoring is one new subscription.

Idea

A subject keeps a list of listeners and notifies them when something happens. The subject knows only the listener interface, never the concrete reactions.

Analogy

A newsletter. The writer publishes once; subscribers join and leave without the writer changing anything, and one bouncing inbox does not stop delivery to the rest.

Cost

The flow of control is no longer visible in one method. Debugging "who reacted to this event" needs logging, and ordering between listeners is not guaranteed unless you design it.

A small typed event bus with error isolation
class EventBus {
    // one listener list per event type; CopyOnWriteArrayList is safe to iterate while others subscribe
    private final Map<Class<?>, List<Consumer<Object>>> listeners = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    private final List<String> errors = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>();

    @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
    <E> Runnable subscribe(Class<E> type, Consumer<? super E> listener) {
        Consumer<Object> l = e -> listener.accept((E) e);
        listeners.computeIfAbsent(type, k -> new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>()).add(l);
        return () -> listeners.get(type).remove(l);           // call it to unsubscribe
    }

    void publish(Object event) {
        for (Consumer<Object> l : listeners.getOrDefault(event.getClass(), List.of())) {
            try {
                l.accept(event);
            } catch (RuntimeException e) {                     // one broken listener must not stop the rest
                errors.add(event.getClass().getSimpleName() + ": " + e.getMessage());
            }
        }
    }

    List<String> errors() { return errors; }
}
The subject publishes and forgets
class OrderService {
    private final EventBus bus;
    OrderService(EventBus bus) { this.bus = bus; }

    void place(String orderId, String userId, long amountPaise) {
        // ... validate, save the order ...
        bus.publish(new OrderPlaced(orderId, userId, amountPaise));   // does not know who listens
    }
}
Subscribe, publish, unsubscribe
EventBus bus = new EventBus();
bus.subscribe(OrderPlaced.class, e -> out.add("email receipt for " + e.orderId()));
bus.subscribe(OrderPlaced.class, e -> { throw new IllegalStateException("loyalty service down"); });
Runnable stopAnalytics = bus.subscribe(OrderPlaced.class, e -> out.add("analytics +" + e.amountPaise()));
bus.subscribe(OrderCancelled.class, e -> out.add("refund " + e.orderId()));

OrderService orders = new OrderService(bus);
orders.place("o-1", "u-7", 49_900);
stopAnalytics.run();                                   // unsubscribe
orders.place("o-2", "u-7", 10_000);
Code that ranObserver.java: the rest of the file, including the main method behind the output below
Observer.java (everything not shown above)
record OrderPlaced(String orderId, String userId, long amountPaise) {}
record OrderCancelled(String orderId) {}

// ... (code shown above) ...

class Demo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<String> out = new ArrayList<>();

// ... (code shown above) ...

        out.forEach(System.out::println);
        System.out.println("errors: " + bus.errors());
        assert out.equals(List.of("email receipt for o-1", "analytics +49900", "email receipt for o-2")) && bus.errors().size() == 2;
    }
}
Output (from running the code above)
email receipt for o-1
analytics +49900
email receipt for o-2
errors: [OrderPlaced: loyalty service down, OrderPlaced: loyalty service down]

Design decisions to state out loud:

  • Synchronous or asynchronous. The bus above calls listeners on the publisher's thread, so a slow listener slows the order. Use an executor or a message queue for slow or remote reactions.
  • Failure isolation. Catch per listener, record, and continue. Decide whether a failed reaction is retried.
  • Ordering. Do not rely on listener order unless you enforce it.
  • Thread safety. CopyOnWriteArrayList lets listeners be added while events are being delivered.
  • Leaks. A listener that is never unsubscribed keeps its object alive. Return an unsubscribe handle.
In production

Spring provides this out of the box: ApplicationEventPublisher.publishEvent(...) and @EventListener methods. @TransactionalEventListener(phase = AFTER_COMMIT) runs the reaction only if the transaction commits, so you never email a receipt for an order that rolled back. Across services, the same pattern becomes a Kafka topic.

ObserverBehavioral
Intent
Notify many dependents of a change without coupling the source to them.
Use when
Several independent reactions follow one event, and the set of reactions changes over time.
Shape
Subject with subscribe and publish; listeners implement one callback; events are immutable records.
Real world
Spring application events, PropertyChangeListener, UI event handlers, Kafka consumers at service scale.
Avoid when
The reactions must all succeed or all fail together with the change. Call them directly in one transaction.
Interview signal
Mention failure isolation and sync vs async. Those are the follow-up questions.

7.2Command

Try it first2 minutes

Name three things you can do with an action once it is an object instead of a method call.

Reveal the answer

Queue it to run later or on another thread; log or persist it (and replay it after a crash); undo it; retry it; batch several into a macro. A thread pool's Runnable tasks are commands; so is each line a machine coding driver parses from input.

A command packages a request (the receiver, the operation, and its arguments) as an object with a uniform interface, usually execute() and optionally undo().

Commands that know how to reverse themselves
interface Command {
    void execute();
    void undo();
}

class Document {
    private final StringBuilder text = new StringBuilder();
    void insert(int pos, String s) { text.insert(pos, s); }
    String delete(int pos, int len) {
        String removed = text.substring(pos, pos + len);
        text.delete(pos, pos + len);
        return removed;
    }
    int length() { return text.length(); }
    @Override public String toString() { return text.toString(); }
}

class InsertCommand implements Command {
    private final Document doc;
    private final int pos;
    private final String s;
    InsertCommand(Document doc, int pos, String s) { this.doc = doc; this.pos = pos; this.s = s; }
    public void execute() { doc.insert(pos, s); }
    public void undo() { doc.delete(pos, s.length()); }
}

class DeleteCommand implements Command {
    private final Document doc;
    private final int pos, len;
    private String removed;                         // remembered so undo can restore it
    DeleteCommand(Document doc, int pos, int len) { this.doc = doc; this.pos = pos; this.len = len; }
    public void execute() { removed = doc.delete(pos, len); }
    public void undo() { doc.insert(pos, removed); }
}

Commands appear in more places than editors:

Use Example
Queues and thread pools executor.submit(runnable): the task is a command
Machine coding drivers Each input line (PARK KA01 CAR) parsed into a command object and executed
Audit and replay Store executed commands; replay them to rebuild state
Retries A failed command is re-queued with its arguments intact
Transactions in memory A key-value store records undo commands per transaction for rollback

7.3Undo and redo

Try it first3 minutes

Type "Hello", type " World", delete the first six characters, undo twice, redo once, then type "!". What is the text, and can you still redo?

Reveal the answer

"Hello World!". The second undo restored the text to "Hello", redo re-applied " World", and typing "!" is a new command, which clears the redo stack, so redo is no longer possible.

Two stacks hold the history
class Editor {
    private final Deque<Command> undoStack = new ArrayDeque<>();
    private final Deque<Command> redoStack = new ArrayDeque<>();

    void run(Command c) {
        c.execute();
        undoStack.push(c);
        redoStack.clear();                          // a new edit invalidates the redo history
    }

    boolean undo() {
        if (undoStack.isEmpty()) return false;
        Command c = undoStack.pop();
        c.undo();
        redoStack.push(c);
        return true;
    }

    boolean redo() {
        if (redoStack.isEmpty()) return false;
        Command c = redoStack.pop();
        c.execute();
        undoStack.push(c);
        return true;
    }
}
The scenario from the question
Document doc = new Document();
Editor ed = new Editor();
ed.run(new InsertCommand(doc, 0, "Hello"));
ed.run(new InsertCommand(doc, 5, " World"));     // "Hello World"
ed.run(new DeleteCommand(doc, 0, 6));            // "World"
ed.undo();                                        // "Hello World"
ed.undo();                                        // "Hello"
ed.redo();                                        // "Hello World"
ed.run(new InsertCommand(doc, 11, "!"));         // "Hello World!", and redo history is gone
Code that ranCommand.java: the rest of the file, including the main method behind the output below
Command.java (everything not shown above)
class Demo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {

// ... (code shown above) ...

        System.out.println(doc + " | redo possible: " + ed.redo());
        assert doc.toString().equals("Hello World!");
    }
}
Output (from running the code above)
Hello World! | redo possible: false

Details that come up as follow-ups:

  • Commands must capture what undo needs. DeleteCommand saves the removed text at execute time.
  • Memory. Cap the undo stack (an ArrayDeque you trim), or merge small edits (consecutive keystrokes become one insert).
  • Snapshots instead of reverse operations. For complex state, store the previous state (the memento pattern) instead of writing an inverse for every command.

7.4State machines with enums

Try it first3 minutes

Write the allowed transitions for an order as a table: rows are states, columns are events (pay, ship, deliver, cancel, return). What should happen for a blank cell?

Reveal the answer

Created: pay to Paid, cancel to Cancelled. Paid: ship to Shipped, cancel to Cancelled. Shipped: deliver to Delivered. Delivered: return to Returned. Cancelled and Returned allow nothing. A blank cell is an illegal transition and must throw.

State pay ship deliver cancel return
CREATED PAID - - CANCELLED -
PAID - SHIPPED - CANCELLED -
SHIPPED - - DELIVERED - -
DELIVERED - - - - RETURNED (within 7 days)
CANCELLED, RETURNED - - - - -

The table is the state diagram from Module 2 written as data. Code it the same way:

Transitions as an EnumMap table
enum OrderStatus { CREATED, PAID, SHIPPED, DELIVERED, CANCELLED, RETURNED }

enum OrderEvent { PAY, SHIP, DELIVER, CANCEL, RETURN }

final class OrderMachine {
    private static final Map<OrderStatus, Map<OrderEvent, OrderStatus>> NEXT = new EnumMap<>(OrderStatus.class);

    private static void allow(OrderStatus from, OrderEvent on, OrderStatus to) {
        NEXT.computeIfAbsent(from, k -> new EnumMap<>(OrderEvent.class)).put(on, to);
    }

    static {                                         // the state diagram, as data
        allow(OrderStatus.CREATED, OrderEvent.PAY, OrderStatus.PAID);
        allow(OrderStatus.CREATED, OrderEvent.CANCEL, OrderStatus.CANCELLED);
        allow(OrderStatus.PAID, OrderEvent.SHIP, OrderStatus.SHIPPED);
        allow(OrderStatus.PAID, OrderEvent.CANCEL, OrderStatus.CANCELLED);
        allow(OrderStatus.SHIPPED, OrderEvent.DELIVER, OrderStatus.DELIVERED);
        allow(OrderStatus.DELIVERED, OrderEvent.RETURN, OrderStatus.RETURNED);
    }

    static OrderStatus next(OrderStatus from, OrderEvent event) {
        OrderStatus to = NEXT.getOrDefault(from, Map.of()).get(event);
        if (to == null) throw new IllegalStateException("cannot " + event + " an order that is " + from);
        return to;
    }
}

The entity applies events in a fixed order: check the transition is legal, check guards that depend on data, run entry actions, then change the state:

Legal transition, then guard, then action
class Order {
    private final String id;
    private OrderStatus status = OrderStatus.CREATED;
    private Instant deliveredAt;

    Order(String id) { this.id = id; }

    void apply(OrderEvent event, Instant now) {
        OrderStatus next = OrderMachine.next(status, event);   // 1. is the transition legal at all?
        // 2. guards that depend on data, not just on the current state
        if (event == OrderEvent.RETURN && now.isAfter(deliveredAt.plus(Duration.ofDays(7))))
            throw new IllegalStateException("return window closed for " + id);
        // 3. actions on entering a state, then commit
        if (next == OrderStatus.DELIVERED) deliveredAt = now;
        status = next;
    }

    OrderStatus status() { return status; }
}
Code that ranEnumState.java: the rest of the file, including the main method behind the output below
EnumState.java (everything not shown above)
class Demo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Instant t = Instant.parse("2026-10-01T10:00:00Z");
        Order o = new Order("o-1");
        try { o.apply(OrderEvent.RETURN, t); throw new AssertionError(); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println(e.getMessage()); }
        o.apply(OrderEvent.PAY, t);
        o.apply(OrderEvent.SHIP, t);
        try { o.apply(OrderEvent.CANCEL, t); throw new AssertionError(); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println(e.getMessage()); }
        o.apply(OrderEvent.DELIVER, t);
        try { o.apply(OrderEvent.RETURN, t.plus(Duration.ofDays(9))); throw new AssertionError(); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println(e.getMessage()); }
        o.apply(OrderEvent.RETURN, t.plus(Duration.ofDays(3)));
        System.out.println("final status " + o.status());
        assert o.status() == OrderStatus.RETURNED;
    }
}
Output (from running the code above)
cannot RETURN an order that is CREATED
cannot CANCEL an order that is SHIPPED
return window closed for o-1
final status RETURNED
Key idea

Every entity with a status field gets a transition table and one method that changes the status. No other code assigns the status directly. This single rule prevents most lifecycle bugs in LLD problems.

7.5The State pattern

Try it first3 minutes

A document can be edited and submitted while a draft; approved (by someone other than the author) or rejected while in review; and nothing once published. Where would the rule "authors cannot approve their own work" live with an enum table, and where with State classes?

Reveal the answer

With an enum, the rule lives in the Document.approve method, which must also check the current status; every method grows a status check. With the State pattern, it lives in InReview.approve, the only place approval exists. Draft and Published do not need to mention approval at all; the interface default throws for them.

In the State pattern, each state is a class implementing the operations it allows; the context delegates to its current state object, and states replace themselves:

Each state implements only what it allows
interface DocState {
    default void edit(Document d, String text) { throw new IllegalStateException(name() + ": cannot edit"); }
    default void submit(Document d) { throw new IllegalStateException(name() + ": cannot submit"); }
    default void approve(Document d, String reviewer) { throw new IllegalStateException(name() + ": cannot approve"); }
    default void reject(Document d, String reason) { throw new IllegalStateException(name() + ": cannot reject"); }
    String name();
}

class Draft implements DocState {
    public void edit(Document d, String text) { d.setBody(text); }
    public void submit(Document d) {
        if (d.body().isBlank()) throw new IllegalStateException("empty document");
        d.moveTo(new InReview());
    }
    public String name() { return "Draft"; }
}

class InReview implements DocState {
    public void approve(Document d, String reviewer) {
        if (reviewer.equals(d.author())) throw new IllegalStateException("authors cannot approve their own work");
        d.log("approved by " + reviewer);
        d.moveTo(new Published());
    }
    public void reject(Document d, String reason) {
        d.log("rejected: " + reason);
        d.moveTo(new Draft());
    }
    public String name() { return "InReview"; }
}

class Published implements DocState {        // everything else falls through to the defaults and throws
    public String name() { return "Published"; }
}
The context delegates and exposes a hook to switch state
class Document {
    private final String author;
    private String body = "";
    private DocState state = new Draft();
    private final List<String> history = new ArrayList<>();

    Document(String author) { this.author = author; }

    // the public API delegates to the current state
    void edit(String text) { state.edit(this, text); }
    void submit() { state.submit(this); }
    void approve(String reviewer) { state.approve(this, reviewer); }
    void reject(String reason) { state.reject(this, reason); }

    // package-private hooks the states use
    void moveTo(DocState next) { history.add(state.name() + " -> " + next.name()); state = next; }
    void setBody(String b) { body = b; }
    void log(String s) { history.add(s); }
    String body() { return body; }
    String author() { return author; }
    String stateName() { return state.name(); }
    List<String> history() { return history; }
}
Code that ranStatePattern.java: the rest of the file, including the main method behind the output below
StatePattern.java (everything not shown above)
class Demo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Document d = new Document("asha");
        d.edit("First draft");
        d.submit();
        try { d.edit("sneaky change"); throw new AssertionError(); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println(e.getMessage()); }
        d.reject("add numbers");
        d.edit("Second draft with numbers");
        d.submit();
        try { d.approve("asha"); throw new AssertionError(); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println(e.getMessage()); }
        d.approve("ravi");
        System.out.println(d.stateName() + " " + d.history());
        assert d.stateName().equals("Published");
    }
}
Output (from running the code above)
InReview: cannot edit
authors cannot approve their own work
Published [Draft -> InReview, rejected: add numbers, InReview -> Draft, Draft -> InReview, approved by ravi, InReview -> Published]

7.6Enum machine or State pattern?

Try it first2 minutes

For each, pick an enum table or the State pattern: (a) a seat that is available, held, or booked; (b) a vending machine where inserting money, selecting a product, and dispensing behave differently in idle, has-money, and dispensing states; (c) a ticket that is open, in progress, resolved, or closed.

Reveal the answer

(a) Enum table: three states, and behavior differs only in which transitions are allowed. (b) State pattern: each state handles several operations with different logic (accept coins, compute change, refuse selection). (c) Enum table, with guards for who may close.

Enum with transition table State pattern
Best when States differ in allowed transitions States differ in behavior across several operations
Where rules live One table plus guards in the entity Spread across state classes, one per state
Adding a state One enum constant and table rows One class
Adding an operation One method on the entity One method on the interface and in each state that allows it
Persistence Trivial: store the enum name Store a name and map it back to a state object
Readability The whole machine on one screen Each state's logic in isolation

Most interview problems start with an enum table. Move to the State pattern when the switch (status) blocks start appearing inside several methods; that is the same smell polymorphism removes from types.

Interview signal

Whichever you choose, draw the state diagram first and say "any transition not drawn throws." Then show where the guard for the trickiest rule lives. That is what interviewers check.

7.7Common mistakes

Common mistakes

  • Observers that must succeed together with the change (debiting a wallet), treated as fire-and-forget events.
  • No failure isolation: one listener's exception stops the others, or worse, rolls back the publisher.
  • Synchronous slow listeners that add their latency to every request.
  • Commands that cannot undo because they did not capture the old value at execute time.
  • Forgetting to clear the redo stack after a new command.
  • Status fields assigned from anywhere (order.setStatus(SHIPPED)) instead of through one transition method.
  • Guards checked before legality, so an illegal event fails with a NullPointerException instead of a clear error.
  • The State pattern for three trivial states, or an enum with switch (status) in every method of a complex machine.

7.8Self-check

Self-checkFive more, after the lessons
  1. When should an event listener run after the database transaction commits, and how do you get that in Spring?
    Reveal

    Whenever the reaction has side effects outside the database (emails, messages, cache updates) that must not happen for a rolled-back change. Use @TransactionalEventListener(phase = AFTER_COMMIT).

  2. How would you implement undo for an operation whose inverse is hard to compute?
    Reveal

    Snapshot the affected state before executing (memento) and restore it on undo, or store the command log and rebuild state from the last checkpoint.

  3. Why does the enum state machine use an EnumMap instead of switch statements?
    Reveal

    The table is data: one place shows the whole machine, it can be printed or tested exhaustively, and adding a transition is a line of data rather than a change inside a method's branches.

  4. In the State pattern, why are the interface's default methods written to throw?
    Reveal

    So each state class overrides only the operations it allows, and every other operation is rejected automatically, with no state having to list what it forbids.

  5. Give one advantage of the enum approach for persistence.
    Reveal

    The state is a plain value: store status = 'SHIPPED' in a column and load it back directly. State objects need a mapping from stored name to class.

Smell to pattern drills

Patterns are answers; smells are the questions. This page trains the reverse lookup interviews need: read a design pressure or a piece of code, name what hurts, and pick the smallest pattern that removes the pain. Twelve drills, a picker you can use during practice, and the patterns you only need to recognize.

On this page

  1. From pressure to pattern
  2. Drills: code smells
  3. Patterns to recognize, not reach for
  4. When patterns hurt

From pressure to pattern

Do not start from a list of patterns and look for places to use them. Start from the change you expect, and ask what makes it expensive today:

  1. Name the likely change. "New payment methods", "new vehicle types", "new notification channels", "pricing rules per city".
  2. Find where that change would land. If it lands in many places, or inside a method that works today, there is a pressure.
  3. Pick the smallest fix. Often polymorphism or a strategy is enough. Reach for heavier patterns only when the smaller one fails.
  4. Say the trade-off. Every pattern adds classes; name what you pay and why it is worth it here.
Pattern pickerPick the pressure you feel in the code. The picker names the pattern, its shape, and when it is the wrong tool.
Key idea

A pattern you cannot justify with a specific expected change is decoration. In an interview, one pattern placed exactly where the variation is beats five patterns placed everywhere.

Drills: code smells

Guided designSmell drill AName the smell, then the fix. Answer before revealing.
  1. 1
    A switch on type in several classes
    Java
    // in FeeService, SpotFinder, and ReceiptPrinter
switch (vehicle.getType()) { case CAR: ... case BIKE: ... case TRUCK: ... }
    Write your answer, then reveal

    Smell: the same type switch repeated, so a new type edits three classes. Fix: polymorphism if the behavior belongs to the vehicle (vehicle.spotSize()); strategy plus factory if it is a business policy that varies independently (pricing). See Module 6.

  2. 2
    Status checks at the top of every method
    Java
    void dispense() { if (state != HAS_MONEY) throw ...; ... }
void insertCoin(int c) { if (state == DISPENSING) throw ...; ... }
void cancel() { if (state == IDLE) throw ...; ... }
    Write your answer, then reveal

    Smell: an implicit state machine spread across methods. Fix: an enum transition table with one apply(event) method, or the State pattern when each state has real behavior. See Module 7.

  3. 3
    A constructor nobody can read
    Java
    new Notification(userId, "Order shipped", null, null, true, false, 3, "en")
    Write your answer, then reveal

    Smell: telescoping constructor; the null, true, and false mean nothing at the call site. Fix: a builder with required fields up front and validation in build(). See Module 4.

  4. 4
    Vendor types inside business code
    Java
    StripeIntent intent = stripe.createPaymentIntent(params);
if (intent.getStatus().equals("requires_action")) order.markPending();
    Write your answer, then reveal

    Smell: the order logic depends on one vendor's API and status strings. Fix: an adapter that implements your PaymentGateway and maps vendor statuses to your own result type. See Module 5.

  5. 5
    Copy-pasted retry and logging blocks
    Java
    for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) { try { log...; return gateway.charge(...); } catch (TimeoutException e) { log... } }
// the same block around refund(), payout(), and verify()
    Write your answer, then reveal

    Smell: cross-cutting behavior duplicated around every call. Fix: decorators (RetryingGateway, LoggingGateway) that wrap the interface once. In Spring, an aspect or a resilience library does the same. See Module 5.

  6. 6
    A service that calls five unrelated services after saving
    Java
    orderRepo.save(o); email.send(...); loyalty.add(...); analytics.track(...); crm.sync(...); fraud.score(...);
    Write your answer, then reveal

    Smell: the order service changes whenever a reaction is added, and one failing reaction breaks ordering. Fix: publish an OrderPlaced event; reactions subscribe (observer). Keep only the steps that must succeed with the order inside the service. See Module 7.

Guided designSmell drill BSix more, mixed difficulty
  1. 1
    Three importers with identical loops

    CsvImporter, JsonImporter, and XmlImporter each parse, validate rows, save valid ones, and count rejects, with the same loop copied three times.

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Smell: duplicated algorithm skeleton. Fix: template method with a final run() and abstract parse/save, or one Importer composed from a Parser and a Sink strategy. See Module 6.

  2. 2
    An if-else ladder of validations

    A withdrawal method has eight if blocks (KYC, limits, fraud, blocked account, daily count...), and product wants to reorder and toggle them per country.

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Smell: a growing ladder with ordering and configuration needs. Fix: a chain or pipeline of Check handlers assembled per country. See Module 6.

  3. 3
    instanceof inside a tree walk
    Java
    long size(Object node) { if (node instanceof File f) return f.size(); if (node instanceof Dir d) { ... } }
    Write your answer, then reveal

    Smell: callers type-check every node. Fix: composite: File and Directory share an FsNode interface; directories sum their children. See Module 5.

  4. 4
    A global settings class used everywhere
    Java
    if (Settings.getInstance().isFeatureOn("newPricing")) ...
    Write your answer, then reveal

    Smell: hidden global dependency; tests share and leak state. Fix: inject a FeatureFlags interface through constructors; keep one instance via DI. See Module 4.

  5. 5
    Undo implemented by copying the whole document after every keystroke
    Write your answer, then reveal

    Smell: memory grows with every edit, and redo is awkward. Fix: command objects with execute and undo, two stacks, and a redo stack cleared on new edits; snapshots only for operations that are hard to invert. See Module 7.

  6. 6
    FixedDeposit extends Account and its withdraw throws
    Write your answer, then reveal

    Smell: a Liskov violation: the subtype cannot keep the parent's promise. Fix: model the capability: a Withdrawable interface implemented only by accounts that allow withdrawals. See Module 3.

Patterns to recognize, not reach for

These come up in conversation or in frameworks. Know one sentence and one example for each; build them only when the pressure is clear.

Pattern One sentence Where you have seen it
Iterator Walk a collection without exposing its structure Iterator, enhanced for loops
Visitor Add operations to a closed set of types without editing them Compilers walking syntax trees; Java 21 pattern-matching switch often replaces it
Mediator Objects talk through one coordinator instead of to each other An elevator controller between floors and cars; a chat room
Memento Save and restore an object's state without exposing internals Snapshot-based undo; game save points
Flyweight Share immutable parts of many small objects Integer.valueOf cache for -128 to 127; glyphs in a text editor
Bridge Separate an abstraction from its implementation so both vary JDBC: the API is one hierarchy, each driver is another
Prototype Create objects by copying a configured instance Copy constructors; template documents
Interpreter Represent a small language's grammar as classes Rule engines, expression evaluators

When patterns hurt

Pattern overuse

  • An interface with one implementation and no testing need.
  • A factory that wraps new for a class that never varies.
  • A strategy for a rule with two cases that will never grow.
  • A singleton for convenience, creating global state.
  • Five patterns in a 90-minute machine coding round, with the core flow unfinished.
  • Naming patterns without the reason: "I used the observer pattern" with no mention of what change it absorbs.
Interview signal

The strongest answer in a design discussion often sounds like: "I considered a strategy here, but pricing has two fixed rules and the interviewer said it will not change, so a single method is clearer. If it starts varying, extracting the strategy is a five-minute refactor." Knowing when not to use a pattern is an SDE-2 signal.

Phase 3: Designing real systemsCoreVery high priority

Module 8: From requirements to classes

This is the method you will run in every LLD round and every machine coding round: clarify, find the entities, assign responsibilities, draw the class diagram, define one service method per use case, find the variation points, then handle state, concurrency, and errors. Each step gets a checklist and the traps it avoids, and a library system is worked end to end.

9 lessons4 figures6 mastery checks

On this page

  1. 8.1The method in seven steps
  2. 8.2Clarify requirements
  3. 8.3Find entities and value objects
  4. 8.4Assign responsibilities
  5. 8.5Services, repositories, and layers
  6. 8.6Find the variation points
  7. 8.7Worked example: library
  8. 8.8Common mistakes
  9. 8.9Self-check
Warm-upWarm-up: one line each
  1. "Design a library system." What is the first thing you do?
    Reveal

    Ask questions: who uses it (members, librarians), which 3-5 use cases matter (search, borrow, return, reserve, fines), what is out of scope, and whether it runs in one process or needs concurrency. Write the answers down before drawing anything.

  2. A library has "books". Is a book one class?
    Reveal

    Usually two: a BookTitle (ISBN, title, author: what you search) and a BookCopy (a physical item with a status: what you lend). Confusing the two is the most common modeling bug in this problem.

  3. Where should "calculate the late fine" live?
    Reveal

    The loan knows its due and return dates, so it computes days overdue; the amount comes from a FinePolicy strategy, because fine rules change. The service coordinates; it does not compute.

  4. What is an anemic domain model?
    Reveal

    Entities with only getters and setters, and every rule in services. It duplicates rules and lets invalid states exist. Push rules that use an entity's own data into the entity.

  5. Which words in a requirement suggest a pattern?
    Reveal

    "Different types of" (polymorphism or strategy), "may change" or "configurable" (strategy), "notify" (observer), "status" or "lifecycle" (state machine), "undo" (command), "steps that all requests pass" (chain).

8.1The method in seven steps

Try it first3 minutes

Without looking ahead, write the steps you would follow from "design X" to a class diagram you are confident in. What does each step produce?

Reveal the answer

Compare with the figure. The key properties of any good method: requirements are written down before modeling; the model (entities, responsibilities, relationships) comes before code; each use case maps to a method; and the hard parts (variation, state, concurrency, errors) are handled explicitly rather than discovered while coding.

Idea

A fixed sequence of small decisions, each with a visible output, so the interviewer can follow your thinking and correct you early.

Analogy

A pilot's checklist. Experienced pilots still use it, because skipping a step under time pressure is how things go wrong.

Cost

It feels slow for the first five minutes. It saves the last thirty, which is where unplanned designs collapse.

Step Output you can show Time in a 45-minute round
1. Clarify Written list of actors, use cases, scope, constraints 4-5 min
2. Entities List of nouns that own data, value objects, enums 3 min
3. Responsibilities One line per class: what it knows, what it does 3 min
4. Class diagram Boxes, relationships, multiplicities 8-10 min
5. APIs Service method signatures, one per use case 4 min
6. Variation Interfaces where change is expected 3 min
7. Hard parts State diagram, concurrency answer, error list 8-10 min, then code the core

8.2Clarify requirements

Try it first3 minutes

Write eight questions you would ask after "Design a parking lot."

Reveal the answer

Actors: who interacts (driver, attendant, admin)? Vehicle types and spot sizes? How many floors and gates; can gates run at the same time (concurrency)? How is the fee computed (hourly, flat, per vehicle type), and can it change? Payment in or out of scope? Do we need reservations, EV charging, or a display board of free spots? Is this one process in memory, or do we persist? What should happen when the lot is full?

The checklist, in the order to ask it:

Ask about Why it changes the design
Actors Each actor usually maps to a set of use cases and permissions
Core use cases (3-5) Each becomes a service method; everything else is out of scope
Types and variations "Several vehicle types", "several split types" mark the strategies
Rules that may change Pricing, limits, eligibility: put them behind interfaces
Lifecycle Anything with a status needs a state machine
Concurrency Several gates, users, or threads acting on the same object
Scale and storage In memory vs persisted; one process vs several
Interface CLI commands, method calls, or REST, and expected output format
Out of scope Write it down: payments, auth, UI, notifications
Interview signal

End the clarification with a summary the interviewer can accept or correct: "So: three vehicle types, three spot sizes, multiple gates in parallel, hourly pricing that may change, no reservations, in-memory. I'll design for that." This sentence is worth more than any diagram that follows it.

8.3Find entities and value objects

Try it first3 minutes

From "members borrow books; each book can have several copies; a member can hold at most 5 books for 14 days; late returns are fined 10 rupees per day", list the classes and classify each as entity, value object, enum, or not a class.

Reveal the answer

Entities: Member, BookCopy, Loan. Entity or value object: BookTitle (identified by ISBN, rarely changes; a record works). Enum: CopyStatus. Policy: FinePolicy (strategy). Not classes: "5 books" and "14 days" (configuration values), "rupees" (part of a Money value object or a long in paise), "late" (a computed fact).

Underline the nouns in the requirements, then filter them:

  • Actors outside the system (the driver at the gate) are often not classes, or only an ID.
  • Attributes (color, due date) belong in a class; they are not classes.
  • Values (money, date range, coordinates, a seat number) become immutable value objects or records.
  • Statuses and kinds with no behavior become enums.
  • Synonyms collapse into one class; use the interviewer's word.

The most valuable modeling move is spotting type vs instance pairs:

Problem Type (described, searched) Instance (has state, gets used)
Library BookTitle BookCopy
Movie booking Movie Show, and per show a ShowSeat
E-commerce Product InventoryUnit
Parking SpotType (size) ParkingSpot
Car rental CarModel Car (with a registration number)

8.4Assign responsibilities

Try it first3 minutes

Where should each rule live: (a) "a member can hold at most 5 books"; (b) "a copy that is on loan cannot be lent again"; (c) "fine = 10 rupees per day late, capped at 500"; (d) "borrowing finds any available copy of the title, checks the member, creates a loan".

Reveal the answer

(a) Member.canBorrow(activeLoans): the member knows its limit. (b) BookCopy.lend(): the copy guards its own status. (c) A FinePolicy strategy, fed the days overdue that Loan.daysOverdue(date) computes. (d) LibraryService.checkout: a use case that coordinates several objects belongs in a service.

Three rules decide most placements:

  1. Information expert: give a responsibility to the class that has the information to do it. Due dates are in Loan, so Loan computes days overdue.
  2. Creator: a class creates objects it contains or closely uses. An Order creates its OrderLines; a service creates a Loan because no entity owns loans.
  3. Coordinator: a use case that spans several entities lives in a service method, which asks entities to do their part and never reaches into their fields.
Watch out

Two opposite failures. An anemic model puts every rule in services, so entities are data bags and rules get duplicated. A god entity pulls unrelated rules into one class (Member that also computes fines and searches the catalog). Ask "whose data does this rule read?" and put it there.

8.5Services, repositories, and layers

Try it first2 minutes

In a machine coding round, which kinds of classes do you need besides entities, and which direction should dependencies point?

Reveal the answer

Services (one method per use case), repositories (store and find entities, in memory behind an interface), strategies or policies (the variation points), exceptions, and a driver or demo that calls services. Dependencies point downward: driver to services, services to entities, repositories, and strategies; never the reverse.

Kind Owns Must not
Entity Its data and invariants (lend, close) Call repositories or other services
Value object An immutable value with validation Have identity or setters
Service A use case: load, ask entities, save, publish Hold data between calls (beyond its collaborators)
Repository Storing and finding entities Contain business rules
Strategy / policy One varying rule Know about storage or the driver
Driver Parsing input and printing output Contain business logic

8.6Find the variation points

Try it first2 minutes

Mark the words that suggest a pattern: "Support cars, bikes, and trucks. Pricing is hourly now but will be per-minute on weekends. Notify the owner when parking time exceeds 4 hours. A spot is free, reserved, or occupied."

Reveal the answer

"Cars, bikes, and trucks": polymorphism on vehicle or spot size. "Pricing ... will be per-minute on weekends": a pricing strategy. "Notify the owner when": an observer or event. "Free, reserved, or occupied": a state machine on the spot.

Phrase in the requirement Likely structure
"different types of X", each behaving differently Polymorphism (X subclasses or an interface)
"may change", "configurable", "depends on the region" Strategy (+ factory to pick it)
"notify", "when X happens, also do Y" Observer / events
"status", "can only ... after ...", "cancel" State machine
"undo", "history", "replay", "queue" Command
"every request must pass checks" Chain of responsibility
"wrap", "add logging or retries to" Decorator
"third-party provider", "legacy system" Adapter

Place an interface only where the requirement or the interviewer signals change. Everything else stays concrete.

8.7Worked example: library

Guided designLibrary management in 25 minutesRun the method; answer each step before revealing
  1. 1
    Clarify

    Members borrow and return books; search is by title; a member may hold 5 books for 14 days; late returns cost 10 rupees per day up to 500. What else do you ask, and what do you put out of scope?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Ask: multiple copies per title (yes); reservations when no copy is free (out of scope for now, likely follow-up); librarian actions (adding copies, marking lost); concurrency (two members borrowing the last copy at two desks: yes, mention it); persistence (in memory). Out of scope: payments of fines, notifications, authentication.

  2. 2
    Entities and responsibilities

    List the classes and one line each.

    Write your answer, then reveal

    BookTitle (record: ISBN, title, author). BookCopy (copy ID, ISBN, status; can lend and take back). Member (ID, max loans; decides if it can borrow). Loan (copy, member, due date, return date; closes, computes days overdue). FinePolicy (interface: days to amount). LibraryService (checkout, return). Repositories for copies and loans.

  3. 3
    Class diagram

    Draw it with multiplicities.

    Write your answer, then reveal

    See the figure below. Note that Loan refers to copy and member by ID, and BookTitle to BookCopy is one to many.

  4. 4
    Service APIs

    Write the method signatures for the two use cases.

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Loan checkout(String memberId, String isbn, LocalDate today) and ReturnReceipt returnCopy(String copyId, LocalDate today). Passing today in makes the logic testable without a clock; in production, inject a Clock.

  5. 5
    Hard parts

    What can go wrong, and what changes are likely?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Errors: unknown member, limit reached, no available copy, returning a copy that is not on loan. Concurrency: two checkouts of the last copy; BookCopy.lend() must be atomic (synchronize per copy, or a conditional update in a database). Likely changes: fine rules (already a strategy), reservations (a queue per title, notified when a copy returns: observer), different limits per membership tier (a policy on Member).

Entities guard their own rules
record BookTitle(String isbn, String title, String author) {}       // what you search for

enum CopyStatus { AVAILABLE, ON_LOAN, LOST }

class BookCopy {                                                    // what sits on the shelf
    private final String copyId;
    private final String isbn;
    private CopyStatus status = CopyStatus.AVAILABLE;

    BookCopy(String copyId, String isbn) { this.copyId = copyId; this.isbn = isbn; }

    void lend() {
        if (status != CopyStatus.AVAILABLE) throw new IllegalStateException(copyId + " is " + status);
        status = CopyStatus.ON_LOAN;
    }
    void giveBack() {
        if (status != CopyStatus.ON_LOAN) throw new IllegalStateException(copyId + " is not on loan");
        status = CopyStatus.AVAILABLE;
    }
    String copyId() { return copyId; }
    String isbn() { return isbn; }
    boolean isAvailable() { return status == CopyStatus.AVAILABLE; }
}

class Member {
    private final String id;
    private final int maxLoans;
    Member(String id, int maxLoans) { this.id = id; this.maxLoans = maxLoans; }
    String id() { return id; }
    boolean canBorrow(int activeLoans) { return activeLoans < maxLoans; }   // the member knows its own limit
}

class Loan {
    private final String id;
    private final String copyId;
    private final String memberId;
    private final LocalDate dueOn;
    private LocalDate returnedOn;

    Loan(String id, String copyId, String memberId, LocalDate borrowedOn, int days) {
        this.id = id; this.copyId = copyId; this.memberId = memberId;
        this.dueOn = borrowedOn.plusDays(days);
    }

    void close(LocalDate on) {
        if (returnedOn != null) throw new IllegalStateException("loan " + id + " already closed");
        returnedOn = on;
    }

    long daysOverdue(LocalDate on) {                                   // the loan knows its dates
        return Math.max(0, ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(dueOn, on));
    }

    boolean isActive() { return returnedOn == null; }
    String id() { return id; }
    String copyId() { return copyId; }
    String memberId() { return memberId; }
}
The fine rule is a strategy
interface FinePolicy {
    long finePaise(long daysOverdue);
}

class PerDayFine implements FinePolicy {
    private final long perDayPaise, capPaise;
    PerDayFine(long perDayPaise, long capPaise) { this.perDayPaise = perDayPaise; this.capPaise = capPaise; }
    public long finePaise(long daysOverdue) { return Math.min(capPaise, daysOverdue * perDayPaise); }
}
In-memory repositories with the queries the use cases need
class CopyRepository {
    private final Map<String, BookCopy> byId = new LinkedHashMap<>();   // insertion order: deterministic demos
    void save(BookCopy c) { byId.put(c.copyId(), c); }
    Optional<BookCopy> find(String copyId) { return Optional.ofNullable(byId.get(copyId)); }
    Optional<BookCopy> firstAvailable(String isbn) {
        return byId.values().stream().filter(c -> c.isbn().equals(isbn) && c.isAvailable()).findFirst();
    }
}

class LoanRepository {
    private final Map<String, Loan> byId = new HashMap<>();
    void save(Loan l) { byId.put(l.id(), l); }
    List<Loan> activeFor(String memberId) {
        return byId.values().stream().filter(l -> l.memberId().equals(memberId) && l.isActive()).toList();
    }
    Optional<Loan> activeForCopy(String copyId) {
        return byId.values().stream().filter(l -> l.copyId().equals(copyId) && l.isActive()).findFirst();
    }
}
Each use case is one service method
record ReturnReceipt(String loanId, long finePaise) {}

class LibraryService {
    private static final int LOAN_DAYS = 14;
    private final Map<String, Member> members;
    private final CopyRepository copies;
    private final LoanRepository loans;
    private final FinePolicy fines;
    private final AtomicLong ids = new AtomicLong(1);

    LibraryService(Map<String, Member> members, CopyRepository copies, LoanRepository loans, FinePolicy fines) {
        this.members = members; this.copies = copies; this.loans = loans; this.fines = fines;
    }

    /** Use case: a member borrows any available copy of a title. */
    Loan checkout(String memberId, String isbn, LocalDate today) {
        Member m = members.get(memberId);
        if (m == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("unknown member " + memberId);
        if (!m.canBorrow(loans.activeFor(memberId).size())) throw new IllegalStateException("loan limit reached");
        BookCopy copy = copies.firstAvailable(isbn).orElseThrow(() -> new IllegalStateException("no copy available"));
        copy.lend();                                                   // the copy guards its own state
        Loan loan = new Loan("L" + ids.getAndIncrement(), copy.copyId(), memberId, today, LOAN_DAYS);
        loans.save(loan);
        return loan;
    }

    /** Use case: a copy comes back; close the loan and compute the fine. */
    ReturnReceipt returnCopy(String copyId, LocalDate today) {
        Loan loan = loans.activeForCopy(copyId).orElseThrow(() -> new IllegalStateException("no active loan for " + copyId));
        loan.close(today);
        copies.find(copyId).orElseThrow().giveBack();
        return new ReturnReceipt(loan.id(), fines.finePaise(loan.daysOverdue(today)));
    }
}
Code that ranLibrary.java: the rest of the file, including the main method behind the output below
Library.java (everything not shown above)
class Demo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        CopyRepository copies = new CopyRepository();
        copies.save(new BookCopy("C1", "978-0134685991"));
        copies.save(new BookCopy("C2", "978-0134685991"));
        LibraryService lib = new LibraryService(Map.of("m1", new Member("m1", 2)), copies, new LoanRepository(), new PerDayFine(1_000, 50_000));
        LocalDate d0 = LocalDate.of(2026, 10, 1);
        Loan a = lib.checkout("m1", "978-0134685991", d0);
        Loan b = lib.checkout("m1", "978-0134685991", d0);
        List<String> out = new ArrayList<>(List.of(a.copyId(), b.copyId()));
        try { lib.checkout("m1", "978-0134685991", d0); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { out.add(e.getMessage()); }
        out.add("fine " + lib.returnCopy(a.copyId(), d0.plusDays(20)).finePaise());
        out.add("fine " + lib.returnCopy(b.copyId(), d0.plusDays(10)).finePaise());
        System.out.println(out);
        assert out.get(2).equals("loan limit reached") && out.get(3).equals("fine 6000") && out.get(4).equals("fine 0");
    }
}
Output (from running the code above)
[C1, C2, loan limit reached, fine 6000, fine 0]

8.8Common mistakes

Common mistakes

  • Drawing classes before agreeing on use cases and scope.
  • One class for a type and its instances (Book with a status, so a title with three copies is three books with duplicated metadata).
  • Anemic entities with every rule in a service, or a god entity that does everything.
  • Services that reach into entity fields (copy.status = ON_LOAN) instead of asking (copy.lend()).
  • No service method per use case, so the driver contains business logic.
  • Interfaces on everything instead of on the variation points the requirements name.
  • Using LocalDate.now() inside business logic, making behavior untestable; pass the date or inject a Clock.
  • Forgetting the hard parts (status transitions, concurrent access, invalid input) until the interviewer asks.

8.9Self-check

Self-checkFive more, after the lessons
  1. What does the "information expert" rule say, and where does it put daysOverdue?
    Reveal

    Give a responsibility to the class that holds the information it needs. The loan holds the due date, so Loan.daysOverdue(date) computes it.

  2. Name the type/instance pair in a movie booking system and why it matters.
    Reveal

    Movie (title, runtime) and Show (a screening at a time on a screen), and per show a ShowSeat with its own status. Seat availability belongs to the show, not to the movie or the physical seat.

  3. Why should a service method take today as a parameter or use an injected Clock?
    Reveal

    So tests control time: overdue fines, expiry, and windows can be tested deterministically without waiting or mocking statics.

  4. What should a repository interface contain in a machine coding round?
    Reveal

    save, findById, and only the queries the use cases need (firstAvailable(isbn), activeFor(memberId)), backed by maps. No business rules.

  5. A requirement says "the late fee may differ for premium members." What changes in the library design?
    Reveal

    Nothing structural: a different FinePolicy is chosen per membership tier (a policy factory, or the member exposes its tier and a map picks the policy). Loan and LibraryService do not change.

Tick an item only when it is true with your notes closed.
