Warm-upWarm-up: one line each
  1. A Booking object holds a List<ShowSeat>. How does that list look in tables?
    Reveal

    As rows on the many side pointing back: each show seat row gets a booking_id foreign key. A collection never becomes a column.

  2. Why store prices as integer paise in the database?
    Reveal

    For the same reason as in Java: binary floating point cannot represent 0.1 exactly, so sums drift. Integers in the smallest unit are exact.

  3. SELECT status and then UPDATE ... SET status = 'HELD' as two statements. What can go wrong?
    Reveal

    Check-then-act (Module 9): two requests both read AVAILABLE and both write HELD. Both users are told they have the seat.

  4. Which HTTP method is not idempotent, and what makes retrying it safe?
    Reveal

    POST. An idempotency key sent by the client lets the server recognize a retry and return the first result instead of acting twice.

11.1When the round asks for tables and APIs

They ask They check
"What tables would you have?" Entities and relationships right; keys; money and time types
"How does the database stop double booking?" A constraint or a conditional update, not an application-level check
"Which queries are hot?" Indexes that match those queries, and no more
"What does the API look like?" Resources and verbs, status codes, idempotency, pagination
Interview signal

Answer from the invariants. "The invariant is one booking per seat per show. So show_seats has the primary key (show_id, seat_id), and holding a seat is one conditional update from AVAILABLE to HELD; zero rows changed means someone else got it, and the API answers 409."

11.2From classes to tables

Try it first3 minutes

Map these classes to tables: Movie; Show (movie, screen, start time); Seat (screen, label); Booking (user, show, seats, total). Where does "seat A4 is held for the 7 pm show" live?

Reveal the answer

Tables movies, shows (with movie_id, screen_id), seats (with screen_id), bookings. The hold belongs to neither the seat (it exists for every show) nor the show (it has many seats), so it gets its own table: show_seats, one row per seat per show, with the status, the holder, and the booking.

In the class diagram In tables
Entity with identity A table with a primary key (usually a surrogate id)
Value object (money, interval, address) Columns on the owner's table (price_paise, start_at, end_at)
One-to-many A foreign key on the many side
Many-to-many A join table with a composite primary key, plus fields of the relationship (a grade, a joined date)
Enum A text column with a CHECK listing the values
Inheritance One table with a type column (simplest); a table per subclass when their fields differ a lot
Money Integer minor units, plus a currency column if there is more than one
Time UTC timestamps; convert to local time only for display
booking.sql: the schema (standard SQL, run on SQLite)
CREATE TABLE movies (
  id           INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  title        TEXT    NOT NULL,
  duration_min INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (duration_min > 0)
);

CREATE TABLE screens (
  id         INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  theater_id INTEGER NOT NULL,                    -- theaters table left out
  name       TEXT    NOT NULL,
  UNIQUE (theater_id, name)
);

CREATE TABLE seats (                              -- physical seats: fixed per screen
  id        INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  screen_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES screens (id),
  label     TEXT    NOT NULL,                     -- 'A1'
  type      TEXT    NOT NULL CHECK (type IN ('REGULAR', 'PREMIUM')),
  UNIQUE (screen_id, label)
);

CREATE TABLE shows (
  id        INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  movie_id  INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES movies (id),
  screen_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES screens (id),
  starts_at INTEGER NOT NULL                      -- UTC, epoch seconds
);

CREATE TABLE bookings (
  id              INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id         INTEGER NOT NULL,
  show_id         INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES shows (id),
  total_paise     INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (total_paise >= 0),
  status          TEXT    NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('CONFIRMED', 'CANCELLED')),
  idempotency_key TEXT    NOT NULL,
  created_at      INTEGER NOT NULL,
  UNIQUE (user_id, idempotency_key)               -- a retried request finds the first booking
);

CREATE TABLE show_seats (                         -- one row per seat per show: the unit of contention
  show_id     INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES shows (id),
  seat_id     INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES seats (id),
  price_paise INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (price_paise >= 0),
  status      TEXT    NOT NULL DEFAULT 'AVAILABLE' CHECK (status IN ('AVAILABLE', 'HELD', 'BOOKED')),
  held_by     INTEGER,                            -- user id, only while HELD
  held_until  INTEGER,                            -- epoch seconds, only while HELD
  booking_id  INTEGER REFERENCES bookings (id),   -- only when BOOKED
  PRIMARY KEY (show_id, seat_id),
  CHECK ((status = 'HELD') = (held_by IS NOT NULL AND held_until IS NOT NULL)),
  CHECK ((status = 'BOOKED') = (booking_id IS NOT NULL))
);

CREATE INDEX shows_by_movie_and_time ON shows (movie_id, starts_at);
CREATE INDEX bookings_by_user ON bookings (user_id, created_at);
Key idea

show_seats is the ShowSeat class from P9. The thing two users fight over gets its own row, and that row becomes the unit of locking in the database, exactly as the object was the unit of locking in memory.

11.3Constraints enforce invariants

Try it first2 minutes

Name the database rule for each invariant: (1) a seat label appears once per screen; (2) a seat is booked at most once per show; (3) a HELD seat always has a holder and an expiry; (4) a driver has at most one live trip.

Reveal the answer

(1) UNIQUE (screen_id, label). (2) The primary key (show_id, seat_id): there is exactly one row per seat per show, and its status can only be one value. (3) A CHECK tying the status to the hold columns. (4) A partial unique index on driver_id over rows whose status is ASSIGNED or STARTED.

Application checks are races between instances; a constraint holds no matter how many instances run or what bug ships next. Put each invariant in the strongest place that can hold it.

Invariant Database rule
A field is always present NOT NULL
One per something (username, seat per show) UNIQUE or PRIMARY KEY
Allowed values; fields that go together CHECK
A referenced row exists FOREIGN KEY
One live row per something (live trip, active subscription) Partial unique index: unique over rows matching a WHERE (PostgreSQL, SQLite; MySQL has no partial indexes)
No two ranges overlap (room bookings) Exclusion constraint in PostgreSQL, as in P14
A partial unique index: at most one live trip per driver ([P17](#p17))
CREATE TABLE trips (
  id        INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  driver_id INTEGER NOT NULL,
  rider_id  INTEGER NOT NULL,
  status    TEXT    NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('ASSIGNED', 'STARTED', 'COMPLETED', 'CANCELLED'))
);
-- at most one live trip per driver: a unique index over live rows only
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX one_live_trip_per_driver ON trips (driver_id) WHERE status IN ('ASSIGNED', 'STARTED');
Watch out

A constraint violation is an expected outcome, not a crash. Catch the unique violation and answer 409 Conflict, or return the existing row when it was an idempotent retry. Letting it surface as a 500 tells the client to retry something that will never succeed.

11.4Indexes come from queries

Try it first2 minutes

Write the three most frequent reads of a booking app and the index each needs.

Reveal the answer

Shows of a movie in a date range: (movie_id, starts_at). The seat map of a show: already served by the primary key (show_id, seat_id). A user's bookings, newest first: (user_id, created_at).

  • Write the queries first, from the use cases, then index exactly those.
  • Composite order: equality columns first, then the range or sort column. (movie_id, starts_at) serves WHERE movie_id = ? AND starts_at BETWEEN ? AND ? ORDER BY starts_at; (starts_at, movie_id) serves it badly.
  • Keys are already indexes. A primary key or unique constraint needs no second index.
  • Every index costs writes and space. Do not index columns no query filters or sorts on.
  • Foreign keys are not indexed automatically in PostgreSQL (MySQL's InnoDB does it); index the ones you join or delete by.

11.5Safe writes under concurrency

Try it first3 minutes

Two users press "hold A4" at the same instant. Write SQL that lets exactly one succeed, with no locks in the application.

Reveal the answer

One statement that checks and writes: UPDATE show_seats SET status = 'HELD', ... WHERE show_id = ? AND seat_id = ? AND status = 'AVAILABLE', then read the affected row count. 1: held. 0: someone else has it, answer 409.

Read, then write: the gap between the statements is the race
SELECT status FROM show_seats WHERE show_id = :show AND seat_id = :seat;
-- the application sees 'AVAILABLE', then:
UPDATE show_seats SET status = 'HELD', held_by = :user, held_until = :now + 600
WHERE show_id = :show AND seat_id = :seat;
One statement: check and write together
UPDATE show_seats
SET status = 'HELD', held_by = :user, held_until = :now + 600
WHERE show_id = :show AND seat_id = :seat
  AND (status = 'AVAILABLE' OR (status = 'HELD' AND held_until < :now));   -- an expired hold counts as free
Tool SQL shape Use when
Unique constraint INSERT; catch the violation Creating something that must be one of a kind (a booking per idempotency key, a username)
Conditional update UPDATE ... WHERE status = 'AVAILABLE'; check the row count A state change on one row (hold a seat, accept an order)
Version column UPDATE ... SET version = version + 1 WHERE id = ? AND version = ? Read, compute in the application, write back (Module 9)
Row lock SELECT ... FOR UPDATE in a transaction, then UPDATE Several dependent reads and writes (a transfer between two wallets, locked in ID order)

Several rows that must change together go in one transaction. Holding seats A1 and A2 is all or nothing:

Text
hold(user, show, seats):
  BEGIN
  for each seat, in seat ID order:          -- one order for everyone: no deadlocks
    run the hold UPDATE; 0 rows changed     -> ROLLBACK, answer 409 naming the seat
  COMMIT, answer 201 with the expiry time

confirm(user, show, seats, idempotencyKey):
  a booking with (user, key) exists         -> return it again: this is a retry
  BEGIN
  insert the booking; unique violation      -> ROLLBACK, return the booking a concurrent retry made
  for each seat, in seat ID order:
    run the confirm UPDATE; 0 rows changed  -> ROLLBACK, answer 409: the hold expired
  COMMIT, answer 201 with the booking
Confirm only your own hold, and only before it expires
UPDATE show_seats
SET status = 'BOOKED', booking_id = :booking, held_by = NULL, held_until = NULL
WHERE show_id = :show AND seat_id = :seat
  AND status = 'HELD' AND held_by = :user AND held_until >= :now;
Code that ransqlcheck.py: the test script that ran the SQL above
sqlcheck.py (complete)
a, b = connect(), connect()             # two clients, like two app servers
a.executescript(R["schema"])
a.executescript("""
INSERT INTO movies VALUES (1, 'Interstellar', 169);
INSERT INTO screens VALUES (1, 10, 'Audi 2');
INSERT INTO seats VALUES (1, 1, 'A1', 'REGULAR'), (2, 1, 'A2', 'REGULAR'), (3, 1, 'A3', 'REGULAR'), (4, 1, 'A4', 'PREMIUM');
INSERT INTO shows VALUES (1, 1, 1, 1000000);
INSERT INTO show_seats (show_id, seat_id, price_paise) VALUES (1, 1, 25000), (1, 2, 25000), (1, 3, 25000), (1, 4, 40000);
""")
RAVI, MEERA = 101, 202
LABEL = {1: "A1", 2: "A2", 3: "A3", 4: "A4"}
now = 900_000

# 1. read-then-write: two clients both believe they got seat A4
p = dict(show=1, seat=4, now=now)
ra = a.execute(R["naive_read"], p).fetchone()[0]
rb = b.execute(R["naive_read"], p).fetchone()[0]
if ra == "AVAILABLE":
    a.execute(R["naive_write"], dict(p, user=RAVI))
if rb == "AVAILABLE":
    b.execute(R["naive_write"], dict(p, user=MEERA))
owner = a.execute("SELECT held_by FROM show_seats WHERE show_id = 1 AND seat_id = 4").fetchone()[0]
say(f"read then write: ravi told held, meera told held; A4 is actually held by {'meera' if owner == MEERA else 'ravi'}")
a.execute("UPDATE show_seats SET status = 'AVAILABLE', held_by = NULL, held_until = NULL WHERE seat_id = 4")

# 2. conditional update: the second client gets 0 rows
n1 = a.execute(R["hold"], dict(p, user=RAVI)).rowcount
n2 = b.execute(R["hold"], dict(p, user=MEERA)).rowcount
say(f"conditional update: ravi {n1} row (held), meera {n2} rows (refused, answer 409)")


def hold(conn, user, seats, t):
    conn.execute("BEGIN IMMEDIATE")
    for s in sorted(seats):
        if conn.execute(R["hold"], dict(show=1, seat=s, user=user, now=t)).rowcount != 1:
            conn.execute("ROLLBACK")
            return f"{LABEL[s]} is taken, rolled back"
    conn.execute("COMMIT")
    return "ok"


def confirm(conn, user, seats, key, t):
    found = conn.execute(R["find_booking"], dict(user=user, key=key)).fetchone()
    if found:
        return found[0], "existing"
    total = sum(conn.execute("SELECT price_paise FROM show_seats WHERE show_id = 1 AND seat_id = ?", (s,)).fetchone()[0] for s in seats)
    conn.execute("BEGIN IMMEDIATE")
    try:
        bid = conn.execute(R["insert_booking"], dict(user=user, show=1, total=total, key=key, now=t)).lastrowid
    except sqlite3.IntegrityError:                    # a concurrent retry inserted it first
        conn.execute("ROLLBACK")
        return conn.execute(R["find_booking"], dict(user=user, key=key)).fetchone()[0], "existing"
    for s in sorted(seats):
        if conn.execute(R["confirm_seat"], dict(show=1, seat=s, user=user, booking=bid, now=t)).rowcount != 1:
            conn.execute("ROLLBACK")
            return None, f"rejected, {LABEL[s]} is no longer held by this user; rolled back, no booking"
    conn.execute("COMMIT")
    return bid, "new"


def status(seat):
    return a.execute("SELECT status FROM show_seats WHERE show_id = 1 AND seat_id = ?", (seat,)).fetchone()[0]


say("hold A1, A2 for ravi: " + hold(a, RAVI, [1, 2], now))
say("hold A2, A3 for meera: " + hold(b, MEERA, [2, 3], now) + f"; A3 is still {status(3)}")
later = now + 11 * 60
say("11 minutes later, hold A2, A3 for meera: " + hold(b, MEERA, [2, 3], later) + " (ravi's hold on A2 expired)")
bid, how = confirm(a, RAVI, [1, 2], "k-12", later)
say(f"ravi confirms A1, A2 after 11 minutes (holds last 10): {how}")
bid, how = confirm(b, MEERA, [2, 3], "k-77", later + 30)
say(f"confirm A2, A3 for meera with key k-77: booking {bid} ({how})")
bid2, how2 = confirm(b, MEERA, [2, 3], "k-77", later + 45)
count = a.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM bookings").fetchone()[0]
say(f"retry with key k-77: booking {bid2} ({how2}); bookings table has {count} row")
assert bid2 == bid and count == 1 and status(2) == "BOOKED" and status(3) == "BOOKED"

# 3. a partial unique index: one live trip per driver
a.executescript(R["trips"])
a.execute("INSERT INTO trips VALUES (1, 7, 501, 'ASSIGNED')")
try:
    a.execute("INSERT INTO trips VALUES (2, 7, 502, 'ASSIGNED')")
    say("second live trip for driver 7: accepted (wrong)")
except sqlite3.IntegrityError as e:
    say(f"second live trip for driver 7: rejected ({e})")
a.execute("UPDATE trips SET status = 'COMPLETED' WHERE id = 1")
a.execute("INSERT INTO trips VALUES (3, 7, 503, 'ASSIGNED')")
say("after trip 1 completes, a new trip for driver 7: accepted")

# 4. CHECK constraints catch an inconsistent row
try:
    a.execute("UPDATE show_seats SET status = 'HELD' WHERE show_id = 1 AND seat_id = 3")
    say("HELD without held_by: accepted (wrong)")
except sqlite3.IntegrityError as e:
    say(f"HELD without held_by or held_until: rejected ({e.args[0].split(':')[0]})")
Output: these statements run on SQLite by a small test script playing the application
read then write: ravi told held, meera told held; A4 is actually held by meera
conditional update: ravi 1 row (held), meera 0 rows (refused, answer 409)
hold A1, A2 for ravi: ok
hold A2, A3 for meera: A2 is taken, rolled back; A3 is still AVAILABLE
11 minutes later, hold A2, A3 for meera: ok (ravi's hold on A2 expired)
ravi confirms A1, A2 after 11 minutes (holds last 10): rejected, A1 is no longer held by this user; rolled back, no booking
confirm A2, A3 for meera with key k-77: booking 1 (new)
retry with key k-77: booking 1 (existing); bookings table has 1 row
second live trip for driver 7: rejected (UNIQUE constraint failed: trips.driver_id)
after trip 1 completes, a new trip for driver 7: accepted
HELD without held_by or held_until: rejected (CHECK constraint failed)
In production

SQLite locks the whole database for writes, so the test runs requests one after another. PostgreSQL and MySQL lock rows: the second UPDATE on the same row waits for the first transaction to finish, then re-checks its WHERE against the new row, which gives the same outcome under real concurrency. A read-then-write pair is still a race at PostgreSQL's default isolation level (READ COMMITTED); stricter levels turn some of these races into serialization errors that the application must retry. Expired holds need no cleanup job for correctness: the hold update treats them as free.

11.6REST APIs

Try it first3 minutes

Design endpoints for: list a movie's shows; see a show's seat map; hold seats; confirm a booking; cancel a booking; list my bookings.

Reveal the answer

See the table below. The points that matter: nouns for resources, POST for actions that create or change state, 201 with the new resource, 409 for a state clash, an idempotency key on confirm, and a cursor on the list.

Endpoint Does Success Typical errors
GET /movies/{id}/shows?city=BLR&date=2026-11-02 A movie's shows 200 404 unknown movie
GET /shows/{id}/seats Seat map with status 200 404
POST /shows/{id}/holds with {seatIds} Hold seats for 10 minutes 201 with expiresAt 409 seat taken; 422 more than 10 seats
POST /bookings with {showId, seatIds} and an Idempotency-Key header Confirm held seats after payment 201 with the booking 409 hold expired
POST /bookings/{id}/cancel Cancel; the row stays as CANCELLED 200 403 not yours; 409 too late
GET /users/me/bookings?limit=20&cursor=... My bookings, newest first 200 with nextCursor 401
Code Meaning Example
200 OK Success with a body Seat map
201 Created A new resource, with its ID Booking confirmed
204 No Content Success, nothing to return A saved card deleted
400 Bad Request Malformed request seatIds missing
401 Unauthorized Not authenticated No token or an expired one
403 Forbidden Authenticated but not allowed Cancelling someone else's booking
404 Not Found No such resource (or hidden from this caller) Unknown show
409 Conflict Clashes with the current state Seat already held
412 Precondition Failed The If-Match version is stale Saving an outdated edit
422 Unprocessable Content Well formed, but breaks a rule 11 seats when the limit is 10
429 Too Many Requests Rate limited; send Retry-After P6
500, 503 Server fault; temporarily unavailable The client retries with backoff

Idempotency keys

  • GET, PUT, and DELETE are idempotent by definition; POST is not. Any POST that creates something or moves money takes an Idempotency-Key header, generated by the client (a UUID) once per user action and reused on every retry.
  • The server stores the key with the user, a fingerprint of the request, and the response. Same key and same request: return the stored response. Same key, different request: an error (the IETF draft suggests 422). Same key while the first request is still running: 409.
  • A UNIQUE (user_id, idempotency_key) constraint makes two concurrent retries safe: only one insert can win.
  • Keys are kept for a bounded time; Stripe, for example, may prune a key once it is at least 24 hours old.

Pagination and concurrent edits

Offset: ?page=3&size=20 Cursor: ?limit=20&cursor=...
Good Simple; can jump to any page Stable while rows are added; fast at any depth
Bad New rows shift pages, so items repeat or are skipped; deep pages scan and discard rows Cannot jump to page 50
Query ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20 OFFSET 40 WHERE (created_at, id) < (?, ?) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20

The cursor is the last row's (created_at, id), encoded so clients treat it as opaque. For edits that may collide (two admins editing one show), use the version column over HTTP: GET returns ETag: "7", the client sends If-Match: "7" with its PUT, and the server answers 412 if the version moved on.

Note

Conventions that read well in an interview: plural nouns (/bookings), actions as sub-resources when they are not plain updates (/bookings/{id}/cancel), a version in the path (/v1), one error shape everywhere ({"code": "SEAT_TAKEN", "message": ..., "details": ...}), money as integer minor units with a currency, and timestamps in ISO 8601 UTC.

11.7Common mistakes

Common mistakes

  • A status column on seats: the seat exists for every show, so its status cannot live there.
  • Double booking prevented only in application code, which breaks with two instances.
  • Read, then write where one conditional UPDATE would do.
  • Not checking the affected row count, so a refused update looks like success.
  • Unique violations surfacing as 500s instead of 409 or the existing row.
  • Indexes on every column, or composite indexes with the range column first.
  • POST endpoints that charge or book without an idempotency key.
  • Offset pagination on a feed that changes while the user scrolls.
  • Floating-point money and local-time timestamps in the schema.

11.8Self-check

Self-checkFive more, after the lessons
  1. Why is show_seats keyed by (show_id, seat_id) rather than having its own id?
    Reveal

    The pair is the natural identity: there must be exactly one row per seat per show. Making it the primary key enforces that and gives the seat-map query its index for free. A surrogate id would still need a unique constraint on the pair.

  2. The hold UPDATE returned 0 rows. What are the possible reasons, and what does the API answer?
    Reveal

    The seat is held by someone else (not expired), or already booked, or the show or seat does not exist. Answer 409 for the first two; check existence first or separately to answer 404 for the last.

  3. Why hold seats in seat ID order inside the transaction?
    Reveal

    Two requests for overlapping seats in opposite orders could each lock one row and wait for the other: a deadlock. One global order removes the cycle, as with wallets in Module 9.

  4. When would you choose SELECT ... FOR UPDATE over a conditional update?
    Reveal

    When the decision needs several reads and the write depends on them, such as a transfer that checks a balance, a daily limit, and the target's cap before writing both rows. A single-row state change is simpler and faster as a conditional update.

  5. Why does a cursor stay correct when new bookings arrive and an offset does not?
    Reveal

    The cursor says "rows older than this one", which does not move when new rows are added at the top. An offset says "skip 40 rows", and new rows push older ones down, so the next page repeats items.

Mastery checklist

Tick an item only when it is true with your notes closed.

Scoping drills: from a one-line prompt to a design

Real prompts are often one line: "Design Uber", "Design a payment system". In an LLD round, that is an invitation to scope: pick the part with interesting objects and rules, find what two users can fight over, say what you leave out, and get agreement within five minutes. This page gives the method and eight drills. Cover each answer, scope the prompt yourself in five minutes, then compare.

On this page

  1. The five-minute method
  2. Drills

The five-minute method

  1. Say the frame out loud. "In this round I will model the core of one service, in one process. Scaling and the distributed parts are a system design conversation; I can note where they would change things."
  2. Find the core loop: the one flow the product exists for (get a ride, get food, sell a seat, move money).
  3. Find the contended resource: what two users or threads could fight over (a driver, a seat, a balance, a stock count). This is where SDE-2 depth shows, so pick a scope that contains one.
  4. Pick three use cases to build and name three to skip. Skipping out loud is a strength: it shows you know what is big.
  5. Name the variation points the interviewer is likely to push: pricing, matching, notification channels, payment methods.
  6. Confirm. "I will build request, match, and complete, with driver assignment under concurrency as the focus. Does that match what you want?"
The interviewer says They want
"Which classes?", "Write the code for...", "How would you add X?" LLD: objects, rules, code
"How many servers?", "100 million users", "Which database and why?" System design: components, data flow, scale
Just "Design X" Ask: "Should I focus on the object model of one service, or on the overall architecture?"
Interview signal

Interviewers score scoping without saying so. A candidate who asks two sharp questions, names the contended resource, and proposes a scope in five minutes has shown more seniority than one who lists twenty features.

Drills

Uber

Try it first5 minutes

Design Uber. Core loop, contended resource, three use cases to build, three to skip, variation points.

Reveal the answer
  • Ask: one city or many? Vehicle types? Can the rider cancel, and until when? Is surge in scope?
  • Core loop: a rider requests; the nearest free driver is assigned; the driver starts and completes; a fare is charged.
  • Contended resource: the driver. Two requests must never get the same one.
  • Build: request and match; start and complete with the fare; rider cancellation that frees the driver.
  • Skip: maps, routing, and ETA; payments; ratings.
  • Variation points: matching strategy, pricing and surge, vehicle types.
  • Worked: P17.

Swiggy

Try it first5 minutes

Design Swiggy (or Zomato).

Reveal the answer
  • Ask: who can cancel, and until when? Is partner assignment automatic? Are coupons in scope?
  • Core loop: place an order; the restaurant accepts and prepares; a partner picks up and delivers.
  • Contended resource: the delivery partner (two orders, one partner), and the order's status (accept racing cancel).
  • Build: the order state machine with the actor allowed for each move; partner assignment; cancellation with refunds by status.
  • Skip: search and menus, live tracking, payments, ratings.
  • Variation points: assignment strategy, cancellation policy, notification channels.
  • Worked: P15.

BookMyShow

Try it first5 minutes

Design BookMyShow.

Reveal the answer
  • Ask: hold seats before payment, and for how long? Several seats at once? What happens if payment fails?
  • Core loop: pick a show, pick seats, hold them, pay, confirm.
  • Contended resource: a seat for one show.
  • Build: the seat map; holding several seats all or nothing with expiry; confirming a hold.
  • Skip: search, reviews, real payments, offers.
  • Variation points: pricing by seat type and day, payment methods.
  • Worked: P9, with tables and an API in Module 11.

A payment system

Try it first5 minutes

Design a payment system (a wallet, as at Paytm or PhonePe).

Reveal the answer
  • Ask: wallet to wallet only, or also bank top-ups and withdrawals? Balance limits? What does the client do on a timeout?
  • Core loop: top up, transfer, see history.
  • Contended resource: balances, with transfers touching two of them.
  • Build: transfers with ordered locking and both ledger rows; idempotency keys; top-up callbacks that may repeat.
  • Skip: card networks, fraud checks, KYC, settlement with banks.
  • Variation points: fee rules, limits per account type, notifications.
  • Worked: P10. If the interviewer means card processing at Stripe's level, that is a system design question; say so and ask.

Facebook

Try it first5 minutes

Design Facebook.

Reveal the answer
  • Ask: which part: posts and the news feed, friend requests, or messaging? (Pick the feed unless told otherwise.)
  • Core loop: a user posts; followers see it in their feed, newest first.
  • Contended resource: less about locks than about work: building a feed by merging the latest posts of everyone followed (a heap merge of k sorted lists), and counters such as likes updated by many users at once.
  • Build: post, follow and unfollow, get the feed with a cursor; likes with an atomic counter.
  • Skip: ranking models, media, comments threads, notifications.
  • Variation points: feed ranking strategy; building feeds when posting (fan-out on write) or when reading (fan-out on read).
  • Practice prompt: social network news feed in the tracker.

Amazon

Try it first5 minutes

Design Amazon.

Reveal the answer
  • Ask: browsing, cart, checkout, or delivery? (Pick cart and checkout.) Is stock reserved at add-to-cart or at checkout?
  • Core loop: add to cart, check out, reserve stock, pay, create the order.
  • Contended resource: the stock count of a product, especially in a flash sale.
  • Build: cart with a pricing pipeline (discount rules); checkout that reserves stock atomically with expiry; order creation with an idempotency key.
  • Skip: search, recommendations, shipping, returns, sellers.
  • Variation points: discount rules, payment methods, reservation timing.
  • Practice prompts: shopping cart and checkout, coupon engine, inventory reservation in the tracker.

WhatsApp

Try it first5 minutes

Design WhatsApp.

Reveal the answer
  • Ask: one-to-one and groups? Delivery and read receipts? Offline users?
  • Core loop: send a message to a chat; members receive it in order; ticks change from sent to delivered to read.
  • Contended resource: the order of messages in one chat; give each chat its own sequence number, assigned atomically.
  • Build: chats and members; send with per-chat sequence numbers; a receipt state machine per message and member; fetching messages after a sequence number for a reconnecting user.
  • Skip: networking, encryption, media, calls.
  • Variation points: delivery channels (online push or offline notification), group permissions.
  • Related: the queue and offsets in P11.

Airbnb

Try it first5 minutes

Design Airbnb.

Reveal the answer
  • Ask: host and guest flows, or booking only? Instant booking or host approval? Cancellation policies?
  • Core loop: search dates, hold a listing, pay, confirm.
  • Contended resource: a listing for a night; a stay of several nights must hold all of them or none.
  • Build: availability per listing per night; booking a date range all or nothing; cancellation policy as a strategy.
  • Skip: search ranking, messaging, reviews, payouts to hosts.
  • Variation points: pricing by night and season, cancellation policies.
  • Related: P14 for date ranges, P9 for holds; hotel booking in the tracker.
Note

Practice this out loud, against a timer, on prompts you have not seen. The timer on the playbook page has a five-minute setting worth using for exactly this.

Problem 1: Parking lot

The most asked LLD problem, and the reference for how a complete solution looks: every file of a working, concurrent, extensible parking lot in plain Java, organized the way Module 10 recommends. Learn this one thoroughly; most other problems reuse its shape.

Uses: M8 method, M6 strategy, M9 locks
Your status

On this page

  2. P1.2Entities and responsibilities

Try it first60 minutes on paper, or 90 minutes in an IDE

Design a parking lot with multiple floors, spots of different sizes, several vehicle types, entry and exit gates that work at the same time, tickets, and hourly pricing that may change. Then compare with this page section by section.

Reveal the answer

A strong answer covers: clarified scope (vehicle and spot types, fit rules, gates in parallel, pricing changes); entities Vehicle, ParkingSpot, Ticket, Receipt, enums for types and sizes; a ParkingLot service with park, unpark, and freeSpots; a spot allocation strategy and a pricing strategy behind interfaces; atomic spot occupation (check and act under the spot's lock); a ticket that can close only once; clear exceptions for a full lot, an unknown ticket, and a vehicle that is already inside; and a plan for extensions (free lists for O(1) allocation, reservations, EV spots, display board events).

P1.1Requirements

Clarifying questions and the answers assumed here:

Question Assumed answer
Vehicle types? Motorcycle, car, truck
Spot sizes and fit rules? Small, medium, large. Motorcycles fit any, cars fit medium or large, trucks fit large only
Floors? Several; prefer lower floors
Gates? Several entry and exit gates running at the same time
Pricing? Hourly by vehicle type; any started hour is charged; rules will change
Payment, reservations, EV charging? Out of scope now; likely follow-ups
Storage? In memory, one process

Functional: park a vehicle and get a ticket; exit with a ticket and get a receipt with the fee; show free spots per size; reject a vehicle when no spot fits.

Rules that must always hold: a spot holds at most one vehicle; a vehicle is parked at most once; a ticket is closed (paid) at most once.

P1.2Entities and responsibilities

Class Knows Does
Vehicle (record) Number, type Validates itself
SpotSize, VehicleType (enums) Constants SpotSize.fitting(type): which sizes a type can use
ParkingSpot ID, floor, size, occupant tryOccupy atomically, release
Ticket Vehicle, spot, entry and exit time close once, returning the duration
Receipt (record) Ticket, spot, minutes, fee Nothing: a result value
SpotAllocationStrategy Preference order Ranks candidate spots for a vehicle
PricingStrategy Rates Fee for a type and duration
TicketRepository Tickets by ID Save, find
ParkingLot (service) Spots, strategies, active vehicles park, unpark, freeSpots

Two placement decisions worth saying out loud: the spot guards "one vehicle per spot" because it owns the occupant; the ticket guards "close once" because it owns the exit time. The service coordinates and never assigns fields directly.

P1.3Class diagram

P1.4Key flows

P1.5Code

The complete solution, in the Module 10 layout. Every file below compiles and the demo runs.

model/ParkingSpot.java
public class ParkingSpot {
    private final String id;
    private final int floor;
    private final SpotSize size;
    private Vehicle occupant;                    // guarded by this

    public ParkingSpot(String id, int floor, SpotSize size) {
        this.id = id;
        this.floor = floor;
        this.size = size;
    }

    /** Check and occupy in one atomic step; false if someone else got here first. */
    public synchronized boolean tryOccupy(Vehicle v) {
        if (occupant != null) return false;
        occupant = v;
        return true;
    }

    public synchronized void release() {
        if (occupant == null) throw new IllegalStateException("spot " + id + " is already free");
        occupant = null;
    }

    public synchronized boolean isFree() { return occupant == null; }
    public String id() { return id; }
    public int floor() { return floor; }
    public SpotSize size() { return size; }
}
model/Ticket.java
import java.time.Duration;
import java.time.Instant;

public class Ticket {
    private final String id;
    private final Vehicle vehicle;
    private final ParkingSpot spot;
    private final Instant entryTime;
    private Instant exitTime;                    // guarded by this

    public Ticket(String id, Vehicle vehicle, ParkingSpot spot, Instant entryTime) {
        this.id = id;
        this.vehicle = vehicle;
        this.spot = spot;
        this.entryTime = entryTime;
    }

    /** Close once; a second close (double exit, double payment) is rejected. */
    public synchronized Duration close(Instant at) {
        if (exitTime != null) throw new IllegalStateException("ticket " + id + " already closed");
        if (at.isBefore(entryTime)) throw new IllegalArgumentException("exit before entry");
        exitTime = at;
        return Duration.between(entryTime, at);
    }

    public String id() { return id; }
    public Vehicle vehicle() { return vehicle; }
    public ParkingSpot spot() { return spot; }
    public Instant entryTime() { return entryTime; }
}
model/SpotSize.java
import java.util.List;

public enum SpotSize {
    SMALL, MEDIUM, LARGE;          // declared smallest first: ordinal order is size order

    /** Sizes a vehicle type can use, smallest first. */
    public static List<SpotSize> fitting(VehicleType type) {
        return switch (type) {
            case MOTORCYCLE -> List.of(SMALL, MEDIUM, LARGE);
            case CAR -> List.of(MEDIUM, LARGE);
            case TRUCK -> List.of(LARGE);
        };
    }
}
strategy/SpotAllocationStrategy.java
import java.util.List;
import parkinglot.model.ParkingSpot;
import parkinglot.model.Vehicle;

/** Decides the order in which free spots are tried. The lot does the atomic occupy. */
public interface SpotAllocationStrategy {
    List<ParkingSpot> candidates(List<ParkingSpot> spots, Vehicle vehicle);
}
strategy/BestFitLowestFloor.java
import java.util.Comparator;
import java.util.List;
import parkinglot.model.ParkingSpot;
import parkinglot.model.SpotSize;
import parkinglot.model.Vehicle;

/** Smallest spot that fits first (keeps large spots for trucks), then the lowest floor. */
public class BestFitLowestFloor implements SpotAllocationStrategy {
    @Override
    public List<ParkingSpot> candidates(List<ParkingSpot> spots, Vehicle vehicle) {
        List<SpotSize> fitting = SpotSize.fitting(vehicle.type());
        return spots.stream()
                .filter(s -> fitting.contains(s.size()) && s.isFree())
                .sorted(Comparator.comparing(ParkingSpot::size).thenComparingInt(ParkingSpot::floor))
                .toList();
    }
}
strategy/HourlyPricing.java
import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.EnumMap;
import java.util.Map;
import parkinglot.model.VehicleType;

/** Per-hour rate by vehicle type; any started hour is charged; minimum one hour. */
public class HourlyPricing implements PricingStrategy {
    private final Map<VehicleType, Long> ratePaise = new EnumMap<>(VehicleType.class);

    public HourlyPricing(long motorcycle, long car, long truck) {
        ratePaise.put(VehicleType.MOTORCYCLE, motorcycle);
        ratePaise.put(VehicleType.CAR, car);
        ratePaise.put(VehicleType.TRUCK, truck);
    }

    @Override
    public long feePaise(VehicleType type, Duration parked) {
        long seconds = parked.getSeconds();
        long hours = Math.max(1, (seconds + 3_599) / 3_600);   // ceiling: 60 min 1 s is two hours
        return hours * ratePaise.get(type);
    }
}
service/ParkingLot.java
import java.time.Duration;
import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.EnumMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong;
import parkinglot.exception.AlreadyParkedException;
import parkinglot.exception.ParkingFullException;
import parkinglot.exception.TicketNotFoundException;
import parkinglot.model.ParkingSpot;
import parkinglot.model.Receipt;
import parkinglot.model.SpotSize;
import parkinglot.model.Ticket;
import parkinglot.model.Vehicle;
import parkinglot.repository.TicketRepository;
import parkinglot.strategy.PricingStrategy;
import parkinglot.strategy.SpotAllocationStrategy;

public class ParkingLot {
    private static final String PENDING = "pending";

    private final List<ParkingSpot> spots;
    private final SpotAllocationStrategy allocation;
    private final PricingStrategy pricing;
    private final TicketRepository tickets;
    private final Map<String, String> activeByVehicle = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();   // number -> ticket id
    private final AtomicLong ticketSeq = new AtomicLong(1);

    public ParkingLot(List<ParkingSpot> spots, SpotAllocationStrategy allocation,
                      PricingStrategy pricing, TicketRepository tickets) {
        this.spots = List.copyOf(spots);
        this.allocation = allocation;
        this.pricing = pricing;
        this.tickets = tickets;
    }

    /** Entry gate: assigns a spot and issues a ticket. Safe to call from many gates at once. */
    public Ticket park(Vehicle v, Instant at) {
        if (activeByVehicle.putIfAbsent(v.number(), PENDING) != null) {   // claim the vehicle first
            throw new AlreadyParkedException(v.number());
        }
        try {
            for (ParkingSpot spot : allocation.candidates(spots, v)) {
                if (spot.tryOccupy(v)) {                                   // atomic per spot
                    try {
                        Ticket t = new Ticket("T" + ticketSeq.getAndIncrement(), v, spot, at);
                        tickets.save(t);
                        activeByVehicle.put(v.number(), t.id());
                        return t;
                    } catch (RuntimeException e) {
                        spot.release();                                    // never leave a spot taken without a ticket
                        throw e;
                    }
                }
            }
            throw new ParkingFullException(v.number());
        } catch (RuntimeException e) {
            activeByVehicle.remove(v.number(), PENDING);                  // undo the claim on any failure
            throw e;
        }
    }

    /** Exit gate: closes the ticket once, computes the fee, frees the spot. */
    public Receipt unpark(String ticketId, Instant at) {
        Ticket t = tickets.findById(ticketId).orElseThrow(() -> new TicketNotFoundException(ticketId));
        Duration parked = t.close(at);                                     // throws on a second exit
        long fee = pricing.feePaise(t.vehicle().type(), parked);
        t.spot().release();
        activeByVehicle.remove(t.vehicle().number());
        return new Receipt(t.id(), t.spot().id(), parked.toMinutes(), fee);
    }

    /** Display board: free spots per size. */
    public Map<SpotSize, Long> freeSpots() {
        Map<SpotSize, Long> free = new EnumMap<>(SpotSize.class);
        for (SpotSize s : SpotSize.values()) free.put(s, 0L);
        for (ParkingSpot s : spots) if (s.isFree()) free.merge(s.size(), 1L, Long::sum);
        return free;
    }
}

repository/InMemoryTicketRepository.java
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Optional;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;
import parkinglot.model.Ticket;

public class InMemoryTicketRepository implements TicketRepository {
    private final Map<String, Ticket> tickets = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    @Override public void save(Ticket t) { tickets.put(t.id(), t); }
    @Override public Optional<Ticket> findById(String id) { return Optional.ofNullable(tickets.get(id)); }
}

public class Demo {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        List<ParkingSpot> spots = List.of(
                new ParkingSpot("F1-S1", 1, SpotSize.SMALL),
                new ParkingSpot("F1-M1", 1, SpotSize.MEDIUM),
                new ParkingSpot("F2-M1", 2, SpotSize.MEDIUM),
                new ParkingSpot("F2-L1", 2, SpotSize.LARGE));
        ParkingLot lot = new ParkingLot(spots, new BestFitLowestFloor(),
                new HourlyPricing(1_000, 4_000, 10_000), new InMemoryTicketRepository());
        Instant t0 = Instant.parse("2026-10-21T09:00:00Z");
        Ticket bike = lot.park(new Vehicle("KA01-B-1", VehicleType.MOTORCYCLE), t0);
        Ticket car = lot.park(new Vehicle("KA01-C-1", VehicleType.CAR), t0);
        Ticket truck = lot.park(new Vehicle("KA01-T-1", VehicleType.TRUCK), t0);
        System.out.println(bike.spot().id() + " " + car.spot().id() + " " + truck.spot().id());
        System.out.println("free: " + lot.freeSpots());
        try {
            lot.park(new Vehicle("KA02-T-2", VehicleType.TRUCK), t0);
        } catch (ParkingException e) {
            System.out.println("rejected: " + e.getMessage());
        }
        Receipt r = lot.unpark(car.id(), t0.plusSeconds(150 * 60));      // 2h30m -> 3 hours
        System.out.println("car paid " + r.feePaise() / 100 + " rupees for " + r.minutes() + " minutes");
        try {
            lot.unpark(car.id(), t0.plusSeconds(160 * 60));
        } catch (IllegalStateException e) {
            System.out.println("rejected: " + e.getMessage());
        }
        check(r.feePaise() == 12_000, "fee");
        check(new HourlyPricing(1_000, 4_000, 10_000).feePaise(VehicleType.CAR, java.time.Duration.ofSeconds(3_601)) == 8_000, "started hour");
        check(lot.freeSpots().get(SpotSize.MEDIUM) == 2, "free medium");

        // 8 gates, 400 cars, 1,000 medium spots on a fresh lot: no spot is ever given twice
        List<ParkingSpot> big = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) big.add(new ParkingSpot("M" + i, i / 100, SpotSize.MEDIUM));
        ParkingLot busy = new ParkingLot(big, new BestFitLowestFloor(), new HourlyPricing(1, 1, 1), new InMemoryTicketRepository());
        Set<String> used = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet();
        ExecutorService gates = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8);
        for (int g = 0; g < 8; g++) {
            int gate = g;
            gates.submit(() -> {
                for (int i = 0; i < 50; i++) {
                    Ticket t = busy.park(new Vehicle("G" + gate + "-" + i, VehicleType.CAR), t0);
                    check(used.add(t.spot().id()), "spot given twice: " + t.spot().id());
                }
            });
        }
        gates.shutdown();
        check(gates.awaitTermination(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS), "gates finished");
        System.out.println("concurrent gates: " + used.size() + " cars, " + used.size() + " distinct spots");
        check(used.size() == 400, "400 parked");
    }

    static void check(boolean ok, String what) { if (!ok) throw new AssertionError(what); }
}

P1.6Concurrency

Three races, each closed at the smallest scope that covers it:

Race Where it is closed How
Two gates take the same spot ParkingSpot.tryOccupy Check and set the occupant under the spot's lock; the loser moves to the next candidate
The same vehicle enters twice ParkingLot.park activeByVehicle.putIfAbsent claims the number before allocating; undone on failure
A ticket is paid twice Ticket.close Synchronized; a second close throws

The candidate list can be stale by the time a gate tries a spot: another gate may have taken it. That is fine, because tryOccupy re-checks under the lock and returns false. Stale reads are acceptable when the final write is atomic and re-checks. That one sentence answers most concurrency follow-ups on this problem.

In production

With several servers, in-process locks stop working. The spot table becomes the arbiter: UPDATE spot SET vehicle = ? WHERE id = ? AND vehicle IS NULL, accepting the spot only if one row changed, and a unique index on the active vehicle number to prevent double entry.

P1.7Deep dives

Guided designExtensions interviewers ask forAnswer each before revealing
  1. 1
    Find a free spot in O(1)

    The strategy scans and sorts all spots on every entry. The lot has 10,000 spots. How do you make allocation constant time?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Keep a free list per size (and per floor if floor preference matters): a ConcurrentLinkedDeque<ParkingSpot> per SpotSize. park polls from the smallest fitting size's deque; unpark offers the spot back. Polling is atomic, so two gates never receive the same spot, and the scan disappears. The strategy then chooses which deque to poll, not which spot.

  2. 2
    Weekend pricing and a free first 30 minutes

    How do these land in the design?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    New PricingStrategy implementations, composed: FreeGracePeriod(30 min, inner) wraps another strategy (a decorator), and WeekendPricing chooses rates by the entry day. Wiring changes; ParkingLot does not. If the rule depends on the entry time, pass the ticket's entry time to the strategy instead of only the duration.

  3. 3
    EV charging spots

    Some spots have chargers, and EVs should prefer them.

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Add a capability to the spot (Set<Feature> features with EV_CHARGER) and a vehicle attribute (electric). A new allocation strategy (or a filter before the default one) puts charger spots first for EVs and last for others, so non-EVs do not block chargers. Pricing may add a charging fee through another strategy.

  4. 4
    A display board at each entrance

    The board shows free spots per size and must update when vehicles enter and leave.

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Publish VehicleParked and VehicleLeft events (observer); each board subscribes and keeps its own counts, or reads freeSpots() on each event. Updating boards must not slow down the gate, so deliver events asynchronously or keep the board update trivially cheap.

  5. 5
    Pay before you leave

    Exit should open only after a successful payment, with several payment methods.

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Give the ticket a lifecycle: ACTIVE, then PAID (after payment succeeds), then EXITED (at the exit gate, within 15 minutes of payment). unpark splits into pay(ticketId, method) and exit(ticketId). Payment methods sit behind a PaymentGateway interface with an adapter per provider, and payment uses an idempotency key so a retried request never charges twice.

  6. 6
    Reservations

    Users can reserve a spot for a time window.

    Write your answer, then reveal

    The spot gains a RESERVED state with an expiry (a state machine: FREE, RESERVED, OCCUPIED). Allocation skips reserved spots unless the vehicle holds that reservation, and a sweeper (or a lazy check on read) releases expired reservations. Reservations need their own entity and repository.

If time is short, cut in this order: the concurrency test (describe it instead), freeSpots, then floor preference. Never cut the full-lot error or the double-exit check.

P1.9What a strong answer shows

  • SDE-2 bar: correct fit rules; strategies only where variation is stated; atomic spot occupation explained with the race; tickets that close once; clean exceptions; running code.
  • Above the bar: separates "which spot" (strategy) from "claim the spot" (atomic lot logic); proposes free lists for O(1); explains stale reads with atomic re-checks; says how locking moves to the database with several servers.
Follow-up questionsPractice saying the answer out loud
  1. Why does the allocation strategy return candidates instead of occupying a spot itself?
    Reveal

    So the policy (which spot is preferable) stays separate from the concurrency rule (claim atomically). Any new strategy is automatically thread-safe because the lot does the claiming.

  2. What happens if a gate crashes after tryOccupy succeeds but before the ticket is saved?
    Reveal

    In memory, the process is gone anyway. With a database, occupy the spot and insert the ticket in one transaction, so both happen or neither does.

  3. Should Ticket compute its own fee?
    Reveal

    It could compute the duration, which it owns, but the fee depends on pricing rules that change independently, so a pricing strategy computes it from the duration and vehicle type.

  4. How would you support a truck occupying two adjacent large spots?
    Reveal

    Allocation must claim several spots atomically: find adjacent free spots, then occupy them in a fixed order (by spot ID) under their locks, releasing any already taken if one fails. The ticket then holds a list of spots.

Problem 2: Vending machine

The canonical State pattern problem. The machine behaves differently for the same button depending on whether money is inside, and the subtle parts are money: escrow until the sale is certain, change that may be impossible to make, and committing every effect together or none at all.

Uses: M7 state pattern, M7 enum or State, M1 value objects

Try it first45 minutes

Design a vending machine that accepts coins and notes, sells products from slots, returns change, supports cancel, and can be put into maintenance. Then compare.

Reveal the answer

A strong answer: states Idle, HasMoney, Maintenance with a diagram and illegal actions rejected; inserted money held in escrow until a sale succeeds; selection checks product, stock, amount, and whether change can be made before changing anything; change planning that does not rely on greedy luck; cancel refunds escrow; and a single place where a sale commits stock, cash, and escrow together.

P2.1Requirements

Question Assumed answer
Money accepted? Coins of 1, 2, 5, 10 rupees; notes of 20, 50, 100
Products? Slots with a code, a product, a price, and a count
Change? From the cash box, which has limited coins; refuse a sale it cannot change
Cancel? Returns exactly the money inserted for this purchase
Admin? Maintenance mode to refill; customers cannot use the machine meanwhile
Concurrency? One customer at a time per machine

Invariants: money inserted for a purchase is either returned or kept with a dispensed product, never lost; stock never goes negative; the cash box never pays out coins it does not have.

P2.2Entities and responsibilities

Class Responsibility

Product (record) Code, name, price
Inventory Products and counts per code; take fails when sold out
CashBox Coin counts; plans change for an amount or reports that it cannot
VendingState Idle, HasMoney, Maintenance: which actions are allowed and what they do
VendingMachine Holds the state and escrow; delegates actions to the state; commits a sale
Sale (record) The product and the change given

P2.5Code

VendingState.java: states as constants with default rejections
interface VendingState {
    default void insert(VendingMachine m, Denomination d) { throw new VendingException(name() + ": cannot accept money"); }
    default Sale select(VendingMachine m, String code) { throw new VendingException(name() + ": insert money first"); }
    default List<Denomination> cancel(VendingMachine m) { return List.of(); }
    String name();

    VendingState IDLE = new VendingState() {
        public void insert(VendingMachine m, Denomination d) {
            m.escrow(d);
            m.moveTo(HAS_MONEY);
        }
        public String name() { return "Idle"; }
    };

    VendingState HAS_MONEY = new VendingState() {
        public void insert(VendingMachine m, Denomination d) { m.escrow(d); }
        public Sale select(VendingMachine m, String code) {
            Sale s = m.sell(code);              // throws, and stays in HAS_MONEY, if it cannot sell
            m.moveTo(IDLE);
            return s;
        }
        public List<Denomination> cancel(VendingMachine m) {
            List<Denomination> refund = m.refundEscrow();
            m.moveTo(IDLE);
            return refund;
        }
        public String name() { return "HasMoney"; }
    };

    VendingState MAINTENANCE = new VendingState() {   // every customer action falls through to the defaults
        public String name() { return "Maintenance"; }
    };
}
VendingMachine.java: delegate, then commit a sale in one place
class VendingMachine {
    private final Inventory inventory;
    private final CashBox cash;
    private final List<Denomination> escrow = new ArrayList<>();   // inserted, not yet kept
    private VendingState state = VendingState.IDLE;

    VendingMachine(Inventory inventory, CashBox cash) { this.inventory = inventory; this.cash = cash; }

    // customer API: synchronized because a machine serves one customer at a time
    synchronized void insert(Denomination d) { state.insert(this, d); }
    synchronized Sale select(String code) { return state.select(this, code); }
    synchronized List<Denomination> cancel() { return state.cancel(this); }
    synchronized void startMaintenance() {
        if (!escrow.isEmpty()) throw new VendingException("customer has money inserted");
        state = VendingState.MAINTENANCE;
    }
    synchronized void endMaintenance() { state = VendingState.IDLE; }
    synchronized String stateName() { return state.name(); }

    // hooks for the states
    void moveTo(VendingState next) { state = next; }
    void escrow(Denomination d) { escrow.add(d); }

    List<Denomination> refundEscrow() {
        List<Denomination> out = List.copyOf(escrow);
        escrow.clear();
        return out;
    }

    Sale sell(String code) {
        Product p = inventory.product(code);
        if (!inventory.inStock(code)) throw new VendingException(code + " is sold out");
        long paid = escrow.stream().mapToLong(d -> d.paise).sum();
        if (paid < p.pricePaise()) throw new VendingException("insert " + (p.pricePaise() - paid) / 100 + " more rupees");
        List<Denomination> change = cash.planChange(paid - p.pricePaise(), escrow)
                .orElseThrow(() -> new VendingException("cannot make change; use exact money or cancel"));
        // every check passed: commit all effects together
        cash.addAll(escrow);
        cash.removeAll(change);
        inventory.take(code);
        escrow.clear();
        return new Sale(p, change);
    }
}
CashBox.java: change planning with backtracking
class CashBox {
    private final Map<Denomination, Integer> count = new EnumMap<>(Denomination.class);

    void add(Denomination d, int n) { count.merge(d, n, Integer::sum); }
    void addAll(List<Denomination> ds) { ds.forEach(d -> add(d, 1)); }
    void removeAll(List<Denomination> ds) { ds.forEach(d -> add(d, -1)); }

    /** Plans change for `amount` using `extra` (coins just inserted) plus the box, or empty if impossible. */
    Optional<List<Denomination>> planChange(long amount, List<Denomination> extra) {
        Map<Denomination, Integer> avail = new EnumMap<>(count);
        extra.forEach(d -> avail.merge(d, 1, Integer::sum));
        Denomination[] ds = Denomination.values();
        List<Denomination> out = new ArrayList<>();
        return plan(amount, ds.length - 1, ds, avail, out) ? Optional.of(out) : Optional.empty();
    }

    // largest denomination first; backtrack when a greedy choice leads to a dead end
    private boolean plan(long left, int i, Denomination[] ds, Map<Denomination, Integer> avail, List<Denomination> out) {
        if (left == 0) return true;
        if (i < 0) return false;
        Denomination d = ds[i];
        int max = (int) Math.min(avail.getOrDefault(d, 0), left / d.paise);
        for (int k = max; k >= 0; k--) {
            for (int j = 0; j < k; j++) out.add(d);
            if (plan(left - k * d.paise, i - 1, ds, avail, out)) return true;
            for (int j = 0; j < k; j++) out.remove(out.size() - 1);
        }
        return false;
    }
}

Product.java
record Product(String code, String name, long pricePaise) {}
Inventory.java
import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.Map;

class Inventory {
    private final Map<String, Product> products = new LinkedHashMap<>();
    private final Map<String, Integer> stock = new LinkedHashMap<>();

    void load(Product p, int count) {
        if (count <= 0) throw new VendingException("load a positive count");
        Product existing = products.putIfAbsent(p.code(), p);
        if (existing != null && !existing.equals(p)) throw new VendingException("slot " + p.code() + " holds " + existing.name());
        stock.merge(p.code(), count, Integer::sum);
    }

    Product product(String code) {
        Product p = products.get(code);
        if (p == null) throw new VendingException("no such product: " + code);
        return p;
    }

    boolean inStock(String code) { return stock.getOrDefault(code, 0) > 0; }

    void take(String code) {
        if (!inStock(code)) throw new VendingException(code + " is sold out");
        stock.merge(code, -1, Integer::sum);
    }
}

public class Demo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Inventory inv = new Inventory();
        inv.load(new Product("A1", "Water", 2_000), 2);
        inv.load(new Product("B2", "Chips", 3_000), 1);
        CashBox cash = new CashBox();
        cash.add(Denomination.COIN_10, 3);
        cash.add(Denomination.COIN_5, 2);
        VendingMachine vm = new VendingMachine(inv, cash);
        List<String> log = new ArrayList<>();

        try { vm.select("A1"); } catch (VendingException e) { log.add(e.getMessage()); }       // Idle: insert money first
        vm.insert(Denomination.NOTE_50);
        Sale s1 = vm.select("A1");                                                              // 50 - 20 = 30 change
        log.add("got " + s1.product().name() + ", change " + s1.change());
        vm.insert(Denomination.NOTE_100);
        try { vm.select("B2"); } catch (VendingException e) { log.add(e.getMessage()); }       // 70 change, box cannot
        log.add("refund " + vm.cancel());
        vm.insert(Denomination.NOTE_20);
        vm.insert(Denomination.COIN_10);
        Sale s2 = vm.select("B2");                                                              // exact money
        log.add("got " + s2.product().name() + ", change " + s2.change());
        vm.insert(Denomination.NOTE_20);
        try { vm.select("B2"); } catch (VendingException e) { log.add(e.getMessage()); }       // sold out, still HasMoney
        log.add("state " + vm.stateName() + ", refund " + vm.cancel());
        log.forEach(System.out::println);
        check(s1.change().stream().mapToLong(d -> d.paise).sum() == 3_000, "change 30");
        check(vm.stateName().equals("Idle"), "idle");
        vm.startMaintenance();
        try { vm.insert(Denomination.COIN_1); throw new AssertionError(); } catch (VendingException e) { System.out.println(e.getMessage()); }
        // greedy would fail here: 60 rupees from {50 x1, 20 x3}; backtracking finds 20+20+20
        CashBox tricky = new CashBox();
        tricky.add(Denomination.NOTE_50, 1);
        tricky.add(Denomination.NOTE_20, 3);
        check(tricky.planChange(6_000, List.of()).orElseThrow().size() == 3, "backtracking change");
        try { inv.load(new Product("A1", "Juice", 2_500), 3); throw new AssertionError(); } catch (VendingException e) { System.out.println("refill rejected: " + e.getMessage()); }
    }

    static void check(boolean ok, String what) { if (!ok) throw new AssertionError(what); }
}

P2.6Hard parts

Why greedy change can fail. Paying 60 rupees from a box holding one 50 and three 20s: greedy takes the 50 and is stuck with 10 to go, but three 20s work. With unlimited coins of standard denominations, greedy is optimal; with limited counts it is not. The cash box tries the largest denomination first and backtracks. That is fast for a machine's handful of denominations and modest coin counts; with large counts, backtracking can explode on impossible amounts, and a bounded-coin dynamic program over the amount (one row per denomination, one column per rupee) gives an answer in time proportional to amount times denominations.

Commit everything or nothing. sell performs every check first (product, stock, amount, change plan) and only then mutates stock, cash, and escrow together. If any check fails, nothing has changed, so the state can stay HasMoney without cleanup.

Concurrency. A machine serves one customer at a time, so its public methods are synchronized: a coin inserted while a selection is running waits. If the machine also talks to a remote inventory or payment service, the sale becomes a small saga: reserve, then charge, then dispense, with compensation on failure.

P2.7Deep dives

Guided designExtensions interviewers ask forAnswer each before revealing
  1. 1
    Card and UPI payments

    How do you add cashless payment without rewriting the states?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Add a payment method abstraction: money in escrow becomes a PaymentAuthorization (cash escrow is one kind, a card authorization is another). Selection captures the authorization for the price instead of planning change. Card and UPI sit behind a PaymentGateway interface with adapters. A new state, AwaitingPayment, may be needed while the card network responds.

  2. 2
    Dispense failure

    The motor jams after payment is committed. What now?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Treat dispensing as a step that can fail: commit stock and cash only after the dispenser confirms, or record the sale as pending and refund automatically if the dispenser reports failure. Add a Faulty state that blocks sales until maintenance. Log every sale with an ID for reconciliation.

  3. 3
    Enum instead of State objects

    Could this machine be an enum with a transition table?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Yes, for three states; the transitions are simple. The State pattern pays off when each state does real work for several actions (HasMoney accumulates escrow, sells, refunds) and when states grow (AwaitingPayment, Faulty, Dispensing). Say why you chose one; both are acceptable.

  4. 4
    Exact-change-only mode

    When the cash box is low, the display should say "exact change only".

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Expose a query on the cash box (can it make change for typical amounts?) and have the display subscribe to cash box changes (observer), or compute it on each sale. It does not change the state machine: it is a display rule, not a state.

P2.8Machine coding plan

Minutes Do
0-7 Clarify; draw the state diagram
7-20 Denomination, Product, Inventory, VendingException
20-35 CashBox with change planning and a quick test of the 60-from-50+20s case
35-55 VendingState constants and VendingMachine with sell committing at the end
55-70 Demo: success, insufficient money, cannot change, sold out, cancel, maintenance
70-75 Walk through, mention the card payment extension

P2.9What a strong answer shows

  • SDE-2 bar: correct state diagram, illegal actions rejected, escrow and refund, change limited by the cash box, stock checks.
  • Above the bar: all checks before any mutation; explains why greedy change fails with limited coins; handles dispense failure and cashless payment without rewriting the states.
Follow-up questionsPractice saying the answer out loud
  1. Why keep inserted money in escrow instead of adding it to the cash box immediately?
    Reveal

    So cancel returns exactly what was inserted, and a failed sale leaves the cash box unchanged. Money moves into the box only when a sale commits.

  2. The State pattern here uses constants with anonymous classes. Is that fine?
    Reveal

    Yes, because the states hold no data of their own; the machine holds the escrow. Stateless state objects can be shared singletons.

  3. How would you test change planning?
    Reveal

    Unit-test CashBox.planChange directly: exact amounts, impossible amounts, the greedy trap case, and that it never uses more coins than available.

  4. What if two products share a slot code by mistake when refilling?
    Reveal

    Inventory.load should reject a code that already holds a different product, unless the operator explicitly replaces it.

Problem 3: LRU cache

Asked as a data structure problem and as a design problem. The data structure answer is a hash map plus a doubly linked list with O(1) get and put. The design answer separates storage from the eviction policy, so LRU, LFU, and FIFO plug in, and explains why a cache read needs a write lock.

Uses: M10 collections, M6 strategy, M9 locks
