Try it first30 minutes

Design a fixed-capacity cache with get(key) and put(key, value) in O(1) that evicts the least recently used entry when full. Then make the eviction policy pluggable and the cache thread-safe.

Reveal the answer

Strong answer: a HashMap<K, Node> for lookup and a doubly linked list with sentinel head and tail for recency; get and put move the node to the front; eviction removes the node before tail and its map entry. For design: a Cache that owns storage and a lock and delegates order to an EvictionPolicy (LRU, FIFO, LFU). Thread safety needs an exclusive lock on reads too, because a read changes recency.

P3.1Requirements

Question Assumed answer
Operations? get(key), put(key, value), remove(key)
Complexity? O(1) for get and put
Capacity? Fixed at construction, positive
Eviction? Least recently used by default; other policies may follow
Does put on an existing key count as a use? Yes: it updates the value and makes the key most recent
Nulls? Not supported (a null value would be indistinguishable from a miss)
Threads? Many threads read and write concurrently

P3.2Entities and responsibilities

Class Responsibility
Cache<K, V> Stores values, enforces capacity, owns the lock, asks the policy who to evict
EvictionPolicy<K> Tracks access order and names the next victim
LruPolicy<K> Recency with a doubly linked list and a map from key to node
FifoPolicy<K> Insertion order with a LinkedHashSet
DoublyLinkedList<K> O(1) add-first, unlink, remove-last with sentinels

P3.3Class diagram

P3.4Key flows

LRU cache simulatorPrefilled with capacity 3 after put(1), put(2), put(3), get(1). Predict the eviction before you press a button.

    Left is most recently used (just after head); right is least recently used (just before tail). Every get and put moves the key to the left; a put into a full cache evicts the rightmost node.

    P3.5Code

    The version to write when asked "implement LRU" with no design discussion:

    ClassicLru.java: map plus doubly linked list with sentinels
    /** The 15-minute version: a map for O(1) lookup, a doubly linked list for O(1) reordering. */
class ClassicLru<K, V> {
    private static final class Node<K, V> {
        final K key;
        V value;
        Node<K, V> prev, next;
        Node(K key, V value) { this.key = key; this.value = value; }
    }

    private final int capacity;
    private final Map<K, Node<K, V>> index = new HashMap<>();
    private final Node<K, V> head = new Node<>(null, null);   // sentinel: most recent is head.next
    private final Node<K, V> tail = new Node<>(null, null);   // sentinel: least recent is tail.prev

    ClassicLru(int capacity) {
        if (capacity <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("capacity must be positive");
        this.capacity = capacity;
        head.next = tail;
        tail.prev = head;
    }

    V get(K key) {
        Node<K, V> n = index.get(key);
        if (n == null) return null;
        unlink(n);
        linkFirst(n);                      // touched: now most recent
        return n.value;
    }

    void put(K key, V value) {
        Node<K, V> n = index.get(key);
        if (n != null) {                   // update counts as a use
            n.value = value;
            unlink(n);
            linkFirst(n);
            return;
        }
        if (index.size() == capacity) {    // evict before inserting
            Node<K, V> lru = tail.prev;
            unlink(lru);
            index.remove(lru.key);
        }
        n = new Node<>(key, value);
        linkFirst(n);
        index.put(key, n);
    }

    private void unlink(Node<K, V> n) {
        n.prev.next = n.next;
        n.next.prev = n.prev;
    }

    private void linkFirst(Node<K, V> n) {
        n.next = head.next;
        n.prev = head;
        head.next.prev = n;
        head.next = n;
    }
}

    The design version, when the interviewer asks for pluggable eviction and threads:

    EvictionPolicy.java
    /** Decides which key leaves when the cache is full. Not thread-safe on its own: the cache locks around it. */
interface EvictionPolicy<K> {
    void onPut(K key);        // a key was inserted or updated
    void onGet(K key);        // a key was read
    void onRemove(K key);     // a key was removed explicitly
    K victim();               // the key to evict next; the policy forgets it
}
    LruPolicy.java
    class LruPolicy<K> implements EvictionPolicy<K> {
    private final DoublyLinkedList<K> order = new DoublyLinkedList<>();
    private final Map<K, DoublyLinkedList.Node<K>> nodes = new HashMap<>();

    public void onPut(K key) { touch(key); }
    public void onGet(K key) { touch(key); }

    public void onRemove(K key) {
        DoublyLinkedList.Node<K> n = nodes.remove(key);
        if (n != null) order.unlink(n);
    }

    public K victim() {
        DoublyLinkedList.Node<K> n = order.removeLast();
        if (n == null) throw new IllegalStateException("nothing to evict");
        nodes.remove(n.key);
        return n.key;
    }

    private void touch(K key) {
        DoublyLinkedList.Node<K> n = nodes.get(key);
        if (n != null) order.unlink(n);
        else nodes.put(key, n = new DoublyLinkedList.Node<>(key));
        order.addFirst(n);
    }
}
    FifoPolicy.java: a second policy to prove the seam
    /** First in, first out: reads do not change the order. */
class FifoPolicy<K> implements EvictionPolicy<K> {
    private final LinkedHashSet<K> order = new LinkedHashSet<>();

    public void onPut(K key) { order.add(key); }      // re-adding an existing key keeps its position
    public void onGet(K key) { }
    public void onRemove(K key) { order.remove(key); }

    public K victim() {
        Iterator<K> it = order.iterator();
        K k = it.next();
        it.remove();
        return k;
    }
}
    Cache.java: storage, capacity, and the lock
    class Cache<K, V> {
    private final int capacity;
    private final Map<K, V> storage = new HashMap<>();
    private final EvictionPolicy<K> policy;
    private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();   // a get changes recency, so reads need the lock too

    Cache(int capacity, EvictionPolicy<K> policy) {
        if (capacity <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("capacity must be positive");
        this.capacity = capacity;
        this.policy = policy;
    }

    Optional<V> get(K key) {
        lock.lock();
        try {
            V v = storage.get(key);
            if (v != null) policy.onGet(key);
            return Optional.ofNullable(v);
        } finally {
            lock.unlock();
        }
    }

    /** Returns the evicted key, if any. */
    Optional<K> put(K key, V value) {
        if (key == null || value == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("null keys and values are not supported");
        lock.lock();
        try {
            K evicted = null;
            if (!storage.containsKey(key) && storage.size() == capacity) {
                evicted = policy.victim();
                storage.remove(evicted);
            }
            storage.put(key, value);
            policy.onPut(key);
            return Optional.ofNullable(evicted);
        } finally {
            lock.unlock();
        }
    }

    boolean remove(K key) {
        lock.lock();
        try {
            if (storage.remove(key) == null) return false;
            policy.onRemove(key);
            return true;
        } finally {
            lock.unlock();
        }
    }

    int size() {
        lock.lock();
        try { return storage.size(); } finally { lock.unlock(); }
    }
}
    Go deeper

    DoublyLinkedList.java

    DoublyLinkedList.java
    class DoublyLinkedList<K> {
    static final class Node<K> {
        final K key;
        Node<K> prev, next;
        Node(K key) { this.key = key; }
    }

    private final Node<K> head = new Node<>(null), tail = new Node<>(null);

    DoublyLinkedList() { head.next = tail; tail.prev = head; }

    void addFirst(Node<K> n) {
        n.next = head.next;
        n.prev = head;
        head.next.prev = n;
        head.next = n;
    }

    void unlink(Node<K> n) {
        n.prev.next = n.next;
        n.next.prev = n.prev;
        n.prev = n.next = null;
    }

    Node<K> removeLast() {
        if (tail.prev == head) return null;
        Node<K> n = tail.prev;
        unlink(n);
        return n;
    }
}
    Demo.java: the same operations, two policies
    Cache<Integer, String> lru = new Cache<>(3, new LruPolicy<>());
Cache<Integer, String> fifo = new Cache<>(3, new FifoPolicy<>());
List<String> out = new ArrayList<>();
for (Cache<Integer, String> c : List.of(lru, fifo)) {
    c.put(1, "a"); c.put(2, "b"); c.put(3, "c");
    c.get(1);                                        // 1 becomes most recent (LRU only)
    out.add("put 4 evicts " + c.put(4, "d").orElse(null));
}
// LRU evicts 2 (least recently used); FIFO evicts 1 (oldest insert)
    Code that ranDemo.java: the complete code behind the output below
    Demo.java (complete)
    public class Demo {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        Cache<Integer, String> lru = new Cache<>(3, new LruPolicy<>());
        Cache<Integer, String> fifo = new Cache<>(3, new FifoPolicy<>());
        List<String> out = new ArrayList<>();
        for (Cache<Integer, String> c : List.of(lru, fifo)) {
            c.put(1, "a"); c.put(2, "b"); c.put(3, "c");
            c.get(1);                                        // 1 becomes most recent (LRU only)
            out.add("put 4 evicts " + c.put(4, "d").orElse(null));
        }
        // LRU evicts 2 (least recently used); FIFO evicts 1 (oldest insert)
        out.forEach(System.out::println);
        check(out.equals(List.of("put 4 evicts 2", "put 4 evicts 1")), "policies");

        ClassicLru<String, Integer> classic = new ClassicLru<>(2);
        classic.put("x", 1); classic.put("y", 2); classic.get("x"); classic.put("z", 3);
        check(classic.get("y") == null && classic.get("x") == 1 && classic.get("z") == 3, "classic");

        // 8 threads hammer a 100-entry cache with 1,000 keys: size never exceeds capacity, nothing throws
        Cache<Integer, Integer> shared = new Cache<>(100, new LruPolicy<>());
        ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8);
        for (int t = 0; t < 8; t++) pool.submit(() -> {
            ThreadLocalRandom r = ThreadLocalRandom.current();
            for (int i = 0; i < 50_000; i++) {
                int k = r.nextInt(1_000);
                if (r.nextBoolean()) shared.put(k, k); else shared.get(k).ifPresent(v -> check(v == k, "value"));
                check(shared.size() <= 100, "capacity");
            }
        });
        pool.shutdown();
        check(pool.awaitTermination(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS), "finished");
        System.out.println("concurrent run finished; size " + shared.size() + " of capacity 100");
    }

    static void check(boolean ok, String what) { if (!ok) throw new AssertionError(what); }
}
    Output (from running the code above)
    put 4 evicts 2
put 4 evicts 1
concurrent run finished; size 100 of capacity 100

    P3.6Concurrency

    The trap: get looks like a read, but it moves the node in the list, so two concurrent gets corrupt the links. A ReadWriteLock with gets under the read lock is therefore wrong for LRU. Options, from simplest:

    Approach Trade-off
    One ReentrantLock (or synchronized) around every operation Correct and simple; all operations serialize. Fine for interviews and most services
    Collections.synchronizedMap(new LinkedHashMap<>(cap, 0.75f, true)) Same, using the JDK's LRU support
    Lock striping: N independent caches, key hash picks one Less contention; LRU becomes approximate across the whole cache
    Approximate recency (Caffeine, Redis) Record accesses in buffers and apply them in batches, or sample keys at eviction time; near-LRU with high concurrency
    In production

    In production Java, use Caffeine rather than hand-written caches: it uses an admission and eviction policy (W-TinyLFU) that beats plain LRU on most workloads and stays fast under concurrency. Redis approximates LRU by sampling a few keys and evicting the least recent among them. The interview version shows you understand what those libraries do.

    P3.7Deep dives

    Guided designExtensions interviewers ask forAnswer each before revealing
    1. 1
      Time-to-live per entry

      Entries must expire 5 minutes after they are written.

      Write your answer, then reveal

      Store an expiry time with each value (record Entry(V value, long expiresAt)). On get, treat an expired entry as a miss and remove it (lazy expiry). To free memory without reads, run a periodic sweep, or keep a PriorityQueue or DelayQueue ordered by expiry. Inject a Clock so tests can move time.

    2. 2
      LFU instead of LRU

      Evict the least frequently used key, breaking ties by least recent. O(1)?

      Write your answer, then reveal

      Keep Map<K, Integer> freq, Map<Integer, LinkedHashSet<K>> keysByFreq, and minFreq. On access, move the key from its frequency set to the next one; if the old set was the minimum and is now empty, increment minFreq. On eviction, remove the first key of keysByFreq.get(minFreq). A new key starts at frequency 1 and resets minFreq to 1. All operations are O(1). It fits behind EvictionPolicy unchanged.

    3. 3
      Loading on a miss

      Callers want get(key, loader) that computes and caches missing values, without two threads loading the same key.

      Write your answer, then reveal

      Single-flight per key: a ConcurrentHashMap<K, CompletableFuture<V>> of in-flight loads; the first caller installs a future with computeIfAbsent and runs the loader, others wait on the same future. Remove the future when it completes, and store the value in the cache.

    4. 4
      Size by bytes, not entries

      Values vary from 1 KB to 5 MB.

      Write your answer, then reveal

      Give the cache a weigher (ToLongFunction<V>) and a maximum weight; evict victims until the total weight fits. Large values may evict many small ones; consider refusing values above a threshold.

    Minutes Do
    0-5 Clarify update semantics, nulls, capacity, threads
    5-25 ClassicLru with sentinels; test the evict-after-get case
    25-40 Extract EvictionPolicy, LruPolicy, Cache with a lock
    40-50 FifoPolicy or LFU to prove the seam

    P3.9What a strong answer shows

    • SDE-2 bar: correct O(1) structure with sentinels; update counts as a use; capacity edge cases; thread safety with one lock and the reason a read lock is wrong.
    • Above the bar: separates policy from storage; implements LFU in O(1) on request; discusses TTL, single-flight loading, and what Caffeine or Redis do differently.
    Follow-up questionsPractice saying the answer out loud
    1. Why a doubly linked list rather than a singly linked one?
      Reveal

      Unlinking a node in O(1) needs its predecessor. With a doubly linked list each node knows prev; a singly linked list would need a walk from the head.

    2. Why sentinel head and tail nodes?
      Reveal

      They remove the special cases for empty lists and for the first and last node, so link and unlink are four assignments each with no null checks.

    3. Your Cache returns Optional<V>. Why not null on a miss?
      Reveal

      Optional forces callers to handle the miss explicitly. It also explains why null values are rejected: a stored null could not be told apart from a miss.

    4. How would you test the LRU order?
      Reveal

      Put keys 1, 2, 3 into a capacity-3 cache, get 1, put 4, and assert that 2 was evicted and 1, 3, 4 remain. Then repeat with an update to an existing key instead of a get.

    Problem 4: Snake and ladder

    A favorite machine coding warm-up because it rewards clean modeling over cleverness: a board that validates itself, dice and rules behind interfaces so tests can script games, a turn queue, and a game loop with a clear end. The same skeleton fits tic-tac-toe, Ludo, and chess.

    Try it first30 minutes

    Design snake and ladder for N players on a configurable board. A player must land exactly on the last cell to win. Variants (two dice, an extra turn on a six) are likely. Write it so a test can play a full game deterministically.

    Reveal the answer

    Strong answer: an immutable Board with one map of jumps (snakes and ladders are both start-to-end jumps), built by a builder that validates direction, range, duplicates, and chains; Dice interface with random and scripted implementations; Rules interface for exact finish and extra turns; a Game with a turn queue (ArrayDeque), playTurn returning the winner when there is one, and a move log; seeded randomness for reproducible games.

    P4.1Requirements

    Question Assumed answer
    Board? Size N (100 by default), configurable snakes and ladders
    Players? Two or more, in a fixed turn order
    Winning? Land exactly on the last cell; overshooting means you stay
    Dice? One six-sided die by default; variants with more dice
    Variants? Extra turn on a six, possibly others
    Input? Board and players from input, then play until someone wins and print the moves

    Invariants: snakes go down and ladders go up; no two jumps start on the same cell; no jump starts where another ends (no chains); the game has at most one winner and no turns after it.

    P4.2Entities and responsibilities

    Class Responsibility
    Board Size and jumps, immutable once built; its builder validates them; resolve(cell) gives the final cell after a snake or ladder
    Dice roll(); RandomDice with a seed, ScriptedDice for tests
    Rules Target cell for a roll (exact finish) and whether a roll earns an extra turn
    Player Name and position
    Game Turn queue, winner, move log; plays one turn or to the end

    Modeling insight worth saying aloud: a snake and a ladder are the same thing, a jump from one cell to another. One map handles both; only the validation differs.

    P4.3Class diagram

    P4.4Key flows

    P4.5Code

    Board.java: one map of jumps, validated by a builder, immutable after build()
    /** Immutable once built, so one board can be shared by many games. */
final class Board {
    private final int size;
    private final Map<Integer, Integer> jumps;   // start cell -> end cell, snakes and ladders alike

    private Board(int size, Map<Integer, Integer> jumps) {
        this.size = size;
        this.jumps = Map.copyOf(jumps);
    }

    static Builder builder(int size) { return new Builder(size); }

    /** Where a piece ends up after landing on `cell`. */
    int resolve(int cell) { return jumps.getOrDefault(cell, cell); }

    int size() { return size; }

    static final class Builder {
        private final int size;
        private final Map<Integer, Integer> jumps = new HashMap<>();

        private Builder(int size) {
            if (size < 10) throw new IllegalArgumentException("board too small");
            this.size = size;
        }

        Builder snake(int head, int tail) {
            if (head <= tail) throw new IllegalArgumentException("snake must go down: " + head + " -> " + tail);
            return addJump(head, tail);
        }

        Builder ladder(int bottom, int top) {
            if (bottom >= top) throw new IllegalArgumentException("ladder must go up: " + bottom + " -> " + top);
            return addJump(bottom, top);
        }

        private Builder addJump(int from, int to) {
            if (from <= 1 || from >= size || to < 1 || to > size) throw new IllegalArgumentException("jump out of range: " + from + " -> " + to);
            if (jumps.containsKey(from)) throw new IllegalArgumentException("cell " + from + " already has a jump");
            if (jumps.containsValue(from) || jumps.containsKey(to)) throw new IllegalArgumentException("chained jumps at " + from + " -> " + to);
            jumps.put(from, to);
            return this;
        }

        Board build() { return new Board(size, jumps); }
    }
}
    Game.java: the turn loop
    class Game {
    private final Board board;
    private final Dice dice;
    private final Rules rules;
    private final Deque<Player> turns = new ArrayDeque<>();
    private final List<String> log = new ArrayList<>();
    private Player winner;

    Game(Board board, Dice dice, Rules rules, List<Player> players) {
        if (players.size() < 2) throw new IllegalArgumentException("need at least 2 players");
        this.board = board;
        this.dice = dice;
        this.rules = rules;
        this.turns.addAll(players);
    }

    /** Plays one turn; returns the winner once someone reaches the last cell. */
    Optional<Player> playTurn() {
        if (winner != null) throw new IllegalStateException("game over: " + winner.name() + " won");
        Player p = turns.poll();
        int roll = dice.roll();
        int from = p.position();
        int target = rules.target(from, roll, board.size());
        int end = board.resolve(target);
        p.moveTo(end);
        log.add(describe(p, roll, from, target, end));
        if (end == board.size()) {
            winner = p;
            return Optional.of(p);
        }
        if (rules.extraTurn(roll)) turns.addFirst(p);    // same player again
        else turns.addLast(p);
        return Optional.empty();
    }

    Player playToEnd(int maxTurns) {
        for (int i = 0; i < maxTurns; i++) {
            Optional<Player> w = playTurn();
            if (w.isPresent()) return w.get();
        }
        throw new IllegalStateException("no winner after " + maxTurns + " turns");
    }

    List<String> log() { return log; }

    private String describe(Player p, int roll, int from, int target, int end) {
        String s = p.name() + " rolled " + roll + ": " + from + " -> " + target;
        if (target == from) return s + " (overshoot, stays)";
        if (end > target) return s + " ladder up to " + end;
        if (end < target) return s + " snake down to " + end;
        return s;
    }
}
    Rules.java
    interface Rules {
    /** Target cell before snakes and ladders, or the current cell if the move is not allowed. */
    int target(int current, int roll, int boardSize);
    boolean extraTurn(int roll);
}
    StandardRules.java
    class StandardRules implements Rules {
    public int target(int current, int roll, int boardSize) {
        int next = current + roll;
        return next > boardSize ? current : next;     // must land exactly on the last cell
    }
    public boolean extraTurn(int roll) { return false; }
}

    class SixGetsAnotherTurn extends StandardRules {
    @Override public boolean extraTurn(int roll) { return roll == 6; }
}

    RandomDice.java
    import java.util.Random;

class RandomDice implements Dice {
    private final Random random;
    private final int count;
    RandomDice(int count, long seed) { this.count = count; this.random = new Random(seed); }   // seed: reproducible games
    public int roll() {
        int sum = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) sum += 1 + random.nextInt(6);
        return sum;
    }
}
    ScriptedDice.java
    import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;
import java.util.List;

class ScriptedDice implements Dice {                 // for tests and demos
    private final Deque<Integer> rolls;
    ScriptedDice(List<Integer> rolls) { this.rolls = new ArrayDeque<>(rolls); }
    public int roll() {
        if (rolls.isEmpty()) throw new IllegalStateException("script ran out of rolls");
        return rolls.poll();
    }
}

    public class Demo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Board board = Board.builder(20).ladder(3, 11).ladder(8, 16).snake(14, 4).snake(19, 2).build();
        List<Player> players = List.of(new Player("Asha"), new Player("Ravi"));
        Dice dice = new ScriptedDice(List.of(3, 6, 3, 2, 4, 3, 6, 5, 4));
        Game game = new Game(board, dice, new StandardRules(), players);
        Player winner = game.playToEnd(100);
        game.log().forEach(System.out::println);
        System.out.println("winner: " + winner.name());
        check(winner.name().equals("Asha"), "winner");
        try { Board.builder(20).snake(5, 9); throw new AssertionError(); } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) { System.out.println("rejected: " + e.getMessage()); }
        try { Board.builder(20).ladder(3, 11).snake(11, 2); throw new AssertionError(); } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) { System.out.println("rejected: " + e.getMessage()); }
        Player w = new Game(Board.builder(100).ladder(2, 38).snake(99, 7).build(), new RandomDice(1, 42), new SixGetsAnotherTurn(),
                List.of(new Player("A"), new Player("B"), new Player("C"))).playToEnd(10_000);
        check(w.position() == 100, "random game ends on 100");
    }

    static void check(boolean ok, String what) { if (!ok) throw new AssertionError(what); }
}

    P4.6Hard parts

    • Determinism. Randomness is injected (Dice), so tests script exact games and a seeded Random reproduces a reported bug.
    • Validation at construction. A board that cannot be built invalid never needs checks during play, and because build() copies the jumps into an immutable map, nothing can change it mid-game.
    • Termination. playToEnd(maxTurns) guards against a board where nobody can win (for example, every path to the end is a snake), instead of looping forever.
    • No concurrency in the classic version: one game runs on one thread. For many games on a server, each game is confined to one thread or guarded by its own lock; games share nothing.

    P4.7Deep dives

    Guided designExtensions interviewers ask forAnswer each before revealing
    1. 1
      Two dice, and three sixes in a row forfeit the turn

      How do these fit?

      Write your answer, then reveal

      Two dice: RandomDice(2, seed) already sums several dice. Three sixes: a new Rules implementation that tracks consecutive sixes per player; since rules now need state per player, either pass the turn history into the rules or let Game keep a counter and ask a Rules method forfeit(consecutiveSixes).

    2. 2
      Pieces capture each other (Ludo-style)

      Landing on an opponent sends them back to start.

      Write your answer, then reveal

      After resolve, check whether another player stands on the end cell (a Map<Integer, Player> of occupancy kept by the game) and move them to 0. This is a rule, so it belongs in Rules or a separate CollisionRule hook called by the game.

    3. 3
      Undo the last move

      A casual mode lets players undo.

      Write your answer, then reveal

      Make each turn a command with the player, previous position, and new position; push it on a stack; undo pops it, restores the position, and puts the player back at the head of the queue (Module 7).

    4. 4
      Run thousands of games on a server

      How do you keep games independent and fast?

      Write your answer, then reveal

      Each Game object is self-contained; store games in a ConcurrentHashMap<gameId, Game> and process each game's moves on one thread at a time (a per-game lock or an actor-style single-threaded executor per game). Boards can be shared because they are immutable after construction.

    P4.9What a strong answer shows

    • SDE-2 bar: validated board; injected dice; exact-finish rule; correct turn order; deterministic tests; clean output.
    • Above the bar: snakes and ladders unified as jumps; rules as a strategy with variants added live; a guard against games that never end; immutable boards shared across games.
    Follow-up questionsPractice saying the answer out loud
    1. Why is Board.resolve a single map lookup instead of looping until no jump applies?
      Reveal

      Chains are rejected at construction, so one lookup is always final. That makes moves O(1) and removes any chance of a cycle.

    2. How would you print the board?
      Reveal

      A separate renderer class reads the board and player positions and formats them; the board itself should not know about console output.

    3. Why use ArrayDeque for turns?
      Reveal

      Taking the next player from the front and putting them at the back (or the front, for an extra turn) are O(1) deque operations, and the order is explicit.

    4. How do you make tic-tac-toe from this skeleton?
      Reveal

      Replace Board with a grid, Dice with player input, and Rules with a win check (row, column, and diagonal counters for O(1) checks). Game, Player, the turn queue, and the log stay the same.

    Problem 5Core45 min LLD / 90 min coding

    Problem 5: Logging framework

    A logging framework is a pattern showcase that is also code you use every day: a shared registry of loggers, levels that filter cheaply, appenders that fan out, formatters as strategies, a template method in the base appender, and an async decorator built on a bounded queue. Knowing how SLF4J and Logback do it is the bonus.

    Uses: M6 template method, M5 decorator, M9 producer-consumer

    Try it first45 minutes

    Design a logging library: named loggers, levels (DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR), several destinations with their own minimum levels and formats, and an option to log without blocking the calling thread. Then compare.

    Reveal the answer

    Strong answer: LogManager.getLogger(name) returning a cached logger; a logger level checked first, with lazy messages (Supplier<String>) so disabled logs cost nothing; appenders behind an interface, each with its own level and formatter; formatters as strategies (plain, JSON); an async appender as a decorator over a bounded queue with a worker thread, a drop counter, and a draining shutdown; reconfiguration that applies to existing loggers.

    P5.1Requirements

    Question Assumed answer
    Levels? DEBUG < INFO < WARN < ERROR; a logger has a minimum level
    Destinations? Console, file, memory (tests); each with its own minimum level and format
    Formats? Plain text and JSON
    Performance? Disabled levels must be nearly free; logging must not block request threads
    Configuration? Change levels and appenders at runtime for all loggers
    Threads? Many threads log at once

    Invariants: a message below the logger's level is never built; a message is written by an appender only if it meets that appender's level; every line logged before shutdown starts is written; when the async queue is full, drops are counted, not silent.

    P5.2Entities and responsibilities

    Class Responsibility Pattern
    LogManager Registry of loggers by name; global configuration Singleton-style registry (static)
    Logger Level check, build LogMessage, fan out to appenders
    LogMessage (record) Time, level, logger, thread, text Value object
    Appender Write a message somewhere Strategy / observer
    LevelAppender Filter by level, format, then write Template method
    Formatter Message to string Strategy
    AsyncAppender Queue and a worker thread around any appender Decorator + producer-consumer
    Chain of responsibility?

    Textbooks often model logging as a chain where an ERROR handler passes to a WARN handler and so on. Real frameworks (Logback, Log4j 2) do what this design does instead: the logger level is a cheap first filter, then every attached appender decides for itself. Mention the textbook framing if asked, and why the fan-out is simpler.

    P5.3Class diagram

    P5.5Code

    Logger.java: cheap level check, lazy message, fan-out
    public class Logger {
    /** Everything a log call reads, swapped as one object so a call never mixes old and new settings. */
    record Settings(Clock clock, LogLevel threshold, List<Appender> appenders) {
        Settings { appenders = List.copyOf(appenders); }
    }

    private final String name;
    private volatile Settings settings;

    Logger(String name, Settings settings) {
        this.name = name;
        this.settings = settings;
    }

    public void debug(String msg) { log(LogLevel.DEBUG, () -> msg); }
    public void info(String msg) { log(LogLevel.INFO, () -> msg); }
    public void warn(String msg) { log(LogLevel.WARN, () -> msg); }
    public void error(String msg) { log(LogLevel.ERROR, () -> msg); }

    /** The message is built only if the level is enabled: no cost for disabled debug logs. */
    public void debug(Supplier<String> msg) { log(LogLevel.DEBUG, msg); }

    public boolean isEnabled(LogLevel level) { return level.atLeast(settings.threshold()); }

    private void log(LogLevel level, Supplier<String> msg) {
        Settings s = settings;                            // one volatile read: a consistent snapshot
        if (!level.atLeast(s.threshold())) return;        // cheap check first
        LogMessage m = new LogMessage(s.clock().instant(), level, name, Thread.currentThread().getName(), msg.get());
        for (Appender a : s.appenders()) a.append(m);     // each appender applies its own level
    }

    void reconfigure(Settings next) { this.settings = next; }
}
    LogManager.java: one logger per name, reconfigurable
    /** One shared registry of loggers: getLogger returns the same Logger for the same name. */
public final class LogManager {
    private static final Map<String, Logger> LOGGERS = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    private static Logger.Settings settings =                       // guarded by LogManager.class
            new Logger.Settings(Clock.systemUTC(), LogLevel.INFO, List.of(new ConsoleAppender(LogLevel.DEBUG, new PlainFormatter())));

    private LogManager() { }

    public static Logger getLogger(String name) {
        Logger existing = LOGGERS.get(name);                         // fast path: no lock once created
        if (existing != null) return existing;
        synchronized (LogManager.class) {                            // creation and configure never interleave
            return LOGGERS.computeIfAbsent(name, n -> new Logger(n, settings));
        }
    }

    /** Applies to existing and future loggers. Tests call this with a fixed clock and a memory appender. */
    public static synchronized void configure(Clock clock, LogLevel level, List<Appender> appenders) {
        settings = new Logger.Settings(clock, level, appenders);
        LOGGERS.values().forEach(l -> l.reconfigure(settings));     // existing loggers switch too
    }

    public static synchronized void shutdown() {
        settings.appenders().forEach(Appender::close);
    }
}
    LevelAppender.java: the template method
    /** Filters by its own level, formats, and writes to a sink. */
abstract class LevelAppender implements Appender {
    private final LogLevel threshold;
    private final Formatter formatter;
    LevelAppender(LogLevel threshold, Formatter formatter) { this.threshold = threshold; this.formatter = formatter; }

    public final void append(LogMessage m) {         // template method: filter, format, write
        if (m.level().atLeast(threshold)) write(formatter.format(m));
    }
    protected abstract void write(String line);
}
    AsyncAppender.java: decorator over a bounded queue
    /** Decorator: callers enqueue and return; one worker thread writes to the wrapped appender. */
final class AsyncAppender implements Appender {
    private static final LogMessage STOP = new LogMessage(null, LogLevel.ERROR, "", "", "");   // unique sentinel
    private final Appender inner;
    private final BlockingQueue<LogMessage> queue;
    private final LongAdder dropped = new LongAdder();
    private final AtomicBoolean closed = new AtomicBoolean();
    private final Thread worker;

    AsyncAppender(Appender inner, int capacity) {
        this.inner = inner;
        this.queue = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(capacity);
        this.worker = new Thread(this::drain, "log-async");
        worker.setDaemon(true);
        worker.start();          // last step of a final class's constructor: every field is already set
    }

    public void append(LogMessage m) {
        if (closed.get() || !queue.offer(m)) dropped.increment();   // never block the caller; count what we lose
    }

    private void drain() {
        try {
            for (LogMessage m = queue.take(); m != STOP; m = queue.take()) inner.append(m);
            List<LogMessage> late = new ArrayList<>();
            queue.drainTo(late);                         // lines that raced with close: write them too
            late.forEach(inner::append);
        } catch (InterruptedException e) {
            Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
        }
    }

    /** Lines logged before close() starts are all written; close is safe to call twice. */
    public void close() {
        if (!closed.compareAndSet(false, true)) return;
        try {
            queue.put(STOP);
            worker.join();
        } catch (InterruptedException e) {
            Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
        }
        inner.close();
    }

    long dropped() { return dropped.sum(); }
}

    Demo.java (complete)
    public class Demo {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        Clock fixed = Clock.fixed(Instant.parse("2026-10-21T10:15:30Z"), ZoneOffset.UTC);
        MemoryAppender all = new MemoryAppender(LogLevel.DEBUG, new PlainFormatter());
        MemoryAppender alerts = new MemoryAppender(LogLevel.ERROR, new JsonFormatter());
        LogManager.configure(fixed, LogLevel.INFO, List.of(all, alerts));

        Logger log = LogManager.getLogger("payments");
        AtomicInteger expensiveCalls = new AtomicInteger();
        log.debug(() -> "state dump " + expensiveCalls.incrementAndGet());   // DEBUG < INFO: supplier never runs
        log.info("charge started for o-42");
        log.error("charge failed for o-42: \"card declined\"");
        all.lines.forEach(System.out::println);
        alerts.lines.forEach(System.out::println);
        System.out.println("expensive debug message built " + expensiveCalls.get() + " times");
        check(all.lines.size() == 2 && alerts.lines.size() == 1 && expensiveCalls.get() == 0, "levels");
        check(LogManager.getLogger("payments") == log, "same logger");

        // async: 4 threads log 2,500 lines each through one AsyncAppender; shutdown drains everything
        MemoryAppender sink = new MemoryAppender(LogLevel.DEBUG, new PlainFormatter());
        AsyncAppender async = new AsyncAppender(sink, 20_000);
        LogManager.configure(fixed, LogLevel.DEBUG, List.of(async));
        Logger busy = LogManager.getLogger("orders");
        List<Thread> threads = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int t = 0; t < 4; t++) {
            Thread th = new Thread(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < 2_500; i++) busy.info("line " + i); }, "worker-" + t);
            threads.add(th);
            th.start();
        }
        for (Thread th : threads) th.join();
        LogManager.shutdown();
        System.out.println("async wrote " + sink.lines.size() + " lines, dropped " + async.dropped());
        check(sink.lines.size() + async.dropped() == 10_000, "every line written or counted");
    }

    static void check(boolean ok, String what) { if (!ok) throw new AssertionError(what); }
}

    P5.6Concurrency

    Concern Handled by
    Two threads ask for the same logger name ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent: one instance
    Reconfiguration while threads log Each logger holds one volatile immutable Settings record (clock, level, appenders), replaced as a whole, so a log call never mixes old and new settings
    A logger created during configure Creation and configure share one lock, so every logger either sees the new settings or is updated by configure
    Many threads writing to one appender The async appender serializes writes on one worker thread; a synchronous file appender would lock around each write
    A slow disk Bounded queue; offer never blocks; drops are counted
    Shutdown A sentinel message and join, so lines logged before shutdown are written; close is idempotent and later lines are counted as dropped
    In production

    This is how SLF4J with Logback works: LoggerFactory.getLogger(...) returns a cached logger; log.debug("order {}", id) uses placeholders so the string is built only if DEBUG is enabled (the same goal as the Supplier here); appenders and encoders are configured per destination; AsyncAppender wraps another appender with a bounded queue and, by default, discards lower-level events when the queue is nearly full. Log4j 2 adds lock-free async loggers using the LMAX Disruptor.

    P5.7Deep dives

    Guided designExtensions interviewers ask forAnswer each before revealing
    1. 1
      Hierarchical levels

      com.shop at INFO, com.shop.payments at DEBUG; loggers inherit the nearest configured ancestor's level.

      Write your answer, then reveal

      Store configured levels by name prefix. When creating or reconfiguring a logger, walk its name from most specific to least (com.shop.payments.Gateway, com.shop.payments, com.shop, root) and take the first configured level. Cache the result in the logger and recompute all loggers when configuration changes.

    2. 2
      Rolling log files

      Start a new file every day or at 100 MB, keeping the last 7.

      Write your answer, then reveal

      A RollingFileAppender with a RollingPolicy strategy (by time, by size, or both) that decides when to roll, and a retention policy that deletes old files. Rolling happens under the appender's lock so no line is split across files.

    3. 3
      Request IDs in every line

      Every log line for one request should include its request ID without passing it to each call.

      Write your answer, then reveal

      A mapped diagnostic context: a ThreadLocal<Map<String, String>> set at the start of a request and cleared at the end (in a finally). Logger copies it into LogMessage, and formatters print it. With async work, copy the context into tasks explicitly, because thread pools reuse threads.

    4. 4
      Never lose ERROR lines

      The queue may drop lines under load, but errors must always be written.

      Write your answer, then reveal

      Make dropping level-aware: when the queue is above, say, 80% full, drop DEBUG and INFO but block briefly (or write synchronously) for WARN and ERROR. Keep the drop counter per level and log it periodically.

    Minutes Do

    P5.9What a strong answer shows

    • SDE-2 bar: clear separation of logger, appender, and formatter; level filtering before work; thread-safe logger registry; a working async appender with shutdown.
    • Above the bar: lazy messages; bounded queue with counted drops and level-aware dropping; reconfiguration of existing loggers; MDC; can explain how Logback and SLF4J map to the design.
    Follow-up questionsPractice saying the answer out loud
    1. Why should log.debug("x=" + compute()) worry you, and what fixes it?
      Reveal

      The string and compute() run even when DEBUG is disabled. Use a Supplier (log.debug(() -> ...)), placeholders (log.debug("x={}", value)), or an isDebugEnabled() guard for expensive work.

    2. Why does LevelAppender.append use final?
      Reveal

      So subclasses cannot skip the level check or formatting; they only supply write. That is the template method's guarantee.

    3. Is LogManager a singleton? Is that a problem for tests?
      Reveal

      It is a static registry, effectively a singleton. Tests stay manageable because configure replaces the clock and appenders for all loggers; in application code, loggers are typically obtained statically by convention, which is an accepted exception to "inject everything".

    4. What happens to a log line if the process crashes with lines still in the async queue?
      Reveal

      They are lost. That is the price of non-blocking logging; for audit trails that must never be lost, write synchronously to durable storage instead of a log.

    Problem 6: Rate limiter

    The LLD version of a rate limiter is about classes and concurrency inside one process: interchangeable algorithms behind one interface, one limiter per key created safely, time injected so behavior is testable, and a check-and-decrement that stays atomic under load. The distributed version (Redis, Lua) is in the HLD handbook.

    Design an in-process rate limiter: each API key gets N requests per time window; premium keys get more; the algorithm should be swappable; it must be correct with many threads. Then compare.

    Reveal the answer

    Strong answer: a Limiter interface with token bucket, sliding window log, and fixed window implementations; a keyed limiter holding a ConcurrentHashMap<String, Limiter> filled with computeIfAbsent and a factory that applies per-tier rules; lazy token refill computed from elapsed time (no timer thread); per-limiter synchronization so check and decrement are atomic; an injected time source for tests; and a plan for idle-key cleanup and multi-instance limits.

    P6.1Requirements

    Question Assumed answer
    Limit by? API key (could be user ID or IP)
    Rules? Free: 10 requests with 5 per second refill; premium: 100 with 50 per second
    Burst behavior? Short bursts are fine up to the capacity
    Response when limited? tryAcquire returns false; the caller returns HTTP 429
    Scope? One process; many threads
    Algorithm? Token bucket by default, swappable

    P6.2Entities and responsibilities

    Class Responsibility
    Limiter One decision: may this request proceed?
    TokenBucket Capacity and refill rate; allows bursts, smooth long-term rate
    SlidingWindowLog Exact limit over any trailing window; one timestamp per request
    FixedWindow Counter per aligned window; cheap; boundary bursts
    KeyedRateLimiter One limiter per key, created by a factory with tier rules
    TimeSource Current time, injected

    P6.3Class diagram

    P6.4Key flows

    Algorithm Memory per key Accuracy Bursts Use when
    Token bucket Two numbers Smooth average rate Up to capacity Default for APIs
    Leaky bucket (queue) A queue Constant output rate Smoothed away Shaping traffic to a fixed rate
    Fixed window counter Two numbers Up to 2x at boundaries At boundaries Cheap, approximate quotas
    Sliding window log One timestamp per request Exact None beyond the limit Low limits where exactness matters
    Sliding window counter Two counters Close approximation Small High volume with near-exact limits

    P6.5Code

    TokenBucket.java: lazy refill, synchronized decision
    /** Holds up to `capacity` tokens, refilled continuously at `perSecond`; each request takes one. Allows bursts. */
class TokenBucket implements Limiter {
    private final long capacity;
    private final double refillPerNano;
    private final TimeSource time;
    private double tokens;                 // guarded by this
    private long lastRefill;               // guarded by this

    TokenBucket(long capacity, double perSecond, TimeSource time) {
        if (capacity <= 0 || perSecond < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("bad bucket config");
        this.capacity = capacity;
        this.refillPerNano = perSecond / 1_000_000_000.0;
        this.time = time;
        this.tokens = capacity;            // start full
        this.lastRefill = time.nanos();
    }

    public synchronized boolean tryAcquire() {
        long now = time.nanos();
        tokens = Math.min(capacity, tokens + (now - lastRefill) * refillPerNano);   // lazy refill: no timer thread
        lastRefill = now;
        if (tokens < 1) return false;
        tokens -= 1;
        return true;
    }
}
    SlidingWindowLog.java
    /** At most `limit` requests in any window of `windowNanos`. Exact, but stores one timestamp per allowed request. */
class SlidingWindowLog implements Limiter {
    private final int limit;
    private final long windowNanos;
    private final TimeSource time;
    private final Deque<Long> accepted = new ArrayDeque<>();   // guarded by this

    SlidingWindowLog(int limit, long windowNanos, TimeSource time) {
        this.limit = limit;
        this.windowNanos = windowNanos;
        this.time = time;
    }

    public synchronized boolean tryAcquire() {
        long now = time.nanos();
        while (!accepted.isEmpty() && now - accepted.peekFirst() >= windowNanos) accepted.pollFirst();   // drop expired
        if (accepted.size() >= limit) return false;
        accepted.addLast(now);
        return true;
    }
}
    FixedWindow.java
    /** Counts requests per aligned window. Cheap, but allows up to 2x the limit across a window boundary. */
class FixedWindow implements Limiter {
    private final int limit;
    private final long windowNanos;
    private final TimeSource time;
    private long windowStart = Long.MIN_VALUE;   // guarded by this
    private int count;                           // guarded by this

    FixedWindow(int limit, long windowNanos, TimeSource time) {
        this.limit = limit;
        this.windowNanos = windowNanos;
        this.time = time;
    }

    public synchronized boolean tryAcquire() {
        long start = Math.floorDiv(time.nanos(), windowNanos) * windowNanos;
        if (start != windowStart) { windowStart = start; count = 0; }      // a new window resets the count
        if (count >= limit) return false;
        count++;
        return true;
    }
}
    KeyedRateLimiter.java
    /** One limiter per key (user, API key, IP), created on first use by a factory that can apply per-tier rules. */
class KeyedRateLimiter {
    private final Map<String, Limiter> limiters = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    private final Function<String, Limiter> factory;

    KeyedRateLimiter(Function<String, Limiter> factory) { this.factory = factory; }

    boolean tryAcquire(String key) {
        return limiters.computeIfAbsent(key, factory).tryAcquire();   // one limiter per key, even under races
    }
}

    Demo.java (complete)
    public class Demo {
    static final long SECOND = 1_000_000_000L;

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        AtomicLong now = new AtomicLong(0);
        TimeSource clock = now::get;                                   // manual time for the demo

        TokenBucket bucket = new TokenBucket(5, 1.0, clock);          // burst of 5, then 1 per second
        int burst = count(bucket, 10);                                 // 5 allowed at t = 0
        now.addAndGet(3 * SECOND);
        int later = count(bucket, 10);                                 // 3 tokens refilled by t = 3 s
        System.out.println("token bucket: " + burst + " allowed in a burst, " + later + " allowed 3 s later");
        check(burst == 5 && later == 3, "bucket");

        now.set(0);
        Limiter fixed = new FixedWindow(10, 60 * SECOND, clock);
        Limiter sliding = new SlidingWindowLog(10, 60 * SECOND, clock);
        now.set(59 * SECOND);                                          // end of the first minute
        int f1 = count(fixed, 10), s1 = count(sliding, 10);
        now.set(61 * SECOND);                                          // two seconds later, a new fixed window
        int f2 = count(fixed, 10), s2 = count(sliding, 10);
        System.out.println("within 2 seconds: fixed window allowed " + (f1 + f2) + ", sliding log allowed " + (s1 + s2));
        check(f1 + f2 == 20 && s1 + s2 == 10, "boundary");

        KeyedRateLimiter api = new KeyedRateLimiter(key ->
                key.startsWith("premium:") ? new TokenBucket(100, 50, clock) : new TokenBucket(10, 5, clock));
        int free = 0, premium = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < 200; i++) { if (api.tryAcquire("free:u1")) free++; if (api.tryAcquire("premium:u2")) premium++; }
        System.out.println("per-key tiers: free key got " + free + ", premium key got " + premium);
        check(free == 10 && premium == 100, "tiers");

        // 8 threads, one key, 100 tokens, no refill: exactly 100 succeed
        KeyedRateLimiter shared = new KeyedRateLimiter(k -> new TokenBucket(100, 0, clock));
        AtomicInteger ok = new AtomicInteger();
        ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8);
        for (int t = 0; t < 8; t++) pool.submit(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) if (shared.tryAcquire("hot")) ok.incrementAndGet(); });
        pool.shutdown();
        check(pool.awaitTermination(20, TimeUnit.SECONDS), "finished");
        System.out.println("8 threads, 8,000 attempts, 100 tokens: " + ok.get() + " allowed");
        check(ok.get() == 100, "concurrency");
    }

    static int count(Limiter l, int attempts) {
        int ok = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < attempts; i++) if (l.tryAcquire()) ok++;
        return ok;
    }

    static void check(boolean ok, String what) { if (!ok) throw new AssertionError(what); }
}

    token bucket: 5 allowed in a burst, 3 allowed 3 s later

    P6.6Concurrency

    Two levels of shared state, two tools:

    • The map of limiters. computeIfAbsent guarantees one limiter per key even when the first two requests for a key race. A get followed by put would let both create their own bucket, doubling the limit.
    • Each limiter's counters. Refill-then-take is a read-modify-write, so tryAcquire is synchronized on the limiter. Different keys never contend; the same hot key serializes, which is correct.

    A lock-free alternative for the token bucket stores tokens and the last refill time in one immutable object inside an AtomicReference and updates it with a compare-and-set loop. It avoids blocking but retries under heavy contention on one key; the synchronized version is easier to get right in an interview.

    Watch out

    Use a monotonic clock (System.nanoTime) for elapsed time, not wall-clock time: wall clocks can jump backward with NTP adjustments, which would produce negative refills or stuck windows.

    P6.7Deep dives

    Guided designExtensions interviewers ask forAnswer each before revealing
    1. 1
      Idle keys fill memory

      Millions of IPs hit the API once each. The map grows forever.

      Write your answer, then reveal

      Expire idle limiters: store the last access time and periodically remove entries idle long enough to be back at their starting state (for a token bucket, capacity / rate seconds, when it is full again; for windows, one window length). Dropping such an entry changes nothing, because a fresh limiter behaves the same. Remove with map.remove(key, limiter) so a limiter replaced in the meantime is not deleted by mistake. Or use a bounded cache with expire-after-access (Caffeine) as the map.

    2. 2
      Several application instances

      The service runs on 10 servers behind a load balancer.

      Write your answer, then reveal

      Giving each instance a tenth of the limit works only if the load balancer spreads each key's traffic evenly, which it usually does not. For a global limit, keep counters in Redis and make the check atomic there (a Lua script for the token bucket, or INCR with EXPIRE for fixed windows). Keep a small local limiter as a first line of defense to protect Redis.

    3. 3
      Different limits per endpoint

      /search is cheap, /export is expensive.

      Write your answer, then reveal

      Key the limiter by apiKey + endpoint, or give requests a cost: tryAcquire(cost) takes cost tokens. Rules come from a configuration map from (tier, endpoint) to (capacity, rate), applied by the factory.

    4. 4
      Tell the client when to retry

      Return a Retry-After header.

      Write your answer, then reveal

      Return a decision object instead of a boolean: allowed, remaining, and retryAfter. For a token bucket, retryAfter is the time until one token refills: (1 - tokens) / refillRate.

    P6.8Machine coding plan

    Minutes Do
    0-7 Clarify keys, rules, burst behavior, threads
    7-15 Limiter, TimeSource
    15-35 TokenBucket with lazy refill; manual-time test of burst and refill
    35-50 SlidingWindowLog or FixedWindow; the boundary test
    50-62 KeyedRateLimiter with tier factory
    62-75 Thread-pool test on one key; walk through Redis for multi-instance

    P6.9What a strong answer shows

    • SDE-2 bar: two algorithms behind one interface; per-key limiters created atomically; synchronized decisions; injected time; correct concurrency test.
    • Above the bar: compares algorithms on memory, accuracy, and bursts; explains the boundary problem; monotonic time; idle-key cleanup; how the design moves to Redis across instances.
    Follow-up questionsPractice saying the answer out loud
    1. Why is lazy refill better than a scheduled task that adds tokens every second?
      Reveal

      No background thread per key, no timer drift, and exact refill at any granularity: tokens are computed from elapsed time whenever a request arrives.

    2. Why does the bucket start full?
      Reveal

      So a new client can make a burst immediately. Starting empty would reject the first requests of every new key, which feels broken. Choose deliberately and say it.

    3. What would go wrong with if (!map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, newBucket())?
      Reveal

      Two concurrent first requests can both create buckets; one overwrites the other, and requests already counted against the lost bucket do not count. computeIfAbsent makes creation atomic.

    4. How do you test a rate limiter without sleeping?
      Reveal

      Inject a manual time source, advance it explicitly between calls, and assert exact counts.

    Problem 7: Expense sharing (Splitwise)

    The most common machine coding problem at Indian product companies, and a test of three things: split types as strategies, money that never loses a paisa, and a balance model that nets debts in both directions. Debt simplification is the classic follow-up.

    Try it first60 minutes

    Users add expenses paid by one person and shared by several, split equally, by exact amounts, or by percentages. Show who owes whom, support settle-up, and simplify debts. Then compare.

    Reveal the answer

    Strong answer: SplitStrategy per split type chosen by a factory; amounts in paise (long) with explicit handling of leftover paise; Expense validated so shares add up to the total; a BalanceSheet of pairwise net debts that never stores both directions; show(user) and settle-up; and a simplification that computes each user's net position and matches largest debtor with largest creditor, giving at most n - 1 transfers.

    P7.1Requirements

    Question Assumed answer
    Split types? Equal, exact amounts, percentages; more may come
    Money? Rupees with paise; no floating point; shares must add up exactly
    Who can be in an expense? Any registered users, including the payer
    Output? Lines like "Ravi owes Asha: 216.66"; only non-zero balances
    Groups? Out of scope at first; a likely follow-up
    Settle up? A payment that reduces a debt; cannot exceed what is owed

    Invariants: the shares of an expense add up to exactly its amount; between two users, at most one direction of debt is stored; the sum of all net positions is zero.

    P7.2Entities and responsibilities

    Class Responsibility
    User (record) ID and name
    Split (record) One user's share in paise
    Expense (record) Payer, amount, shares; rejects shares that do not add up
    SplitStrategy Turns an amount, users, and inputs into shares
    EqualSplit, ExactSplit, PercentSplit One rule each, including leftover paise
    SplitFactory Maps a SplitType to its strategy
    BalanceSheet Pairwise net debts; settle-up; net positions
    DebtSimplifier Net positions to a short list of transfers
    ExpenseService Use cases: add user, add expense, settle, show, simplify

    P7.3Class diagram

    P7.4Key flows

    Adding an expense: validate users and amount, ask the strategy for shares, build the Expense (which re-checks the total), then for every share record "share owner owes payer that amount" in the balance sheet. The payer's own share nets to nothing because addDebt ignores a debt to oneself.

    P7.5Code

    SplitStrategy.java
    interface SplitStrategy {
    /** @param values per-user inputs: unused for EQUAL, paise for EXACT, percent for PERCENT */
    List<Split> split(long amountPaise, List<String> users, List<Long> values);
}
    EqualSplit.java: the leftover paisa is assigned, not lost
    class EqualSplit implements SplitStrategy {
    public List<Split> split(long amount, List<String> users, List<Long> ignored) {
        long base = amount / users.size();
        long leftover = amount % users.size();             // e.g. 100.00 / 3 leaves 1 paisa
        List<Split> out = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < users.size(); i++) {
            out.add(new Split(users.get(i), base + (i < leftover ? 1 : 0)));   // first users absorb the leftover paise
        }
        return out;
    }
}
    PercentSplit.java: floor, then hand out the remainder
    class PercentSplit implements SplitStrategy {
    public List<Split> split(long amount, List<String> users, List<Long> percents) {
        if (percents.size() != users.size()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("one percent per user");
        if (percents.stream().mapToLong(Long::longValue).sum() != 100) throw new IllegalArgumentException("percents must add up to 100");
        List<Split> out = new ArrayList<>();
        long assigned = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < users.size(); i++) {
            long share = amount * percents.get(i) / 100;   // floor
            out.add(new Split(users.get(i), share));
            assigned += share;
        }
        // hand out the paise lost to flooring, one each, in order
        for (int i = 0; assigned < amount; i = (i + 1) % out.size(), assigned++) {
            Split s = out.get(i);
            out.set(i, new Split(s.userId(), s.amountPaise() + 1));
        }
        return out;
    }
}
    BalanceSheet.java: net in both directions
    /** Pairwise net debts: owes.get(a).get(b) > 0 means a owes b that many paise. Never both directions at once. */
class BalanceSheet {
    private final Map<String, Map<String, Long>> owes = new TreeMap<>();   // sorted: stable output

    synchronized void addDebt(String debtor, String creditor, long amount) {
        if (debtor.equals(creditor) || amount == 0) return;
        long reverse = get(creditor, debtor);                 // creditor already owes debtor?
        if (reverse >= amount) {
            put(creditor, debtor, reverse - amount);          // net it off
        } else {
            put(creditor, debtor, 0);
            put(debtor, creditor, get(debtor, creditor) + amount - reverse);
        }
    }

    /** A settle-up payment from `payer` to `payee` is a debt in the opposite direction. */
    synchronized void recordPayment(String payer, String payee, long amount) {
        if (amount > get(payer, payee)) throw new IllegalArgumentException(payer + " owes " + payee + " only " + get(payer, payee));
        addDebt(payee, payer, amount);
    }

    synchronized long get(String debtor, String creditor) {
        return owes.getOrDefault(debtor, Map.of()).getOrDefault(creditor, 0L);
    }

    /** Net position per user: positive = is owed money, negative = owes money. */
    synchronized Map<String, Long> netPositions() {
        Map<String, Long> net = new TreeMap<>();
        owes.forEach((d, m) -> m.forEach((c, amt) -> {
            net.merge(d, -amt, Long::sum);
            net.merge(c, amt, Long::sum);
        }));
        return net;
    }

    synchronized Map<String, Long> debtsOf(String user) {
        return new LinkedHashMap<>(owes.getOrDefault(user, Map.of()));
    }

    private void put(String d, String c, long amt) {
        Map<String, Long> m = owes.computeIfAbsent(d, k -> new TreeMap<>());
        if (amt == 0) m.remove(c); else m.put(c, amt);
        if (m.isEmpty()) owes.remove(d);
    }
}
    DebtSimplifier.java: greedy on net positions
    class DebtSimplifier {
    /** Settles net positions with at most n - 1 transfers: largest debtor pays largest creditor, repeat. */
    List<Transfer> simplify(Map<String, Long> net) {
        Comparator<long[]> byAmount = Comparator.comparingLong((long[] a) -> a[1]).reversed();
        PriorityQueue<long[]> creditors = new PriorityQueue<>(byAmount);   // [userIndex, amount]
        PriorityQueue<long[]> debtors = new PriorityQueue<>(byAmount);
        List<String> ids = new ArrayList<>(net.keySet());
        for (int i = 0; i < ids.size(); i++) {
            long v = net.get(ids.get(i));
            if (v > 0) creditors.add(new long[] {i, v});
            else if (v < 0) debtors.add(new long[] {i, -v});
        }
        List<Transfer> out = new ArrayList<>();
        while (!creditors.isEmpty() && !debtors.isEmpty()) {
            long[] c = creditors.poll(), d = debtors.poll();
            long x = Math.min(c[1], d[1]);
            out.add(new Transfer(ids.get((int) d[0]), ids.get((int) c[0]), x));
            if (c[1] > x) creditors.add(new long[] {c[0], c[1] - x});
            if (d[1] > x) debtors.add(new long[] {d[0], d[1] - x});
        }
        return out;
    }
}
    ExpenseService.java
    class ExpenseService {
    private final Map<String, User> users = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();   // users may be added while expenses are
    private final List<Expense> expenses = new ArrayList<>();
    private final SplitFactory splits;
    private final BalanceSheet balances;
    private final AtomicLong ids = new AtomicLong(1);

    ExpenseService(SplitFactory splits, BalanceSheet balances) { this.splits = splits; this.balances = balances; }

    void addUser(User u) {
        if (users.putIfAbsent(u.id(), u) != null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("duplicate user " + u.id());
    }

    Expense addExpense(String paidBy, long amountPaise, SplitType type, List<String> participants, List<Long> values, String note) {
        requireUser(paidBy);
        participants.forEach(this::requireUser);
        if (amountPaise <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("amount must be positive");
        List<Split> shares = splits.forType(type).split(amountPaise, participants, values);
        Expense e = new Expense("E" + ids.getAndIncrement(), paidBy, amountPaise, note, shares);
        synchronized (this) {
            expenses.add(e);
            for (Split s : shares) balances.addDebt(s.userId(), paidBy, s.amountPaise());   // everyone owes the payer
        }
        return e;
    }

    void settle(String payer, String payee, long amountPaise) { balances.recordPayment(payer, payee, amountPaise); }

    List<String> show(String userId) {
        List<String> out = new ArrayList<>();
        balances.debtsOf(userId).forEach((c, amt) -> out.add(name(userId) + " owes " + name(c) + ": " + rupees(amt)));
        return out;
    }

    List<String> simplified() {
        List<String> out = new ArrayList<>();
        for (Transfer t : new DebtSimplifier().simplify(balances.netPositions()))
            out.add(name(t.from()) + " pays " + name(t.to()) + ": " + rupees(t.amountPaise()));
        return out;
    }

    private void requireUser(String id) { if (!users.containsKey(id)) throw new IllegalArgumentException("unknown user " + id); }
    private String name(String id) { return users.get(id).name(); }
    static String rupees(long paise) { return paise / 100 + "." + String.format("%02d", paise % 100); }
}

    import java.util.List;

record Expense(String id, String paidBy, long amountPaise, String description, List<Split> splits) {
    Expense {
        long sum = splits.stream().mapToLong(Split::amountPaise).sum();
        if (sum != amountPaise) throw new IllegalArgumentException("splits add up to " + sum + ", not " + amountPaise);
        splits = List.copyOf(splits);
    }
}
    SplitType.java
    enum SplitType { EQUAL, EXACT, PERCENT }
    ExactSplit.java
    import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

class ExactSplit implements SplitStrategy {
    public List<Split> split(long amount, List<String> users, List<Long> exact) {
        if (exact.size() != users.size()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("one amount per user");
        long sum = exact.stream().mapToLong(Long::longValue).sum();
        if (sum != amount) throw new IllegalArgumentException("exact amounts add up to " + sum + " paise, not " + amount);
        List<Split> out = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < users.size(); i++) out.add(new Split(users.get(i), exact.get(i)));
        return out;
    }
}
    SplitFactory.java
    import java.util.EnumMap;
import java.util.Map;

class SplitFactory {
    private final Map<SplitType, SplitStrategy> strategies = new EnumMap<>(SplitType.class);

    SplitFactory() {
        strategies.put(SplitType.EQUAL, new EqualSplit());
        strategies.put(SplitType.EXACT, new ExactSplit());
        strategies.put(SplitType.PERCENT, new PercentSplit());
    }

    SplitStrategy forType(SplitType type) { return strategies.get(type); }
}

    public class Demo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        ExpenseService app = new ExpenseService(new SplitFactory(), new BalanceSheet());
        for (String[] u : new String[][] {{"u1", "Asha"}, {"u2", "Ravi"}, {"u3", "Meera"}, {"u4", "Kabir"}}) app.addUser(new User(u[0], u[1]));

        app.addExpense("u1", 100_000, SplitType.EQUAL, List.of("u1", "u2", "u3", "u4"), List.of(), "dinner");  // 1,000 / 4
        app.addExpense("u2", 10_000, SplitType.EQUAL, List.of("u1", "u2", "u3"), List.of(), "cab");            // 100 / 3
        app.addExpense("u3", 120_000, SplitType.EXACT, List.of("u1", "u2", "u3", "u4"),
                List.of(30_000L, 20_000L, 40_000L, 30_000L), "groceries");
        app.addExpense("u4", 50_000, SplitType.PERCENT, List.of("u1", "u4"), List.of(40L, 60L), "tickets");
        for (String u : List.of("u1", "u2", "u3", "u4")) app.show(u).forEach(System.out::println);
        System.out.println("-- simplified --");
        List<String> plan = app.simplified();
        plan.forEach(System.out::println);
        check(plan.size() <= 3, "at most n - 1 transfers");
        try { app.addExpense("u1", 1_000, SplitType.EXACT, List.of("u1", "u2"), List.of(500L, 400L), "bad"); throw new AssertionError(); }
        catch (IllegalArgumentException e) { System.out.println("rejected: " + e.getMessage()); }
        check(new EqualSplit().split(10_000, List.of("a", "b", "c"), List.of()).stream().mapToLong(Split::amountPaise).sum() == 10_000, "no paisa lost");
    }

    static void check(boolean ok, String what) { if (!ok) throw new AssertionError(what); }
}

    Check one line by hand: Ravi owes Asha 250.00 for dinner, Asha owes Ravi 33.34 for the cab (she absorbed the leftover paisa as the first participant), so Ravi owes Asha 216.66 net.

    P7.6Hard parts

    Money. long paise everywhere; conversion to rupees only when printing. Every division (equal and percent) produces leftover paise, and the strategy must assign them deterministically so shares add up. Expense re-validates the sum, so a buggy new strategy fails loudly instead of corrupting balances.

    Netting. Without netting, "Asha owes Ravi 33.34" and "Ravi owes Asha 250.00" both exist and the display is confusing. addDebt subtracts from the reverse direction first.

    Simplification. Minimizing the number of transfers exactly is NP-hard in general (it hides a subset-sum problem). The greedy on net positions is the standard answer: it never needs more than n - 1 transfers and runs in O(n log n). Say both facts.

    Concurrency. Two users adding expenses at once both update the balance sheet: its methods are synchronized, and the service adds the expense and its debts in one synchronized block so readers never see half an expense. With a database, an expense and its ledger rows go in one transaction.

    P7.7Deep dives

    Guided designExtensions interviewers ask forAnswer each before revealing
    1. 1
      Groups

      Expenses belong to groups (a trip, a flat), and balances are shown per group and overall.

      Write your answer, then reveal

      Add a Group (ID, name, members) and a groupId on Expense. Keep one BalanceSheet per group plus an overall one (or derive overall by summing group sheets). Validate that every participant is a member of the group.

    2. 2
      A new split type: by shares (2:1:1)

      How does it fit?

      Write your answer, then reveal

      A ShareSplit strategy: total shares = sum of inputs, each user gets amount * share / total floored, leftover paise handed out in order. Register it in the factory. Nothing else changes, which is the point of the strategy.

    3. 3
      Edit or delete an expense

      A user fixes a wrong amount.

      Write your answer, then reveal

      Never edit balances in place. Reverse the old expense (add the opposite debts) and apply the new one, or recompute balances from the expense list. Keep an audit trail of versions. Simplest correct approach: balances are derived data, rebuildable from expenses.

    4. 4
      Multiple currencies

      A trip abroad mixes rupees and dollars.

      Write your answer, then reveal

      Store amount and currency on each expense, keep a balance sheet per currency (do not convert silently), and convert only at settlement using a rate captured at that time. Money becomes a value object with a currency (Module 1).

    P7.9What a strong answer shows

    • SDE-2 bar: strategies for split types; paise as long; shares that always add up; netted pairwise balances; clear output; validation errors.
    • Above the bar: explains why exact minimization is NP-hard and why greedy gives at most n - 1 transfers; treats balances as derived data for edits; per-currency sheets; synchronized updates or a transaction around expense plus ledger.
    Follow-up questionsPractice saying the answer out loud
    1. Why long paise instead of BigDecimal?
      Reveal

      All amounts are whole paise and sums fit easily in a long, so integer arithmetic is exact and fast. BigDecimal works too; choose one and never mix in double.

    2. Who gets the leftover paisa in an equal split, and does it matter?
      Reveal

      Any deterministic rule works (first participants, or the payer); what matters is that it is consistent, documented, and the shares add up exactly.

    3. Why does Expense validate the sum when the strategy already did?
      Reveal

      Defense in depth: the record's invariant holds regardless of which strategy produced the shares, including future ones.

    4. How would you show "you are owed 216.66 in total"?
      Reveal

      Read the user's net position from netPositions(): positive means owed, negative means owing.

    Problem 8Core60 min LLD / 90 min coding

    Problem 8: Elevator system

    The elevator problem tests whether you can model behavior over time: each car is a state machine that serves stops in sweeps (LOOK), a dispatcher strategy picks a car for each hall call, and a single-writer controller turns button presses from many threads into safe, ordered updates. A tick-based simulation makes it all testable.

    Uses: M7 state machines, M6 strategy, M9 producer-consumer

    Try it first60 minutes

    Design a controller for N elevator cars in a building with F floors: hall buttons (up and down at each floor), car buttons (destination floors), and a policy for which car answers a call. Show how a car decides where to go next and how concurrent button presses are handled.

    Reveal the answer

    Strong answer: an Elevator that keeps up and down stop sets and runs LOOK (continue while there are stops ahead, then reverse); hall calls carry the direction the passenger wants; car buttons derive direction from the car's position; a DispatchStrategy (nearest car, with a cost for cars that must finish a sweep first); an ElevatorSystem that queues commands from any thread and applies them on one controller thread per tick; a state diagram for idle, moving, doors open, and out of service.

    P8.1Requirements

    Question Assumed answer
    Cars and floors? N cars, floors 0 to F - 1
    Buttons? Hall: up or down at each floor. Car: any floor
    Scheduling? Serve in sweeps; do not change direction while stops remain ahead
    Car choice? Minimize the estimated time to reach the caller
    Concurrency? Buttons are pressed at any time from many places
    Out of scope Weight limits, door sensors, express zones (likely follow-ups)

    Invariants: a car never moves beyond the top or bottom floor; doors open only when stopped at a floor; every accepted request is eventually served while the car is in service; a passenger who wants to go down is not picked up by a car that is going up (unless that floor is where it turns).

    P8.2Entities and responsibilities

    Class Responsibility
    Direction (enum) UP, DOWN, IDLE
    Elevator Position, direction, up and down stop sets; one simulation step at a time using LOOK
    DispatchStrategy Chooses a car for a hall call
    NearestCarStrategy Cost = distance if the caller is on the way, else finish the sweep and come back
    ElevatorSystem Command inbox, cars, dispatch, the tick loop, the event log
