    Key idea

    Why a stack of write layers and not an undo log? Both work for one client. An undo log writes into the shared store at once and undoes on rollback, so other clients would see uncommitted values (a dirty read). Layers keep uncommitted writes private until the outermost commit, which is what "other clients see only committed data" requires. The undo-log version (Module 7) is the right answer only when the prompt has a single client.

    P16.6Concurrency

    Race Defense
    A reader sees half of a commit commit holds the write lock while applying every write; readers take the read lock, so they see all of it or none
    Two transactions write the same key Each records the key's version on first touch; commit checks every recorded version under the write lock; the second commit gets ConflictException
    Read X, write Y, while another commit changes X Reads are recorded too, so the commit fails; this prevents decisions made on stale data (write skew)
    Two threads share one session Not supported: a session is one client's state, like a database connection; give each thread its own
    Purge runs during reads Purge takes the write lock; reads never depend on purge because they check expiry themselves
    Watch out

    The classic bug in this problem: incr written as get then put in two steps, with no version check. Eight threads doing 500 increments each end with fewer than 4,000 because two threads read the same value and both write value + 1. The demo's counter is the test for exactly that, and it passes only because conflicting commits fail and retry.

    In production

    This is optimistic concurrency control, the scheme behind Redis WATCH / MULTI / EXEC (a watched key changed, so EXEC returns nil and the client retries) and behind conditional writes in DynamoDB. Databases such as PostgreSQL use multiversion concurrency control instead: each transaction reads from a snapshot taken at its start, and conflicting writes to one row are detected at write time.

    P16.7Deep dives

    Guided designExtensions interviewers ask forAnswer each before revealing
    1. 1
      COUNT(value): how many keys hold this value

      The classic follow-up, and it must stay fast inside transactions.

      Write your answer, then reveal

      Keep a reverse index value -> count in the store, updated in commit for each write (decrement the old value, increment the new). Inside a transaction, the count must include pending writes: compute it as the store's count plus a delta from the layers (for each key the layers change, subtract its committed value's count and add its pending value's). Expired entries complicate it: either purge before counting or count only live entries, and say which.

    2. 2
      Snapshot reads

      Reads here see the latest committed value, so a long transaction can read X before a commit and Y after it.

      Write your answer, then reveal

      The commit check catches it (X's version changed), so committed results are still correct, but the transaction may compute with an inconsistent view before failing. Snapshot reads fix that: keep a few versions per key and have each transaction read the newest version not newer than its start version. That is multiversion concurrency control; old versions are garbage-collected once no open transaction can read them.

    3. 3
      Durability

      The process restarts and data must survive.

      Write your answer, then reveal

      A write-ahead log: on each outermost commit, append the transaction's writes as one record and flush before acknowledging, then apply to memory. On restart, replay the log. Periodic snapshots bound replay time; the log is truncated after a snapshot. Redis offers both (AOF and RDB).

    4. 4
      Active expiry

      Millions of keys expire and are never read again.

      Write your answer, then reveal

      Lazy expiry alone leaks memory. Add a sweeper: a DelayQueue or a min-heap by expiry time, polled by a background thread that removes due keys under the write lock (checking the entry is still the same version, since the key may have been rewritten). Redis samples random keys with a TTL several times a second instead of keeping a heap.

    P16.8Machine coding plan

    Minutes Do
    0-8 Clarify nesting rules, visibility, TTL, concurrency; write the invariants
    8-25 Store with get / put / delete; a command driver reading lines like SET a 10
    25-50 Session layers: begin, nested rollback, commit merging; tombstones for deletes
    50-65 TTL with an injected clock; lazy expiry; purge
    65-80 Versions and the commit check; the concurrent counter test
    80-90 Walk through COUNT, snapshots, and the write-ahead log

    P16.9What a strong answer shows

    • SDE-2 bar: layered pending writes with read-your-writes; tombstones; nested rollback and commit; outermost commit applied atomically; lazy TTL with an injected clock.
    • Above the bar: versions checked at commit with a retry loop; why layers beat an undo log with many clients; COUNT with transaction deltas; snapshot reads and the write-ahead log.
    Follow-up questionsPractice saying the answer out loud
    1. Why does a delete inside a transaction need a tombstone instead of removing the key from the layer?
      Reveal

      Removing it from the layer would make the read fall through to the store and return the committed value, so the delete would be invisible. The tombstone says "absent" and stops the search at that layer.

    2. An inner transaction commits and then the outer one rolls back. What does the store contain?
      Reveal

      Nothing from either. An inner commit only merges into its parent layer; the outer rollback drops that layer with everything merged into it.

    3. Why inject the clock?
      Reveal

      TTL tests must not sleep. With a clock passed in, the test moves time forward 31 seconds instantly and checks the key reads as absent.

    4. Why a read-write lock rather than a ConcurrentHashMap?
      Reveal

      A commit changes several keys and must appear all at once. ConcurrentHashMap makes each key's update atomic, not a group of them; the write lock makes the whole commit one step for every reader.

    Problem 17: Ride-hailing matching

    Uber and Ola in LLD form. Three ideas carry it: a spatial index so "drivers near me" does not scan the whole city, an atomic claim on the driver so two riders never get the same car, and a price locked in when the ride is booked. Everything else (matching rule, surge rule, fare formula) is a strategy you can swap.

    Uses: M9 atomics, M6 strategy, M7 state machines, M10 collections

    Try it first45 minutes

    Design the core of a ride-hailing app: drivers go online and send locations; a rider requests a ride of a vehicle type; the system assigns the nearest available driver within a radius; the driver starts and completes the trip and a fare is computed with surge pricing; the rider can cancel before pickup. Thousands of requests arrive at once. Then compare.

    Reveal the answer

    Strong answer: a GridIndex of cells to drivers, so a nearby search scans only the cells a radius can touch; Driver with an atomic status (OFFLINE, AVAILABLE, ON_TRIP) and a compare-and-set tryReserve; a RideService that ranks candidates with a MatchingStrategy and reserves the first one still free, moving on when one is taken; one active ride per rider via putIfAbsent; a Trip state machine (ASSIGNED, STARTED, COMPLETED, CANCELLED) with driver and rider checks; surge computed at request time and stored on the trip; PricingStrategy for the fare; and release of the driver on both end states.

    P17.1Requirements

    Question Assumed answer
    Drivers? Go online and offline; send a location every few seconds; one vehicle type each
    Matching? Nearest available driver of the requested type within 3 km; no driver means a clear error
    Trip lifecycle? Assigned, started by the driver at pickup, completed by the driver with the distance driven
    Cancellation? Rider may cancel before pickup; the driver becomes available again
    Pricing? Base fare plus a per-km rate by vehicle type, times a surge multiplier fixed when the ride is booked
    Surge? Fewer free drivers near the pickup means a higher multiplier
    Out of scope Payments, ratings, driver accept/decline, routing and ETA (deep dives)

    Invariants: a driver is on at most one trip; a rider has at most one active ride; only the trip's driver starts and completes it; the surge on a trip never changes after booking; every trip that ends frees its driver exactly once.

    P17.2Entities and responsibilities

    Class Responsibility
    Driver Atomic status, latest location; tryReserve, release, goOnline, goOffline
    GridIndex Drivers by 1 km cell; moves a driver between cells; near(point, radius)
    Trip Rider, driver, surge, fare; status changed only through checked moves
    TripStatus, DriverStatus (enums) The two state machines
    MatchingStrategy Order to try candidates in (nearest first)
    SurgePolicy, PricingStrategy Multiplier from supply; fare from type, distance, surge
    RideService Request, start, complete, cancel; one active ride per rider

    P17.5Code

    RideService.java: rank, reserve, move on
    class RideService {
    private final GridIndex index = new GridIndex(1.0);                    // 1 km cells
    private final Map<String, Driver> drivers = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    private final Map<String, Trip> trips = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    private final Map<String, String> activeTripOfRider = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    private final AtomicLong tripSeq = new AtomicLong();
    private final MatchingStrategy matching;
    private final SurgePolicy surge;
    private final PricingStrategy pricing;
    private final double radiusKm;

    RideService(MatchingStrategy matching, SurgePolicy surge, PricingStrategy pricing, double radiusKm) {
        this.matching = matching; this.surge = surge; this.pricing = pricing; this.radiusKm = radiusKm;
    }

    void addDriver(Driver d) { drivers.put(d.id(), d); index.add(d); }
    void updateLocation(String driverId, Location at) { index.update(driver(driverId), at); }

    Trip requestRide(String riderId, Location pickup, Location drop, VehicleType type) {
        String tripId = "T" + tripSeq.incrementAndGet();                   // a refused request just skips a number
        if (activeTripOfRider.putIfAbsent(riderId, tripId) != null)          // one live ride per rider
            throw new IllegalStateException(riderId + " already has an active ride");
        try {
            List<Driver> ranked = matching.rank(index.near(pickup, radiusKm), pickup, type);
            int surgePercent = surge.multiplierPercent(ranked.size());
            for (Driver d : ranked) {
                if (!d.tryReserve()) continue;                               // taken a moment ago: try the next
                Trip t = new Trip(tripId, riderId, d, pickup, drop, surgePercent);
                trips.put(tripId, t);
                return t;
            }
            throw new NoDriverException("no " + type + " within " + radiusKm + " km of " + riderId);
        } catch (RuntimeException e) {
            activeTripOfRider.remove(riderId, tripId);
            throw e;
        }
    }

    void startTrip(String tripId, String driverId) { trip(tripId).start(driverId); }

    long completeTrip(String tripId, String driverId, long meters) {
        Trip t = trip(tripId);
        long fare = t.complete(driverId, meters, pricing);
        finish(t);
        return fare;
    }

    void cancelTrip(String tripId, String riderId) {
        Trip t = trip(tripId);
        t.cancel(riderId);                                                   // throws once the ride has started
        finish(t);
    }

    private void finish(Trip t) {                                            // runs once: only one terminal move succeeds
        driver(t.driverId()).release();
        activeTripOfRider.remove(t.riderId(), t.id());
    }

    Driver driver(String id) {
        Driver d = drivers.get(id);
        if (d == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("no driver " + id);
        return d;
    }

    Trip trip(String id) {
        Trip t = trips.get(id);
        if (t == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("no trip " + id);
        return t;
    }
}
    Driver.java: one atomic status
    class Driver {
    private final String id;
    private final VehicleType type;
    private final AtomicReference<DriverStatus> status = new AtomicReference<>(DriverStatus.OFFLINE);
    private volatile Location location;                         // written by GridIndex.update under this driver's lock

    Driver(String id, VehicleType type, Location at) { this.id = id; this.type = type; this.location = at; }

    /** The only way a driver gets a trip: one compare-and-set, so two requests can never both win. */
    boolean tryReserve() { return status.compareAndSet(DriverStatus.AVAILABLE, DriverStatus.ON_TRIP); }

    void release() {
        if (!status.compareAndSet(DriverStatus.ON_TRIP, DriverStatus.AVAILABLE))
            throw new IllegalStateException(id + " is not on a trip");
    }

    boolean goOnline() { return status.compareAndSet(DriverStatus.OFFLINE, DriverStatus.AVAILABLE); }
    boolean goOffline() { return status.compareAndSet(DriverStatus.AVAILABLE, DriverStatus.OFFLINE); }   // not mid-trip

    boolean isAvailable() { return status.get() == DriverStatus.AVAILABLE; }
    String id() { return id; }
    VehicleType type() { return type; }
    Location location() { return location; }
    void moveTo(Location to) { location = to; }
}
    GridIndex.java: cells of drivers
    /** Drivers bucketed by square cells, so "who is near" scans a few cells instead of every driver. */
class GridIndex {
    private final double cellKm;
    private final Map<Long, Set<Driver>> cells = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    GridIndex(double cellKm) { this.cellKm = cellKm; }

    void add(Driver d) {
        synchronized (d) { cell(key(d.location())).add(d); }
    }

    /** Location pings for one driver are serialized by the driver's lock; the driver is never in two cells. */
    void update(Driver d, Location to) {
        synchronized (d) {
            long from = key(d.location()), next = key(to);
            if (from != next) {
                cell(from).remove(d);
                cell(next).add(d);
            }
            d.moveTo(to);
        }
    }

    /** Drivers within radiusKm: scan the cells the circle can touch, then filter by real distance. */
    List<Driver> near(Location p, double radiusKm) {
        int r = (int) Math.ceil(radiusKm / cellKm);
        long cx = (long) Math.floor(p.x() / cellKm), cy = (long) Math.floor(p.y() / cellKm);
        List<Driver> out = new ArrayList<>();
        for (long x = cx - r; x <= cx + r; x++)
            for (long y = cy - r; y <= cy + r; y++) {
                Set<Driver> s = cells.get(key(x, y));
                if (s == null) continue;
                for (Driver d : s) if (d.location().distanceTo(p) <= radiusKm) out.add(d);
            }
        return out;
    }

    private Set<Driver> cell(long key) { return cells.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet()); }
    private long key(Location l) { return key((long) Math.floor(l.x() / cellKm), (long) Math.floor(l.y() / cellKm)); }
    private static long key(long cx, long cy) { return (cx << 32) ^ (cy & 0xffffffffL); }
}
    Trip.java: checked moves
    class Trip {
    private final String id, riderId, driverId;
    private final Location pickup, drop;
    private final VehicleType type;
    private final int surgePercent;                            // locked in when the ride is booked
    private TripStatus status = TripStatus.ASSIGNED;           // guarded by this
    private long farePaise;                                    // guarded by this; set on completion

    Trip(String id, String riderId, Driver driver, Location pickup, Location drop, int surgePercent) {
        this.id = id; this.riderId = riderId; this.driverId = driver.id(); this.type = driver.type();
        this.pickup = pickup; this.drop = drop; this.surgePercent = surgePercent;
    }

    synchronized void start(String byDriver) {
        requireDriver(byDriver);
        move(TripStatus.STARTED);
    }

    synchronized long complete(String byDriver, long meters, PricingStrategy pricing) {
        requireDriver(byDriver);
        move(TripStatus.COMPLETED);
        farePaise = pricing.farePaise(type, meters, surgePercent);
        return farePaise;
    }

    synchronized void cancel(String byRider) {
        if (!riderId.equals(byRider)) throw new IllegalArgumentException(byRider + " did not book " + id);
        move(TripStatus.CANCELLED);
    }

    private void move(TripStatus to) {
        if (!status.canMoveTo(to)) throw new IllegalStateException(id + " cannot go from " + status + " to " + to);
        status = to;
    }

    private void requireDriver(String who) {
        if (!driverId.equals(who)) throw new IllegalArgumentException(who + " is not the driver of " + id);
    }

    String id() { return id; }
    String riderId() { return riderId; }
    String driverId() { return driverId; }
    int surgePercent() { return surgePercent; }
    synchronized TripStatus status() { return status; }
    synchronized long farePaise() { return farePaise; }
}

    TripStatus.java
    import java.util.Set;

enum TripStatus {
    ASSIGNED, STARTED, COMPLETED, CANCELLED;

    boolean canMoveTo(TripStatus to) {
        return switch (this) {
            case ASSIGNED -> Set.of(STARTED, CANCELLED).contains(to);
            case STARTED -> to == COMPLETED;                       // no cancelling a ride in progress
            case COMPLETED, CANCELLED -> false;
        };
    }
}
    DriverStatus.java
    enum DriverStatus { OFFLINE, AVAILABLE, ON_TRIP }
    Location.java
    /** A point on a flat city map, in kilometres. Real systems use latitude and longitude (see the deep dives). */
record Location(double x, double y) {
    double distanceTo(Location o) { return Math.hypot(x - o.x, y - o.y); }
}
    VehicleType.java
    enum VehicleType {
    AUTO(3_000, 1_500), MINI(4_000, 1_100), SEDAN(6_000, 1_500);

    final long basePaise, perKmPaise;

    MatchingStrategy.java
    import java.util.List;

interface MatchingStrategy {
    /** Candidates in the order to try them; the service reserves the first one still free. */
    List<Driver> rank(List<Driver> nearby, Location pickup, VehicleType type);
}
    NearestDriver.java
    import java.util.Comparator;
import java.util.List;

class NearestDriver implements MatchingStrategy {
    @Override
    public List<Driver> rank(List<Driver> nearby, Location pickup, VehicleType type) {
        return nearby.stream()
                .filter(d -> d.type() == type && d.isAvailable())
                .sorted(Comparator.comparingDouble((Driver d) -> d.location().distanceTo(pickup)).thenComparing(Driver::id))
                .toList();
    }
}
    SurgePolicy.java
    interface SurgePolicy {
    /** Price multiplier in percent (100 = no surge) from free drivers of the type near the pickup. */
    int multiplierPercent(int freeDriversNearby);
}
    SupplySurge.java
    class SupplySurge implements SurgePolicy {
    @Override
    public int multiplierPercent(int free) {
        if (free >= 3) return 100;
        return free == 2 ? 125 : 150;
    }
}
    PricingStrategy.java
    interface PricingStrategy {
    long farePaise(VehicleType type, long meters, int surgePercent);
}
    StandardPricing.java
    class StandardPricing implements PricingStrategy {
    @Override
    public long farePaise(VehicleType type, long meters, int surgePercent) {
        long base = type.basePaise + type.perKmPaise * meters / 1_000;
        return (base * surgePercent + 50) / 100;                  // rounded half up
    }
}

    class NoDriverException extends RuntimeException {
    NoDriverException(String message) { super(message); }

    // 10 drivers, 30 riders, each rider sends the request twice at the same moment
RideService busy = new RideService(new NearestDriver(), new SupplySurge(), new StandardPricing(), 3.0);
Location stadium = new Location(50, 50);
for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) {

ConcurrentLinkedQueue<Trip> booked = new ConcurrentLinkedQueue<>();
AtomicInteger noDriver = new AtomicInteger(), duplicate = new AtomicInteger();
CountDownLatch go = new CountDownLatch(1);
ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(16);
for (int i = 0; i < 60; i++) {
    String rider = "fan" + (i % 30);
    pool.submit(() -> {
        go.await();
        try { booked.add(busy.requestRide(rider, stadium, home, VehicleType.MINI)); }
        catch (NoDriverException e) { noDriver.incrementAndGet(); }
        catch (IllegalStateException e) { duplicate.incrementAndGet(); }
        return null;
    });
}
go.countDown();
pool.shutdown();
check(pool.awaitTermination(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS), "finished");

        svc.updateLocation("D2", office);                                  // D2 is now 8 km away, in another cell
        System.out.println(a.id() + " completed, 8 km, fare " + fare + " paise");

        Trip r2 = svc.requestRide("ravi", home, office, VehicleType.MINI);
        say(r2, "ravi");
        attempt(() -> svc.requestRide("ravi", home, office, VehicleType.MINI));

        Trip m = svc.requestRide("meera", home, office, VehicleType.SEDAN);
        say(m, "meera");
        svc.startTrip(m.id(), "D4");
        attempt(() -> svc.cancelTrip(m.id(), "meera"));
        attempt(() -> svc.requestRide("kiran", home, office, VehicleType.AUTO));
        check(fare == 12_800, "fare");
        check(r2.driverId().equals("D3") && r2.surgePercent() == 125, "rematch");

        // 10 drivers, 30 riders, each rider sends the request twice at the same moment
        RideService busy = new RideService(new NearestDriver(), new SupplySurge(), new StandardPricing(), 3.0);
        Location stadium = new Location(50, 50);
        for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
            Driver d = new Driver("S" + i, VehicleType.MINI, new Location(50 + i * 0.1, 50));
            busy.addDriver(d);
            d.goOnline();
        }
        ConcurrentLinkedQueue<Trip> booked = new ConcurrentLinkedQueue<>();
        AtomicInteger noDriver = new AtomicInteger(), duplicate = new AtomicInteger();
        CountDownLatch go = new CountDownLatch(1);
        ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(16);
        for (int i = 0; i < 60; i++) {
            String rider = "fan" + (i % 30);
            pool.submit(() -> {
                go.await();
                try { booked.add(busy.requestRide(rider, stadium, home, VehicleType.MINI)); }
                catch (NoDriverException e) { noDriver.incrementAndGet(); }
                catch (IllegalStateException e) { duplicate.incrementAndGet(); }
                return null;
            });
        }
        go.countDown();
        pool.shutdown();
        check(pool.awaitTermination(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS), "finished");
        Set<String> driversUsed = new HashSet<>(), riders = new HashSet<>();
        for (Trip t : booked) { driversUsed.add(t.driverId()); riders.add(t.riderId()); }
        check(booked.size() == 10, "every driver booked once");
        check(driversUsed.size() == 10, "no driver twice");
        check(riders.size() == 10, "no rider twice");
        check(noDriver.get() + duplicate.get() == 50, "the rest refused");
        System.out.println("30 riders x 2 requests at once for 10 drivers: 10 trips, 10 different drivers, no rider with two rides");
    }

    static void say(Trip t, String rider) {
        System.out.println(t.id() + ": " + rider + " -> " + t.driverId() + ", surge " + t.surgePercent() + "%");
    }

    static void attempt(Runnable r) {
        try { r.run(); } catch (RuntimeException e) { System.out.println("rejected: " + e.getMessage()); }
    }

    static void check(boolean ok, String what) { if (!ok) throw new AssertionError(what); }
}

    P17.6Concurrency

    Race Defense
    Two requests pick the same driver tryReserve is a compare-and-set from AVAILABLE to ON_TRIP; the loser tries its next candidate
    A rider double-taps "Book" activeTripOfRider.putIfAbsent; the second request fails at once; a failed request removes only its own entry
    A driver goes offline while being matched goOffline is a compare-and-set from AVAILABLE, so it fails once the driver is reserved, and a reserve fails once the driver is offline
    Rider cancels as the driver starts the trip Both go through Trip's synchronized moves; one wins, the other gets an illegal-move error
    A driver's location changes during a search Pings for one driver are serialized by the driver's lock; a search may see a slightly old position, which is fine for "near"
    Key idea

    The pattern is the same as parking spots in P1 and partners in P15: search without locks, then claim with one atomic step, and treat a failed claim as "try the next one". Locking the whole service, or even the whole cell, while searching would make every request in a busy area wait in line.

    Watch out

    Do not compute the fare from the surge at completion time. Surge can rise during a 40-minute ride, and the rider agreed to the multiplier shown when booking. Store it on the trip, the same reason P15 stores prices on the order.

    In production

    Real systems index locations with hexagonal cells (Uber's H3) or geohashes, keep driver locations in an in-memory store sharded by city, and match in short batches (every couple of seconds, solve an assignment problem over all waiting riders and free drivers) instead of greedily one request at a time, which gives lower total pickup time. The driver must also accept the offer, so assignment is an offer with a timeout, as in the P15 deep dive.

    P17.7Deep dives

    Guided designExtensions interviewers ask forAnswer each before revealing
    1. 1
      Latitude and longitude instead of a flat map

      Cells of 1 km and distance with hypot only work on a plane.

      Write your answer, then reveal

      Use the haversine formula for distance, and cells that are a fixed angle (a geohash prefix, or an H3 cell at a chosen resolution). A cell is about 1 km tall everywhere but narrower in longitude away from the equator, so scan neighbors by cell adjacency rather than a fixed count, and always filter by real distance. The design does not change: the index is behind near(point, radius).

    2. 2
      The driver can decline

      The driver has 15 seconds to accept the ride.

      Write your answer, then reveal

      Add OFFERED between reserving and assigning. Reserve the driver (so nobody else offers them the same ride), send the offer, start a timer (P12). Accept: create the trip as ASSIGNED. Decline or timeout: release the driver, remember the decline, and offer the next candidate. The rider sees "finding your driver" for the whole sequence.

    3. 3
      Better surge

      "Fewer free drivers" ignores demand.

      Write your answer, then reveal

      Compute supply and demand per cell over a sliding window: requests in the last 5 minutes against free drivers now, smoothed and capped (say 1x to 3x). Recompute every 30 seconds per cell rather than on each request. It stays a SurgePolicy; the trip still stores the multiplier it was booked with.

    4. 4
      Pool rides

      Two riders share a car going the same way.

      Write your answer, then reveal

      The driver gains a seat capacity instead of a boolean: an atomic counter claimed with compare-and-set up to the limit, as in batched deliveries in P15. Matching for the second rider prefers drivers already on a pool trip whose route detour stays under a limit. Each rider has their own trip and fare; the driver is released when the last one ends.

    P17.8Machine coding plan

    Minutes Do
    0-8 Clarify matching radius, cancellation window, fare formula, surge; write the invariants
    8-25 Location, VehicleType, Driver with the atomic status; TripStatus
    25-45 RideService.requestRide with a plain list scan first; NearestDriver; NoDriverException
    45-60 Trip moves; start, complete with StandardPricing, cancel; release on both end states
    60-75 Replace the scan with GridIndex; location updates
    75-90 Concurrent booking test; walk through offers, geohash, and batch matching
    Note

    Starting with a plain list scan and swapping in the grid later is deliberate: the grid sits behind one method, so the swap touches nothing else, and you never run out of time with a half-built index and no working flow.

    P17.9What a strong answer shows

    • SDE-2 bar: atomic driver claim with fallback to the next candidate; one active ride per rider; trip state machine with actor checks; pricing and matching as strategies; driver released on every end state.
    • Above the bar: a spatial index with a clear cost argument; surge locked at booking; driver offers with timeouts; batch matching and H3 or geohash in production.
    Follow-up questionsPractice saying the answer out loud
    1. Why an AtomicReference for the driver's status instead of a synchronized method?
      Reveal

      Every transition is "if status is X, set it to Y", which is exactly one compare-and-set. It never blocks, and matching threads that lose simply try the next driver.

    2. Why does the grid scan cells and then filter by distance?
      Reveal

      Cells are squares and the search area is a circle. The cells give a cheap superset; the distance check removes drivers in the corners of the scanned square.

    3. What happens if the rider cancels and the driver presses Start at the same moment?
      Reveal

      Both go through the trip's synchronized moves. Cancel first: the trip is CANCELLED, the driver is released, and Start fails. Start first: the trip is STARTED and Cancel fails because a started ride cannot be cancelled. Never both.

    4. Why release the driver in the service rather than inside Trip?
      Reveal

      The trip records what happened to it; freeing the driver is a step in the booking flow, done once after a successful end move. Keeping it in one finish method makes "released exactly once" easy to check.

    Patterns by pressure

    Pressure you feel Pattern Shape in one line Where you have used it Lesson
    Callers pick a concrete class with if/switch on a type Factory One method returns the right implementation of an interface List.of, Spring BeanFactory M4
    A constructor with many optional parameters Builder Fluent setters on a helper, build() validates and creates HttpRequest.newBuilder(), Lombok @Builder M4
    Exactly one instance must exist Singleton Private constructor, one static instance; prefer one DI bean Runtime.getRuntime(), Spring singleton beans M4
    A class has the wrong interface for your code Adapter Wrap it and translate calls InputStreamReader, Arrays.asList M5
    Add behavior around calls, in combinations Decorator Same interface, wraps another instance, adds before or after BufferedInputStream, Collections.unmodifiableList M5
    Control access: lazy, remote, cached, secured Proxy Same interface, decides whether and how to call the real one Spring @Transactional proxies M5
    A subsystem is too complicated for callers Facade One simple class in front of many JdbcTemplate, SLF4J M5
    Treat a tree of parts like a single part Composite Leaf and container share one interface File systems, UI containers M5
    One step's algorithm varies Strategy Interface for the step, injected implementation Comparator, pricing rules M6
    Same steps, some differ by subtype Template method Base class fixes the order, subclasses fill the steps HttpServlet.service calling doGet M6
    A request passes through a list of checks Chain of responsibility Each handler handles or passes on Servlet filters, Spring Security M6
    Others must react to a change without coupling Observer Subject keeps listeners and notifies them Spring @EventListener M7
    Actions must be queued, logged, or undone Command An action as an object with execute (and undo) Runnable tasks, editor undo M7
    Behavior depends on a mode with rules for moving between modes State Enum transitions or one class per state Order lifecycles, vending machines M7
    Key idea

    Name the pressure before the pattern: "pricing rules will change per city, so pricing is a strategy." If you cannot name a pressure, you do not need the pattern.

    SOLID in one line each

    Principle One line The smell when it is broken
    Single responsibility A class has one reason to change A class you edit for unrelated feature requests
    Open/closed Add behavior by adding code, not editing working code A switch on type that grows with every feature
    Liskov substitution A subtype works everywhere its parent does Overrides that throw UnsupportedOperationException or skip rules
    Interface segregation Clients depend only on methods they use Implementations full of empty methods
    Dependency inversion Depend on interfaces; inject the implementation new of infrastructure classes inside business logic

    UML relationships as Java

    Relationship Arrow In Java Example
    Inheritance Solid line, hollow triangle at the parent extends Car extends Vehicle
    Realization Dashed line, hollow triangle at the interface implements TokenBucket implements Limiter
    Composition Filled diamond at the whole Field created and owned by the whole; dies with it Order owns its OrderLines
    Aggregation Hollow diamond at the whole Field passed in; the part outlives the whole Team has Players
    Association Solid line, open arrow A field that refers to another object Booking refers to a Show
    Dependency Dashed line, open arrow Parameter, local variable, or return type only Service uses a Request

    Full lesson: M2 The six relationships.

    Collections that solve LLD problems

    Need Use Cost
    Lookup by key HashMap O(1) average
    Least recently used eviction LinkedHashMap(cap, 0.75f, true) with removeEldestEntry, or map plus doubly linked list O(1)
    Sorted keys; nearest key below or above (time slots, intervals) TreeMap with floorEntry, ceilingEntry O(log n)
    Next item by priority or time PriorityQueue with a Comparator O(log n) add and poll
    Queue, stack, undo and redo ArrayDeque (not Stack, not LinkedList) O(1) at both ends
    Keys that are an enum EnumMap, EnumSet Array-backed, ordered
    Counts or totals shared by threads ConcurrentHashMap.merge, LongAdder Atomic per key
    Producer-consumer handoff ArrayBlockingQueue (bounded) Blocks when full or empty
    Run something later or repeatedly ScheduledExecutorService, DelayQueue See P12
    A read-only copy to return List.copyOf, Map.copyOf O(n), immutable

    Concurrency tools

    Problem Tool Remember
    Check-then-act on a map computeIfAbsent, putIfAbsent, merge Atomic per key; keep the function short and side-effect free
    A shared counter AtomicLong, LongAdder LongAdder for hot counters read rarely
    An invariant across several fields synchronized or ReentrantLock Guard every read and write of those fields with the same lock
    Many readers, few writers ReentrantReadWriteLock Worth it only when reads are long or frequent
    Two locks in one operation Lock in a global order (by ID) Prevents deadlock (P10)
    Wait until something is available BlockingQueue, or Condition with await in a while loop Never if around await
    A stop flag read by another thread volatile boolean Visibility only, not atomicity
    Run tasks on threads ExecutorService; Future.get() surfaces exceptions Always shutdown()
    A request that must take effect once putIfAbsent(key, CompletableFuture) Duplicates wait for the first result (P10)
    Lost updates in a database Version column, conditional update Optimistic: retry on conflict (M9)

    Tables and APIs on one screen

    Need Answer More
    One per something UNIQUE or a primary key; catch the violation and answer 409 M11
    One live row per something Partial unique index ... WHERE status IN (...) M11
    A contended state change UPDATE ... WHERE status = 'AVAILABLE', then check rows changed = 1 M11
    Several rows all or nothing One transaction; rows in ID order; any 0-row update rolls back M11
    Hot queries Index equality columns first, then the range or sort column M11
    A POST that is retried Idempotency-Key header, unique per user in the table M11
    A list that changes while paging Cursor of the last (created_at, id) M11
    Status codes 201 created, 400 malformed, 401 who are you, 403 not allowed, 404 missing, 409 state clash, 422 breaks a rule, 429 slow down M11

    Every worked problem in one line

    Problem The idea to remember
    P1 Parking lot Spot allocation and pricing as strategies; claim a spot atomically, try the next on failure
    P2 Vending machine States with illegal actions rejected; money in escrow until a sale commits stock, cash, and change together
    P3 LRU cache Hash map plus doubly linked list, O(1); or LinkedHashMap in access order
    P4 Snake and ladder Board as data, a game loop that owns turns, dice and rules pluggable
    P5 Logging framework Levels and appenders; one immutable settings snapshot; async with a bounded queue
    P6 Rate limiter Token bucket or sliding window per key; atomic updates per key
    P7 Splitwise Split strategies, amounts in paise with leftovers assigned, net balances; simplify by matching the largest debtor and creditor
    P8 Elevator LOOK scheduling per car, a dispatch strategy, one controller thread
    P9 Movie booking ShowSeat per seat per show; holds with expiry; all seats or none
    P10 Digital wallet Ordered locking, both ledger rows, idempotency keys
    P11 Pub-sub queue Partitions, consumer groups, offsets committed after processing
    P12 Task scheduler A priority queue by time, a worker pool, cancellation and recurrence
    P13 Tic-tac-toe O(1) win check with row, column, and diagonal counters; undo through the move history
    P14 Meeting rooms Half-open intervals; TreeMap floor and ceiling; a lock per room
    P15 Food delivery Transitions that name their actor; partner claimed atomically, released if the order changed
    P16 Key-value store Write layers per transaction, tombstones, versioned commit with retry
    P17 Ride matching Grid index, compare-and-set on the driver, surge locked at booking

    Java you type in every round

    Records, enums with data, exceptions, switch expressions
    /** Value object: immutable, equality by value, validation in the compact constructor. */
record Money(long paise) {
    Money {
        if (paise < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative amount");
    }
    Money plus(Money o) { return new Money(Math.addExact(paise, o.paise)); }
}

/** Enum with data and behavior: no switch needed at the call site. */
enum VehicleType {
    BIKE(1), CAR(2), TRUCK(4);
    final int slots;
    VehicleType(int slots) { this.slots = slots; }
}

/** Domain exception: unchecked, named for the rule that was broken. */
static class SlotUnavailable extends RuntimeException {
    SlotUnavailable(String id) { super("slot " + id + " is taken"); }
}

/** Switch expression over an enum: the compiler checks every case is handled. */
static String size(VehicleType t) {
    return switch (t) {
        case BIKE -> "small";
        case CAR -> "medium";
        case TRUCK -> "large";
    };
}
    Map idioms that remove null checks
    Map<String, List<String>> byCity = new HashMap<>();
byCity.computeIfAbsent("Pune", k -> new ArrayList<>()).add("asha");    // group without null checks
Map<String, Integer> count = new HashMap<>();
for (String w : List.of("a", "b", "a")) count.merge(w, 1, Integer::sum);  // counting
int missing = count.getOrDefault("z", 0);
EnumMap<VehicleType, Integer> free = new EnumMap<>(VehicleType.class);  // compact, ordered by enum
free.put(VehicleType.CAR, 10);
    Sorting, grouping, nearest keys, heaps, stacks
    List<Order> orders = List.of(new Order("ravi", "Pune", 300), new Order("asha", "Delhi", 500), new Order("meera", "Pune", 500));
List<Order> sorted = orders.stream()
        .sorted(Comparator.comparingLong(Order::amount).reversed().thenComparing(Order::user))
        .toList();
Map<String, Long> totalByCity = orders.stream()
        .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Order::city, TreeMap::new, Collectors.summingLong(Order::amount)));

TreeMap<Integer, String> bookings = new TreeMap<>(Map.of(9, "standup", 14, "review"));  // start hour -> meeting
Map.Entry<Integer, String> before11 = bookings.floorEntry(11);    // latest start at or before 11
Map.Entry<Integer, String> after11 = bookings.ceilingEntry(11);   // earliest start at or after 11

PriorityQueue<Order> biggestFirst = new PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.comparingLong(Order::amount).reversed());
biggestFirst.addAll(orders);
Deque<String> undo = new ArrayDeque<>();                          // use ArrayDeque, not Stack
undo.push("type a");
undo.push("type b");
    The two-minute LRU cache
    Map<Integer, String> lru = new LinkedHashMap<>(16, 0.75f, true) {   // true = access order
    @Override
    protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry<Integer, String> eldest) { return size() > 2; }
};
lru.put(1, "a");
lru.put(2, "b");
lru.get(1);           // 1 is now most recent
lru.put(3, "c");      // evicts 2
    Atomic updates from a thread pool
    ConcurrentHashMap<String, Long> hits = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4);
List<Future<?>> futures = new ArrayList<>();
for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++)
    futures.add(pool.submit(() -> hits.merge("home", 1L, Long::sum)));   // atomic read-modify-write
for (Future<?> f : futures) f.get();                                    // wait, and surface exceptions
pool.shutdown();

    Edge cases to say out loud

    Area Ask or test
    Input Null, empty, zero, negative, duplicate, unknown ID
    Capacity Full, exactly at the limit, one over
    Time Exactly at expiry; clock injected for tests; time zones for schedules
    Money Integer paise, never double; rounding remainder assigned on purpose
    State Every invalid transition rejected with a clear error
    Concurrency Two users on the same resource; the same request twice
    Extension The next likely feature lands as a new class, not an edit everywhere

    Interview playbook

    How to run both LLD rounds minute by minute: the LLD discussion (diagrams and key code in 45 to 60 minutes) and the machine coding round (runnable code in 90 to 120 minutes). With a clarifying checklist, phrases that show seniority, recovery moves, a round timer, and a rubric to score your mocks.

    On this page

    1. Two rounds, two different jobs
    2. The clarifying checklist
    3. Running the LLD discussion round
    4. Running the machine coding round
    5. Phrases that show seniority
    6. When things go wrong
    7. Red flags
    8. Other practical rounds

    Two rounds, two different jobs

    LLD discussion Machine coding
    Format Whiteboard, doc, or drawing tool; 45 to 60 minutes Your IDE; 90 to 120 minutes; sometimes a 2 to 3 hour take-home
    What you produce Requirements, class diagram, key flows, the core code Code that compiles and runs a demo of the main flows
    What is scored Modeling, extensibility, reasoning about trade-offs and concurrency, communication Working code first, then structure, readability, edge cases, extensibility
    Typical twist "Now add X. What changes?" "You have 15 minutes: add X" or a reviewer reads your code afterwards
    Biggest risk Drawing for 40 minutes and never showing code Nothing runs at the end

    The clarifying checklist

    Ask these in the first 5 to 10 minutes and write the answers down as a numbered requirements list. The interviewer is scoring whether you find the hard parts yourself.

    1. Actors and core use cases. Who uses it, and which 3 to 5 flows must work? "Which of these should the demo show?"
    2. Rules. Limits, pricing, validation, what happens when something fails or runs out.
    3. Lifecycles. Which entities move through states (order, booking, payment)? Draw them later.
    4. Concurrency. Can two users act on the same thing at once? Which operation must never happen twice?
    5. Scale inside one process. Roughly how many entities? In memory is fine? (It almost always is.)
    6. Interface. Method calls, a command-line driver, or REST? Is there a given input format?
    7. Out of scope. Persistence, authentication, UI, real payments. Say what you will skip.
    8. What will change. "Are new vehicle types or pricing rules likely?" The answers are your variation points.

    Finish with the invariants, the rules that must always hold ("a seat is never sold twice", "a balance is never negative"). They decide where the locks and the validations go.

    Running the LLD discussion round

    Phase (45 min plan) Produce Say
    Clarify (5) Numbered requirements, scope, invariants "Let me confirm scope before designing."
    Entities (5) Nouns that own data and rules; value objects; enums "Seat is the physical seat; ShowSeat is its state for one show."
    Class diagram (10) Classes with key fields and methods; relationships with multiplicity; interfaces at variation points "Pricing varies by city, so it sits behind an interface."
    Flows (10) One sequence diagram for the main use case; a state diagram if there is a lifecycle "Here is what happens when two users pick the same seat."
    Code the core (10) The class where the hard rule lives, with real method bodies "This method is the invariant; everything else is plumbing."
    Extend (5) Concurrency answer, one new requirement placed in the design, trade-offs "Adding EV charging is a new spot type and a new pricing strategy; nothing else changes."

    Use Module 8's seven-step method for the middle phases. In a 60-minute round, spend the extra time on code: interviewers remember the candidate who wrote the tricky method correctly.

    Running the machine coding round

    Phase (90 min plan) Do Watch out for
    Clarify (8) The checklist above; agree on the demo scenarios Starting to code before agreeing on what "done" means
    Model (10) Class list in comments or on paper; interfaces at variation points Designing for features nobody asked for
    Skeleton (12) Packages, records, enums, exceptions, repository interfaces, an empty Main that compiles Spending 20 minutes on a framework setup
    Core flow (35) Services and strategies; one happy path end to end first; extend the demo as each feature lands Perfecting one class while others do not exist
    Edges (13) Validation, error cases, concurrency if asked; the edge-case list from the cheat sheet New features at this point
    Demo (7) Main runs every agreed scenario with readable output; tests if allowed Output that needs explaining
    Walkthrough (5) Explain structure, patterns with their reasons, and where the next feature plugs in Apologizing for the code instead of explaining it

    Rules that save rounds:

    • Compile by minute 30, happy path by minute 65. If you are behind, cut scope out loud: "I will skip the refund flow and come back if time allows."
    • Type the starter skeleton while you think about the model; it compiles in ten minutes and gives you the driver, exceptions, and repositories.
    • Write the driver early and grow it. A demo that ran at minute 50 can only get better.
    • In-memory repositories behind interfaces, IDs from an AtomicLong or a prefix plus counter. Never a database unless asked.
    • One exception family for domain errors, with messages a user could read.
    • No pattern without a pressure. A strategy for pricing that varies is good; a factory for one class is noise.
    • Stop adding features 10 minutes before the end. Rename, delete dead code, and write three lines of assumptions at the top of Main.

    Module 10 covers layout, IDs, tests, and the driver in detail.

    Phrases that show seniority

    Moment Say
    Scoping "I will design for these four use cases and leave refunds as an extension; tell me if refunds matter."
    Choosing a pattern "Pricing rules differ by city and will grow, so pricing is a strategy. Spot selection is fixed, so it stays a method."
    Rejecting a pattern "I could add a factory here, but there is one implementation and no sign of more. I will extract it when a second one appears."
    Concurrency "The race is two bookings for the last seat. I lock per seat in sorted order, so different seats never wait on each other and overlapping requests cannot deadlock."
    Trade-off "One lock per show is simpler and correct; per-seat locks scale better. At our load, I would start with per show."
    Extension "A new vehicle type is a new enum value and a new pricing rule; no existing class changes."
    Testing "I injected the clock so expiry is testable without sleeping."

    When things go wrong

    Situation Move
    A new requirement mid-way Restate it, say which classes change and which do not, then change the fewest. This is the extensibility test, not an interruption.
    You are stuck on an algorithm Say the simple correct version first ("a linear scan works; we can index later"), make it work, then improve.
    You find a bug in your design Say so and fix it: "this allows a double booking; the check has to move inside the lock." Owning it scores better than hiding it.
    The interviewer pushes back Ask what they are worried about, then either defend with the trade-off or adopt the better idea. Both are fine; silence is not.
    A pattern name you do not know Ask what problem it solves in this context; often you already know the idea under another name.
    Running out of time Stop and summarize: what works, what is missing, how you would finish it. A clear plan for the rest earns partial credit.

    Red flags

    Red flag Why it hurts Instead
    A Manager or System class that does everything Shows no modeling; nothing can change without editing it Give each rule to the class that owns its data
    Getters and setters on every field Anyone can break invariants Methods named after behavior: book, release, debit
    instanceof and switch on types everywhere Every new type edits old code Polymorphism or a strategy
    double for money Rounding errors in a payment answer Integer paise or BigDecimal
    Five patterns, no running code Looks like memorization The minimum design that runs, then extensions
    synchronized on every method, or none anywhere Either no concurrency thinking or no understanding of it Name the shared state, then protect only that
    Silent typing for ten minutes The interviewer cannot score what they cannot hear Narrate decisions, not keystrokes

    Other practical rounds

    Some companies add rounds that test the same skills on code you did not write, or grow one problem in stages. Formats change, so ask your recruiter which rounds you will get. Stripe is known for debugging (bug squash) and integration rounds; Uber and many Indian product companies run classic machine coding; API and table design often appears inside design rounds.

    Round What happens How to prepare
    Multi-part coding One problem in three or four parts; each part adds a requirement to your own code Solve handbook problems, then do their deep dives as the next parts against your own code; keep rules in small functions or strategies so part 3 does not rewrite part 1
    Bug squash An unfamiliar repository with a failing test or a bug report; find and fix the cause Reproduce first; read the code path; state a hypothesis out loud and confirm it with one print or breakpoint; fix the cause, add a test, run the whole suite
    Integration Add a feature to an unfamiliar codebase using a provided API or SDK and its docs Read the docs for auth, errors, and pagination before coding; make one call work end to end and print the response; wrap the API in one client class (adapter)
    Refactoring or code review Improve working but messy code without changing behavior, or review a pull request Smell drills; add a test that pins current behavior before changing anything; small steps that each compile
    API and table design Design endpoints and tables for a feature Module 11
    Note

    The bugs planted in debugging rounds are usually ordinary: off by one, null or empty input, == on strings, a shared mutable default, integer overflow, time zones, floating-point money, an unhandled error or retry path. Scan for them while you read, and narrate what you rule out.

    Practice with the timer and the rubric

    Round timerRun it during every mock. It tells you which phase you should be in, so you notice drift while you can still fix it.
    0:00
      Score a mockScore each row right after a mock, honestly. The weakest row decides what you practice next week.

      A weekly routine that works:

      1. One timed problem from the handbook with the timer running, then compare section by section and set the status.
      2. One practice prompt from the tracker that you have not seen, in the other round format.
      3. Score both on the rubric, and practice the weakest row next week.
      4. Every other week, a mock with a friend or a recorded solo session: watching yourself think out loud is uncomfortable and very effective.
      Interview signal

      What separates SDE-2 from SDE-1 answers: scoping the problem without being led; naming the invariants and protecting them under concurrency; placing variation behind interfaces for reasons you can state, and refusing patterns you cannot justify; managing the clock; and handling a new requirement by changing the fewest classes.

      Glossary

      Every term used in the handbook in one line each, with a link to where it is explained. Search finds these too.

      A
      Abstraction
      Exposing what an object does through an interface while hiding how it does it. Read more
      Adapter
      A wrapper that converts one interface into the one your code expects. Read more
      Aggregation
      A has-a relationship where the part is passed in and can outlive the whole (hollow diamond). Read more
      Association
      One class holds a reference to another as a field (solid line). Read more
      At-least-once delivery
      Messages are never lost but may repeat, because the offset is committed after processing; handlers must be idempotent. Read more
      Atomic operation
      A read-modify-write that no other thread can interleave with, such as incrementAndGet or merge. Read more
      B
      BlockingQueue
      A thread-safe queue whose put waits when full and take waits when empty; the producer-consumer building block. Read more
      Builder
      A helper with fluent setters and a validating build() for objects with many optional parts. Read more
      C
      Chain of responsibility
      A list of handlers where each one handles the request or passes it to the next. Read more
      Check-then-act
      A race where a thread checks a condition and acts on it, but another thread changes it in between. Read more
      Class diagram
      UML boxes for classes with fields and methods, joined by relationship lines with multiplicities. Read more
      Cohesion
      How closely the parts of a class belong together; high cohesion means one clear purpose. Read more
      Command
      An action packaged as an object with execute (and undo), so it can be queued, logged, or reversed. Read more
      Compare-and-set (CAS)
      An atomic update that succeeds only if the value is still what you read; the basis of lock-free atomics. Read more
      Composite
      Leaves and containers share one interface, so a tree is used like a single object. Read more
      Composition
      Building behavior by holding other objects rather than inheriting; in UML, a part owned by and dying with its whole (filled diamond). Read more
      ConcurrentHashMap
      A thread-safe map with atomic per-key operations: computeIfAbsent, merge, putIfAbsent. Read more
      Conditional update
      An UPDATE whose WHERE clause includes the expected state, so the check and the write are one statement; zero rows changed means someone else won. Read more
      Consumer group
      Consumers that share a topic's partitions, so each message is processed once per group. Read more
      Coupling
      How much one class depends on another's details; low coupling lets classes change independently. Read more
      Cursor pagination
      Paging by "rows after this one" using the last row's sort key, instead of an offset; stable while rows are added. Read more
      D
      Deadlock
      Threads each hold a lock the other needs, so none can continue; prevented by a global lock order. Read more
      Decorator
      A wrapper with the same interface that adds behavior before or after delegating; stackable. Read more
      Dependency (UML)
      A class uses another only as a parameter, local variable, or return type (dashed arrow). Read more
      Dependency injection
      Passing an object its collaborators (usually through the constructor) instead of letting it create them. Read more
      Dependency inversion
      High-level policy depends on interfaces, and low-level details implement them. Read more
      Double-entry ledger
      Every money movement writes a debit and an equal credit, so balances can be rebuilt and checked. Read more
      DRY
      Do not repeat yourself: one authoritative place for each piece of knowledge. Read more
      E
      Encapsulation
      Keeping state private and changing it only through methods that protect its rules. Read more
      Entity
      An object with an identity that persists while its state changes, such as an order or a seat. Read more
      F
      Facade
      One simple class in front of a complicated subsystem. Read more
      Factory
      A method or class that decides which implementation to create, so callers depend only on the interface. Read more
      Fixed rate and fixed delay
      Fixed rate starts runs on a clock rhythm; fixed delay waits a set time after each run ends. Read more
      G
      God class
      One class that knows and does everything; a sign that responsibilities were never assigned. Read more
      H
      Half-open interval
      A range [start, end) that includes its start and excludes its end, so back-to-back ranges do not overlap. Read more
      I
      Idempotency key
      A client-chosen ID that makes a retried request return the first result instead of acting twice. Read more
      Immutability
      An object whose state cannot change after construction; safe to share and to use as a map key. Read more
      Inheritance
      A subclass reuses and specializes a parent class (extends); strong coupling, so use it for true is-a cases. Read more
      Interface segregation
      Clients should depend only on the methods they use; prefer small, focused interfaces. Read more
      Invariant
      A rule that must always hold, such as a balance never going negative; encapsulation exists to protect invariants. Read more
      L
      Law of Demeter
      Talk to your direct collaborators, not to their collaborators (avoid a.getB().getC().do()). Read more
      Lazy expiry
      Treating an expired hold or entry as free when it is next read, instead of relying on a timer to clear it. Read more
      Liskov substitution
      A subtype must work anywhere its parent is expected, keeping the parent's promises. Read more
      Lock granularity
      How much state one lock guards: one global lock is simple, per-object locks allow more parallelism. Read more
      Lock ordering
      Acquiring several locks in one global order (for example by ID) so no deadlock cycle can form. Read more
      LOOK scheduling
      An elevator serves stops in its current direction and reverses at the last requested floor. Read more
      LRU cache
      A fixed-size cache that evicts the least recently used entry; a hash map plus a doubly linked list. Read more
      M
      Machine coding round
      An interview where you write runnable, well-structured code for a design problem in 90 to 120 minutes. Read more
      Multiplicity
      How many objects take part at each end of a relationship: 1, 0..1, *, 1..*. Read more
      O
      Observer
      A subject keeps a list of listeners and notifies them of changes, without knowing what they do. Read more
      Offset
      A message's position in a partition; a consumer group's committed offset says where it resumes. Read more
      Open/closed principle
      Extend behavior by adding new code rather than editing working code. Read more
      Optimistic locking
      Read a version, write only if the version is unchanged, retry on conflict. Read more
      P
      Partial unique index
      A unique index over only the rows that match a condition, such as one live trip per driver. Read more
      Partition
      An ordered, append-only slice of a topic; order is guaranteed only within one partition. Read more
      Polymorphism
      One call, many behaviors: the object's type decides which method runs, replacing type switches. Read more
      Producer-consumer
      Producers put work on a queue and consumer threads take it, decoupling their speeds. Read more
      Proxy
      A stand-in with the same interface that controls access to the real object (lazy, cached, secured, remote). Read more
      R
      Race condition
      A result that depends on how threads interleave; usually a lost update or check-then-act. Read more
      Read-write lock
      Many readers at once or one writer alone; useful when reads dominate. Read more
      Rebalance
      Reassigning a consumer group's partitions when a member joins or leaves. Read more
      Record
      A Java class for immutable data: fields, constructor, equals, hashCode, and toString generated. Read more
      Repository
      An interface for storing and finding entities, so services do not depend on the storage. Read more
      S
      Scoping
      Turning a one-line prompt into a buildable design: the core loop, the contended resource, three use cases to build and three to skip. Read more
      Sequence diagram
      UML lifelines and arrows showing which object calls which, in time order, for one use case. Read more
      Service
      A class that coordinates entities to carry out a use case; holds little state of its own. Read more
      Single responsibility
      A class should have one reason to change. Read more
      Single-writer principle
      Only one thread changes a piece of state; others send it commands through a queue. Read more
      Singleton
      A class with exactly one instance; usually better as one bean created by dependency injection. Read more
      Smell
      A surface sign in code that a design pressure is building up, such as a growing switch on type. Read more
      Spatial index
      A structure that finds nearby points without scanning all of them, such as a grid of cells, a geohash, or H3. Read more
      State diagram
      UML states and labeled transitions (event, guard, action) for one object's lifecycle. Read more
      State pattern
      One class per state, each handling events its own way and choosing the next state. Read more
      Strategy
      An interface for one varying step, with implementations chosen and injected at runtime. Read more
      T
      Template method
      A base class fixes the order of steps and lets subclasses fill in some of them. Read more
      Thread pool
      A fixed set of worker threads that run submitted tasks from a queue (ExecutorService). Read more
      Token bucket
      A rate limiter that refills tokens at a steady rate up to a capacity; each request spends one. Read more
      Tombstone
      A marker that records a delete, so a lookup stops there instead of falling through to older data. Read more
      Type vs instance
      Separating what something is (a seat) from its state in one context (a seat for one show). Read more
      V
      Value object
      An immutable object compared by value, such as Money or a date range; validates itself. Read more
      Variation point
      The place in a design where change is expected, hidden behind an interface. Read more
      Volatile
      A field modifier that makes writes visible to other threads; it does not make compound updates atomic. Read more
      W
      Write-ahead log
      An append-only log of changes, flushed before a change is acknowledged, so a restart can replay it. Read more
      Y
      YAGNI
      You are not going to need it: do not build for features nobody has asked for. Read more

      Roadmap and revision

      A 12-week plan at two LLD sessions a week (about 5 hours), with problems from week 4 and mocks from week 7. If you run the HLD handbook at the same time, interleave as shown below and expect about 18 weeks for both.

      On this page

      1. Weekly plan
      2. Revision rules
      3. Mock interviews
      4. Using the handbook at work

      Weekly plan

      Each session is about 2 to 2.5 hours. Start every session by clearing the revision queue on the home page (15 to 20 minutes).

      Week Session 1 Session 2
      1 M1 Objects and responsibilities M2 Relationships and UML
      2 M3 SOLID M4 Creational + M5 Structural (first half)
      3 M5 (second half) + M6 Strategy, template, chain M7 Observer, command, state
      4 Smell drills + P1 Parking lot as a 60-minute LLD discussion M8 Requirements to classes + P2 Vending machine
      5 M9 Concurrency (races, locks, atomics) M9 (queues, deadlock, optimistic) + P3 LRU cache
      6 M10 Machine coding craft, rebuilding the starter project P4 Snake and ladder as a 90-minute machine coding round + P13 Tic-tac-toe as a 30-minute LLD discussion
      7 P5 Logging + P6 Rate limiter P7 Splitwise in 90 minutes; first mock
      8 P8 Elevator P9 Movie ticket booking
      9 M11 Tables and APIs, using P9 as the example P10 Digital wallet
      10 P14 Meeting rooms + four scoping drills P15 Food delivery in 90 minutes; mock
      11 P11 Pub-sub queue + P12 Task scheduler as LLD discussions P16 Key-value store in 90 minutes
      12 P17 Ride matching Four more scoping drills + two unseen prompts from the tracker; 120-minute mock

      After week 12: one practice prompt a week, alternating the LLD and machine coding formats, plus the revision queue, until your interviews.

      Running it next to the HLD handbook

      With three design sessions a week, do two HLD sessions and one LLD session in weeks 1 to 6 (the LLD foundations are shorter), then switch to one HLD and two LLD sessions while the LLD problems run. Module 11 sits well next to the HLD data modeling material. Some problems pair naturally across the two handbooks, so schedule them in the same week: the rate limiter (classes here, Redis and distribution there), the pub-sub queue with the HLD queues module, the task scheduler with the HLD scheduler case, and movie booking with the HLD ticketing case.

      Revision rules

      • Spaced review: set a status after every problem and practice prompt. The queue brings them back after 1, 2, 4, 10, or 30 days.
      • Recode, do not reread: on review, close the page, open an empty project, and rebuild the core with a timer (30 minutes for the class diagram and the core class, 60 for a full run). Then compare.
      • One-line misses: keep a running list of what you forgot ("no lock ordering", "money as double", "forgot the state diagram"). Read it before every mock.
      • Mastery checklists: revisit them at the end of each phase; untick anything that is no longer true.

      Mock interviews

      When Format Focus
      Week 7 45-minute LLD discussion with a peer, a Starter prompt Clarifying, a clean class diagram, the core method in code
      Week 10 90-minute machine coding, a Core prompt you have not seen Compile by 30, happy path by 65, a demo that runs
      Week 12 120-minute machine coding, a Stretch prompt, starting from a one-line prompt you scope yourself Scoping, concurrency, extension in the last 20 minutes
      Then Every 1 to 2 weeks, alternating formats Rotate prompts from the tracker

      Score each mock with the rubric on the interview playbook and note the weakest row; that decides the next week's revision.

      Using the handbook at work

      • Code review: each module's "Common mistakes" box is a review checklist. The most useful at work: M3 for responsibilities and dependencies, M9's thread-safety checklist for anything shared between threads.
      • Before adding a feature: find the variation point first (M8). If the feature edits a growing switch, it is time for a strategy or polymorphism.
      • Lifecycles: orders, payments, cards, and loans are state machines. Write the transition table before the code (M7); most status bugs are missing guards.
      • Money paths: idempotency keys, ledgers, and ordered locking from P10 apply directly to payment and repayment services.
      • Schema and API reviews: Module 11's checks (constraints for invariants, indexes from queries, conditional updates, idempotency keys, cursor pagination) work as a review checklist for any new endpoint.
      • Tests: inject time and randomness (M10) so behavior that depends on them can be tested without sleeping.

      Your problems

      How to use practice prompts

      Practice prompts have no write-up of their own. Each one combines ideas from the problems and modules listed under it. Attempt it in one of the two formats (a 45-minute LLD discussion or a 90-minute machine coding round), then reread the linked material to check your design, and set your status honestly.

      Status When to choose it
      Could not solve it You could not get a coherent design or running core without help
      Solved with hints You needed to look something up for the core design or code
      Solved independently Design and working core inside the time box, trade-offs explained
      Needs revision You did it before, but a redo went badly
      Can teach it Done twice, weeks apart, and you can answer every follow-up

      Back up or move your progress

      Progress saves to your account automatically. Use this only to move progress by hand, for example from a private window.
